leads.caseName: Iseman v. Coffey County Board of Zoning Appeals
leads.text:
1 
No. 129,117  
 
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF KANSAS  
 
JIM and DIANA ISEMAN and 
BILL and KARA REYNOLDS,  
Appellees/Cross -Appellants , 
 
v. 
 
COFFEY COUNTY BOARD OF ZONING APPEALS, et al., 
Appellees , 
 
v. 
 
DANNY HAWKINS and LAURA HAWKINS, 
Appellants/Cross -Appellees . 
 
 
SYLLABUS BY THE COURT 
 
1. 
 An indispensable party is a party who must be included in an action before it may 
properly go forward.  
 
2. 
A necessary party must be included in an action either as plaintiffs or defendants 
unless there is a valid excuse for their nonjoinder . 
 
3. 
Under intervention of right, a party  must show (1) timely application, (2) a 
substantial interest in the subject matter of the litigation, and (3) inadequate 
representation of the intervenor's interests by other parties . 
 
 
2 
4. 
 A motion for relief under K.S.A. 60 -260(b)(6) must be made within a reasonable 
time. 
 
5. 
 Cities and counties are vested with general zoning authority to protect public 
health, safety, and welfare , but such authority does not extend to land used for 
agricultural purposes.  
 
Appeal from Coffey District Court; MICHAEL E. WARD, judge. Oral argument held September 8, 
2026. Opinion filed November 20 , 2026. Affirmed.  
 
P. Bernard Irvine , of Irvine Law, LLC, of Manhattan, for appellants /cross-appellees Danny 
Hawkins and Laura Hawkins.  
 
Terence E. Leibold , of Petefish, Immel, Hird, Johnson & L eibold, L.L.P., of Lawrence, for 
appellee s/cross-appellants Jim and Diana Iseman and Bill and Kara Reynolds . 
 
Before HILL, P.J., SCHROEDER and COBLE, JJ. 
 
 SCHROEDER, J.:  In this timely appeal by Danny Hawkins an d Laura Hawkins  (the 
Landowners),  we are tasked with determin ing whether the use of their land qualifies as 
agricultural use when its primary purpose is to hunt specially bred and managed      
domesticated deer in a confi ned, fenced -in area. The adjacent neighbors have safety 
concerns related to the operation of the hunting facility. The zoning administrator for 
Coffey County (administrator) determined the Landowners needed a special use permit to 
operate the hunting facility as the land no longer qualified as being used for agricultural 
purposes. The Board of Zoning Appeals (the Board) disagreed.  The district court found 
the Board's decision was unreasonable and contrary to the law . Upon an extensive review 
of the record,  we find the land is currently being used as a recreational  hunting preserve  
 
3 
as defined by the county zoning regulations , and the district court was correct to find the 
Landowners  need a special use per mit. We affirm. 
 
FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND 
 
 The Landowners  own real property  in Coffey County  as joint tenants  where they 
operate about a 100-acre domesticated deer hunting facility . Their land is adjacent to land 
owned by Jim and Diana Iseman and Bill and Kara Reynolds (the Neighbors).  
 
On July 1, 2019, the administrator  sent the Landowners  a letter explaining the 
Landowners  needed to set up an administrative hearing to determine whether they were 
violating zoning regulations by operating a privately  owned deer hunting preserve. About 
a week later, on July 9, 2019, the administrator sent the Landowners  another letter 
referring to  a discussion she had with Laura that day . The letter stated it had two 
enclosures—the A-1 agricultural district zoning regulations and a special use application, 
which required a $150 fee . The letter did not explicitly state  the Landowners  were 
violating any zoning regulations. The administrator explained  that "the filing deadline for 
the August Planning Board meeting is July 18, 2019 by 5:00 p.m."  
 
On July 25, 2019, the administrator mailed a nother  letter to the Landowners,  
referring to  a discussion she had with Laura on July 22, 2019 . The letter explained the 
administrator performed an investigation and concluded the Landowners  were violating 
Coffey County zoning regulations  by operating a privately  owned deer hunting preserve.  
The letter acknowledged the administrator had  received the Landowners ' appeal 
paperwork but not the associated fee.  The administrator explained the Landowners  had 
30 days from the date of th e letter to appeal to the Board. On August 19, 2019, the 
Landowners  filed an application for an appeal  from a decision of the administrator , 
specifically  appealing the July 25, 2019 decisio n. 
 
 
4 
On August 28, 2019, a different interim  administrator  sent the Landowners  a 
letter, stating he had received the Landowners'  application and fee, but the  application 
was incomplete because the legal description  on the application  was merely a property 
description, not a proper legal description.  The interim administrator explained the Board  
would hear  the Landowners ' appeal at the next Board meeting if it received the missing 
information  by September 9, 2019 . The Landowners  completed their application on 
August 30, 2019. 
 
In October  2019, the Board held a hearing  to review the administrator's decision. 
The Board ultimately reversed the administrator's findings  because "the land appears to 
be a privately owned natural wildlife habitat and reserve which is considered an 
agricultural use and these regulations do not require a special use [] zoning permit or 
occupancy certificate for it."  
 
The Neighbors filed a petition for review of the Board 's determination  in district 
court case No. 19-CV-46, naming only the Board of County Commissioners of the 
County of Coffey  (Commissioners ) and the  Board as defendants  (collectively the 
County) . The Landowners  were not named as a party.  
 
The Neighbors asserted the Landowners  failed to timely appeal the administrator's 
decision  to the Board and the Board erred in allowing the appeal to proceed. The 
Neighbors also asserted the Board's finding that the Landowners  were using the land for 
agricultural use , which was not subject to the County's zoning regulations , was arbitrary, 
capricious, unreasonable, and contrary to the law. The Neighbors asked the district court 
to find the Board's determination unlawful and reinstate the administrator's decision that 
the Landowners  violated the county's  zoning regulations. The petition was later amended 
to correct the name of one of the parties but substantively did not change. In response, the 
County acknowledged  the appeal was untimely but proceeded with the merits of the case 
 
5 
and denied the Landowners  used the property as a privately owned for -profit hunting 
preserve.  
 
 In November 2020, the  parties—which excluded the Landowners—filed 
competing motions for summary judgment.  The district court found it had jurisdiction to 
hear the appeal from the Board; the material facts were largely undisputed ; and the court 
ultimately granted the Neighbors ' motion for summary judgment. The district court found 
the Board's decision contrary to the law and , therefore , unreasonable. The district court 
explained the  Landowners  were operating a recreational hunting preserve , which was not 
an agricultural use  of the land  and required a special use permit . 
 
 About one month after the district court issued its order, the Landowners  wrote a 
letter to the district court stating the Neighbors appealed the B oard's decision to the 
district court without the  Landowners' knowledge. The Landowners  filed an entirely new 
lawsuit in the district court , in case No. 21-CV-21, against the County and the Neighbors . 
The Landowners  claimed they informally learned of the Neighbors ' appeal of the Board's 
decision to the district court in May 2020  but were never formally notified of the appeal 
or of any hearings. The Landowners  petitioned for declaratory judgment, injunctive 
relief, and inverse condemnation. Specifically, the Landowners  claimed:  (1) They were 
indispensable parties to the appeal  as the appeal related to their property , which caused 
the district court to lack jurisdiction based on an absent, indispensable party ; (2) failure to 
include them  violated their due process right s and resulted in an uncompensated 
confiscation of their property interest ; and (3) in the alternative, the County's actions 
resulted in a taking of  the Landowners ' property interest for public use . The Landowners  
filed a motion for summary judgment  largely elaborating on the points made in their 
petition . 
 
The district court  denied the Landowners ' motion for summary judgment , 
interpreted the motion as a motion to intervene  in 19-CV-46, and reopened the evidence 
 
6 
and the judgment issued in that case . The Neighbors filed a motion to alter or amend the 
district court's order , arguing the Landowners ' interests were adequately represented by 
the other defendants , the motion to intervene was untimely , and the district court's 
judgment could not be set aside . The district court denied the Neighbors ' motion to alter 
or amend. The Landowners  then filed a response to the Neighbors ' original motion for 
summary judgment  and joined in the County's motion  for summary judgment . 
 
 The district court found the Landowners ' appeal of the administrator's decision to 
the Board was timely filed  as the administrator's decision was confusin g and inconsistent 
and was timely as to the first time the decision was made in writing  on July 25, 2019 . 
Substantively, the district court found it was not factually or legally correct for the B oard 
to classify the Landowners ' hunting site as a "private natural wildlife habitat and reserve." 
The administrator's classification of the land as a hunting preserve wa s consistent with 
the actual use of the land, the zoning regulations, and Kansas law. The district court set 
aside the B oard's decision as unreasonable and contrary to the law.  
 
The Neighbors timely cross -appealed. Additional facts are set forth as necessary.  
 
ANALYSIS 
 
Jurisdiction  
 
 Before addressing the merits, we must first determine if the Landowners ' appeal 
from the administrator 's decision was timely filed.  
 
Subject matter jurisdiction is a question of law subject to unlimited review and can 
be raised at any time. Nicholson v. Mercer , 319 Kan. 712, 714, 559 P.3d 350 (2024).  
 
 
7 
 Article 10 , section 106 of the Coffey County Zoning Regulations addresses 
appeals. The regulations state : "Appeals shall be made within 30 days after a decision has 
been made by the Zoning Administrator  by filing an application for appeal ." Article 10, 
section 106A. The party appealing the zoning administrator's decision shall  file the 
appeal with the recording secretary, state the grounds for the appeal, include the 
property's legal description, provide  an ownership list and a filing fee, and provide any 
other necessary information. Article 10, section 106B.  
 
 Here, the record reflects that, on July 9, 2019, the administrator determined  the 
Landowners  were using their real property as a hunting preserve , which required a special 
use permit. The administrator's decision was not in writing. At the Board hearing on 
October 16, 201 9, the Landowners  contended the meeting on July 9 was informal and 
was not an administrative hearing . 
 
The Landowners  received a letter on July 25, 2019, which was the first time the 
administrator put her decision in writing.  The letter  stated in part:  
 
"As per my discussion with Mrs. Hawkins on July 22, 2019, you brou ght in the 
appeal paperwork without the fee. The appeal application is not complete without the fee 
as you were advised at our meeting and the appeal documentation will not be placed on 
the Planning Board agenda for August 21, 2019.  
 
"Your 80-acre tract . . . is in violation of the Zoning Regulations for operating a 
privately-owned hunting preserve for deer as per my investigation and findings on May 2, 
2019.  
 
"You must stay the operation unless a S

leads.text:
- 857 -
Nebraska Supreme Court Advance Sheets
322 Nebraska Reports
HINRICHSEN v. RCTS PROPERTIES
Cite as 322 Neb. 857
Alex E. Hinrichsen and Janice M. Hinrichsen,  
appellees, v. RCTS Properties,  
L.L.C., appellant.
___ N.W.3d ___
Filed November 20, 2026.    No. S-25-777.
 1. Foreclosure: Equity.  An action to foreclose on real estate is an action 
in equity.
 2. Equity: Appeal and Error.  On appeal from an equity action, an appel -
late court decides factual questions de novo on the record and, as to 
questions of both fact and law, is obligated to reach a conclusion inde -
pendent of the trial court’s determination.
 3. Limitations of Actions.  Which statute of limitations applies is a ques -
tion of law.
 4. ____. The point at which a statute of limitations begins to run is a fac -
tual question to be determined from the facts of each case.
 5. Secured Transactions: Acceleration Clauses.  Where acceleration of 
the maturity of a security agreement and note is made optional with 
the holder of the security agreement, some affirmative action must be 
taken by the holder evidencing the holder’s election to take advantage 
of the acceleration provision, and until such action, the provision has no 
operation.
 6. Foreclosure: Mortgages: Limitations of Actions.  An action to fore -
close a real estate mortgage may be brought within the statutory 10-year 
limitations period for foreclosing mortgages, even though an action on 
the debt is time barred.
Appeal from the District Court for Buffalo County: John H. 
Marsh , Judge. Affirmed.
Bradley Holbrook and Samantha Merrill, of Jacobsen, Orr, 
Lindstrom & Holbrook, P.C., L.L.O., for appellant.

Nebraska Supreme Court Advance Sheets
322 Nebraska Reports
HINRICHSEN v. RCTS PROPERTIES
Cite as 322 Neb. 857
Drew A. Graham, of Svehla Law Offices, P.C., L.L.O., for 
appellees.
Funke, C.J., Cassel, Stacy, Papik, Freudenberg, 
Bergevin, and V aughn, JJ.
Papik, J.
Many years after RCTS Properties, L.L.C., stopped mak -
ing installment payments on a debt it owed Alex and Janice 
Hinrichsen, the Hinrichsens filed an action to judicially fore -
close real property pledged as security for the debt. RCTS did 
not dispute the validity of the debt or that most installment 
payments remained unpaid. Rather, RCTS argued that the 
Hinrichsens waited too long to institute foreclosure proceed -
ings. RCTS primarily contended that the statute of limitations 
began running over 10 years before the initiation of foreclo -
sure proceedings when a member of RCTS and the guarantor 
of RCTS’ obligation filed for bankruptcy and the Hinrichsens 
filed a proof of claim in those bankruptcy proceedings. 
RCTS argued that its member’s filing for bankruptcy and the 
Hinrichsens’ filing of a proof of claim accelerated the debt 
and therefore started the statute of limitations clock. The dis -
trict court found no merit to RCTS’ arguments and entered 
a decree of foreclosure in favor of the Hinrichsens. Now on 
appeal, RCTS renews its statute of limitations’ arguments. We 
find no merit to those arguments and therefore affirm.
I. BACKGROUND
1. Execution of Promissory Note, Deed  
of Trust, and Guaranty
In December 2010, RCTS purchased a building in Elm 
Creek, Nebraska, from the Hinrichsens. RCTS paid a portion 
of the purchase price upfront, but the remaining $100,000 was 
financed by the Hinrichsens. This case concerns that $100,000 
obligation.
On December 31, 2010, RCTS executed a promissory note 
in favor of the Hinrichsens for $100,000. The note required 
- 859 -
Nebraska Supreme Court Advance Sheets
322 Nebraska Reports
HINRICHSEN v. RCTS PROPERTIES
Cite as 322 Neb. 857
RCTS to repay the loan in monthly installments starting in 
March 2011, with a final payment due in January 2026. Chad 
Messersmith and Jeffrey Moore, the sole members and owners 
of RCTS, signed the note on behalf of the company. RCTS 
also executed a deed of trust to secure the loan, which named 
the Hinrichsens as beneficiaries. The terms of the deed of 
trust obligated RCTS to pay the debt in accordance with the 
terms of the promissory note. Around the same time the parties 
executed the deed of trust, Messersmith signed a personal guar -
anty. The guaranty obligated Messersmith to pay the $100,000 
in the event RCTS failed to do so.
Both the promissory note and the deed of trust contained 
an acceleration clause. In the event RCTS defaulted, the note 
granted the Hinrichsens the option to “elect to declare the 
entire remaining balance immediately due and payable.” The 
deed of trust likewise provided the Hinrichsens with the option 
to “require immediate payment in full of all sums secured by 
[the deed of trust].”
2. RCTS Fails to Make Payments on Note
For over a year, RCTS made installment payments on the 
note. But after a May 2012 payment, it made no further 
payments.
3. Messersmith’s Bankruptcy
In August 2012, Messersmith filed for bankruptcy in his 
personal capacity. As part of his bankruptcy case, Messersmith 
disclosed the personal guaranty on the note with a balance 
of $95,026.
About a month after Messersmith filed for bankruptcy, 
the Hinrichsens, through counsel, filed a proof of claim in 
the bankruptcy proceedings for $121,624.96. The parties agree 
that this amount represented Messersmith’s liability on the 
guaranty, combined with his liability on another obligation 
he owed the Hinrichsens. The Hinrichsens attached both the 
note and the personal guaranty for the $100,000 loan to 
the proof of claim. The proof of claim did not state that 
- 860 -
Nebraska Supreme Court Advance Sheets
322 Nebraska Reports
HINRICHSEN v. RCTS PROPERTIES
Cite as 322 Neb. 857
the Hinrichsens were accelerating the debt, and it made no 
demand of Messersmith.
Through the bankruptcy proceedings, Messersmith’s personal 
liability on the guaranty was discharged, and the Hinrichsens 
received no payment.
4. Parties Exchange Demands
In October 2022, after more than a decade of not paying 
under the note, RCTS demanded reconveyance of the deed 
of trust from the trustee. Counsel for RCTS claimed that the 
promissory note was no longer enforceable due to the expi -
ration of the limitations period. The Hinrichsens declined to 
reconvey the deed of trust.
In December 2023, the Hinrichsens, for the first time, 
demanded payment from RCTS in the amount of $222,952.87. 
This amount included over a decade of default interest. The 
demand letter sent by the Hinrichsens’ counsel declared that, 
should RCTS fail to cure the default, the Hinrichsens “have 
authorization to accelerate the loan and immediately com -
mence foreclosure.” The letter also stated that “[s]hould the 
loan be further accelerated,” RCTS had the right to rein -
state the loan after “further acceleration” by paying the total 
loan amount due. RCTS did not pay in response to the 
Hinrichsens’ demand.
5. Foreclosure Proceedings
In February 2024, the Hinrichsens initiated an action for 
judicial foreclosure of the deed of trust. In response, RCTS 
raised the affirmative defense of the statute of limitations and 
asked the district court for a declaration that the deed of trust 
was no longer enforceable.
Shortly after the parties submitted their initial pleadings 
in the foreclosure proceedings, RCTS moved for a separate 
trial on the statute of limitations pursuant to Neb. Rev. Stat. 
§ 25-221 (Reissue 2016). The district court granted the motion. 
At the separate trial, the district court received evidence of the 
facts recited above.
- 861 -
Nebraska Supreme Court Advance Sheets
322 Nebraska Reports
HINRICHSEN v. RCTS PROPERTIES
Cite as 322 Neb. 857
RCTS argued that based on the evidence introduced at trial, 
it was entitled to prevail on statute of limitations grounds. 
RCTS asserted that the Hinrichsens’ act of filing a proof of 
claim in Messersmith’s bankruptcy constituted an election to 
accelerate the debt under the optional acceleration clause in the 
note and commenced the running of the 10-year statute of limi -
tations governing the foreclosure action. See Neb. Rev. Stat. 
§ 25-202(1) (Reissue 2016).
In an order entered following the trial, the district court 
disagreed, finding that the submission of a proof of claim was 
not a clear and unequivocal act of acceleration as required 
by Nebraska law. Because RCTS had not proved that the 
Hinrichsens’ claim was barred, the district court allowed 
the action to proceed.
Shortly thereafter, RCTS filed a motion for a new trial or, 
in the alternative, to alter or amend the district court’s order. 
Because we understand the substance of RCTS’ motion as a 
request that the district court modify its order related to the 
statute of limitations, we refer to it as a “motion to alter or 
amend.” In support of its motion, RCTS argued that the mere 
filing of bankruptcy by Messersmith automatically accelerated 
the debt. The district court declined to modify its order finding 
that the statute of limitations had not yet run.
The Hinrichsens then moved for summary judgment. At 
the hearing on the summary judgment motion, counsel for 
RCTS made a new, narrower statute of limitations argument. 
RCTS claimed that even if the statute of limitations did not bar 
the Hinrichsens from bringing the foreclosure action, a differ -
ent statute of limitations—the 5-year statute of limitations for 
actions on written contracts, see Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-205(1) 
(Reissue 2016)—limited its indebtedness. RCTS asked the 
district court, in calculating its indebtedness, to exclude any 
installment payments that were due more than 5 years prior to 
the initiation of the foreclosure action in February 2024.
The district court granted partial summary judgment as to 
RCTS’ liability and determined that the amount of the lien 
- 862 -
Nebraska Supreme Court Advance Sheets
322 Nebraska Reports
HINRICHSEN v. RCTS PROPERTIES
Cite as 322 Neb. 857
was a remaining issue of fact. That issue proceeded to trial, 
and both parties presented testimony as to the date of default, 
the interest rate, and the total amount of the lien. Janice also 
testified at this trial. When asked what she was hoping to 
achieve in filing a proof of claim in Messersmith’s 2012 bank -
ruptcy, Janice stated that the goal was to “get our money that 
he owed us.”
The district court ultimately found that the Hinrichsens 
were entitled to foreclosure of their mortgage in the amount 
of $247,068.43. This amount included all of RCTS’ missed 
installment payments. The district court’s decree stated that 
should RCTS fail to pay its indebtedness within 20 days from 
the entry of the decree, an order was to be issued for the sale 
of the real estate with proceeds from that sale applied to the 
amount due to the Hinrichsens.
RCTS filed this appeal, which we moved to our docket.
II. ASSIGNMENTS OF ERROR
RCTS assigns several errors on appeal, but we have con -
densed and paraphrased those assignments as follows: The dis -
trict court erred (1) by finding that the statute of limitations on 
the foreclosure action did not start running in 2012 as a result 
of an acceleration of RCTS’ debt due to either Messersmith’s 
bankruptcy or the Hinrichsens’ filing of a proof of claim 
therein and (2) by including all of RCTS’ missed installment 
payments in calculating the amount of the lien.
III. STANDARD OF REVIEW
[1,2] An action to foreclose on real estate is an action in 
equity. Beckner v. Urban , 309 Neb. 677, 962 N.W.2d 497 
(2021), modified on denial of rehearing 310 Neb. 746, 968 
N.W.2d 855 (2022). On appeal from an equity action, an 
appellate court decides factual questions de novo on the record 
and, as to questions of both fact and law, is obligated to reach 
a conclusion independent of the trial court’s determination. 
Kortmeyer v. Hendrix, ante  p. 102, 38 N.W.3d 918 (2026).

SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA 

OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027 

_________________________ 

SC-2026-0255 
_________________________ 

Ex parte Meta Platforms, Inc. 

PETITION FOR WRIT OF MANDAMUS 

(In re: Steven Burns et al. 

v. 

Meta Platforms, Inc.) 

(St. Clair Circuit Court: CV-23-900235) 

STEWART, Chief Justice. 

SC-2026-0255 
2 

 Meta Platforms, Inc. ("Meta"), pe titions this Court for a writ of 
mandamus directing the St. Clair Circ uit Court ("the circuit court") to 
dismiss the action commenced agains t it by Steven Burns, Charmaine 
Starnes, Sandra Garrison, David Wa ng, Monica Wang, Kristi Briggs-
Holley, and Heather Weaver ("the plaintiffs"). Because the circuit court 
lacks personal jurisdiction over Meta, we grant the petition and issue the 
writ. 
Facts and Procedural History 
 Meta operates the social-media pl atform known as Facebook. Meta, 
which was formerly known as "Facebook, Inc.," is a Delaware corporation 
with its principal place of business located in California. In 2018, a 
nationwide class action was commenced in the federal District Court for 
the Northern District of California alleging that Meta had improperly 
permitted Facebook users' private in formation to be shared with third 
parties ("the class action"). See In re Facebook, Inc. Consumer Priv. User 
Profile Litig., 655 F. Supp. 3d 899 (N.D. Cal. 2023). Following a proposed 
settlement of the class action, the plaintiffs were permitted to opt out of 
the class action. 
SC-2026-0255 
3 

 On October 11, 2023, the plainti ffs commenced an action in the 
circuit court asserting various tort theories of recovery against Meta, 
including claims of frau d, breach of privacy, conversion, the tort of 
outrage, and wantonness. The factu al allegations included in the 
plaintiffs' complaint were consistent with the facts alleged in the class 
action. The plaintiffs' generally allege that, notwithstanding Facebook's 
terms of service or Facebook users' privacy settings, Meta permitted 
third-party software developers to access users' personal data. The 
complaint included the following allegations: 
"[Meta] is a corporation organized under the laws of the State 
of Delaware and which conducts business in this County and 
throughout Alabama. Its principal office is located in Menlo 
Park, California. Its registered agent for service in Alabama 
is Corporation Service Company Inc. … 

"The events giving rise to the claims made the basis of this 
lawsuit arise from each Plaint iff's personal use of their 
personal internet connected devices, including their cell 
phone devices. Each Plaintiff's use of their personal internet 
connected devices, including th eir cell phone devices, have 
regularly taken place in St. Clair County, Alabama. 

"…. 

"Plaintiffs are each Facebook users that each have ownership 
of their mobile devices, inte rnet-connected devices and/or 
other personal internet-connect ed hardware devices. Each 
Plaintiff maintains custody of their internet-connected device 
in Alabama. [Meta] relies on Plaintiffs to operate their 
SC-2026-0255 
4 

Alabama-based mobile devices and hardware devices to 
'download' or otherwise allow [Meta] to place its software onto 
the Plaintiff's device; i.e. an 'App'. With out Plaintiffs' 
hardware device, [Meta] would have no means of distributing 
its software product known as 'Facebook'. In order to convince 
the Plaintiffs and other users to download Facebook, Meta has 
made representations about the Plaintiff's property/data 
contained on their persona devices, and made representations 
that the Plaintiffs and other users have the ability to control 
access and distribution of pr operty and data when using 
'Facebook'. Meta has suppresse d many facts related to the 
Plaintiffs and users' data. This Complaint contains 
allegations that show that Me ta's privacy settings were a 
misrepresentation and a suppr ession of facts to the 
Plaintiffs." 

The plaintiffs alleged that Meta improperly shared the personal 
information of approximately 87 mill ion Facebook users, 1,385,169 of 
which were from Alabama. 
 On September 2, 2025, Meta moved to dismiss the plaintiffs' action, 
arguing, among other reasons, that the circuit court lacked personal 
jurisdiction over Meta. In its motion, Meta argued that the plaintiffs had 
not alleged any suit-related conduct by Meta in Alabama. Nor, Meta 
argued, had the plaintiffs alleged an y facts that could support general 
personal jurisdiction in Alabama. In response to Meta's motion, each 
plaintiff submitted a similarly worded affidavit stating, in part: 
"I use Meta's Facebook platform usually on my personal cell 
phone which is primarily located within St. Clair County. My 
SC-2026-0255 
5 

data and personal information in Facebook is held in the 
'Facebook App' and that App is located on my cell phone here 
in Alabama. My data and personal information has been 
created by me through my use, and input here in Alabama on 
my personal device." 

The plaintiffs also submitted documents regarding Meta's operation of a 
data center in Huntsville and its pl ans to construct a data center in 
Montgomery. 
 On February 27, 2026, the circui t court entered an order denying 
Meta's motion to dismiss, concludi ng that it had specific personal 
jurisdiction over the plaintiffs' cl aims against Meta. This petition 
followed. 
Standard of Review 
" ' "A writ of mandamus is an extraordinary 
remedy, and is appropriat e when the petitioner 
can show (1) a clear legal right to the order sought; 
(2) an imperative duty upon the respondent to 
perform, accompanied by a refusal to do so; (3) the 
lack of another adequate remedy; and (4) the 
properly invoked jurisdicti on of the court. Ex 
parte Inverness Constr. Co., 775 So. 2d 153, 156 
(Ala. 2000)." ' 

"Ex parte Gulf Health Hosps., Inc., 321 So. 3d 629, 632 (Ala. 
2020)(quoting Ex parte BOC Grp., Inc., 823 So. 2d 1270, 1272 
(Ala. 2001)). 

" ' "[A] petition for a writ of mandamus 
is the proper device by which to 
SC-2026-0255 
6 

challenge the denial of a motion to 
dismiss for lack of in personam 
jurisdiction. See Ex parte McInnis, 820 
So. 2d 795 (Ala. 2001); Ex parte Paul 
Maclean Land Servs., Inc., 613 So. 2d 
1284, 1286 (Ala. 1993). ' "An appellate 
court considers de no vo a trial court's 
judgment on a party's motion to 
dismiss for lack of personal 
jurisdiction." ' Ex parte Lagrone, 839 
So. 2d 620, 623 (Ala. 2002)(quoting 
Elliott v. Van Kleef, 830 So. 2d 726, 729 
(Ala. 2002)). Moreover, '[t]he plaintiff 
bears the burden of proving the court's 
personal jurisdiction over the 
defendant.' Daynard v. Ness, Motley, 
Loadholt, Richardson & Poole, P.A., 
290 F.3d 42, 50 (1st Cir. 2002)." 

" 'Ex parte Dill, Dill, Carr, Stonbraker & 
Hutchings, P.C., 866 So. 2d 519, 525 (Ala. 2003). 

" ' " 'In considering a Rule 12(b)(2), 
Ala. R. Civ. P., motion to dismiss for 
want of personal ju risdiction, a court 
must consider as true the allegations of 
the plaintiff's complaint not 
controverted by the defendant's 
affidavits, Robinson v. Giarmarco & 
Bill, P.C., 74 F.3d 253 (11th Cir. 1996), 
and Cable/Home Communication Corp. 
v. Network Productions, Inc., 902 F.2d 
829 (11th Cir. 1990), and "where the 
plaintiff's complaint and the 
defendant's affidavits conflict, the ... 
court must construe all reasonable 
inferences in favor of the plaintiff." 
Robinson, 74 F.3d at 255 (quoting 
SC-2026-0255 
7 

Madara v. Hall, 916 F.2d 1510, 1514 
(11th Cir. 1990)).' " 

" 'Wenger Tree Serv. v. Royal Truck & Equip., Inc., 
853 So. 2d 888, 894 (Ala. 2002)(quoting Ex parte 
McInnis, 820 So. 2d 7 95, 798 (Ala. 2001)). 
However, if the defend ant makes a prima facie 
evidentiary showing that the Court has no 
personal jurisdiction, "t he plaintiff is then 
required to substantiate the jurisdictional 
allegations in the complaint by affidavits or other 
competent proof, and he may not merely reiterate 
the factual allegations in the complaint." 
Mercantile Capital, LP v. Federal Transtel, Inc., 
193 F. Supp. 2d 1243, 1247 (N.D. Ala. 2002)(citing 
Future Tech. Today, Inc. v. OSF Healthcare Sys., 
218 F.3d 1247, 1249 (11th Ci r. 2000)). See also 
Hansen v. Neumueller GmbH, 163 F.R.D. 471, 
474-75 (D. Del. 1995)("When a defendant files a 
m o t i o n t o d i s m i s s p u r s u a n t t o F e d . R . C i v . P . 
12(b)(2), and supports that motion with affidavits, 
plaintiff is required to controvert those affidavits 
with his own affidavits or other competent 
evidence in order to su rvive the motion.")(citing 
Time Share Vacation Club v. Atlantic Resorts, 
Ltd., 735 F.2d 61, 63 (3d Cir. 1984)).' 

"Ex parte Covington Pike Dodge, Inc., 904 So. 2d 226, 229-30 
(Ala. 2004)." 

Ex parte Kentucky Farm Bureau Mut. Ins. Co., 428 So. 3d 21, 24-25 (Ala. 
2025). If the complaint does not a llege a factual basis upon which 
personal jurisdiction could be based, then there is nothing to "controvert 
by affidavit," and the de fendant need not make an initial evidentiary 
SC-2026-0255 
8 

showing. See Ex parte Northstar Battery Co., 99 So. 3d 1204, 1207-08 
(Ala. 2012) (stating that, in order to shift the evidentiary burden as to 
personal jurisdiction to the defendan t, the complaint must allege facts 
upon which personal jurisdiction could be based), and Ex parte McNeese 
Title, LLC, 82 So. 3d 670, 673-74 (Ala. 2011) (holding that the failure to 
specifically allege the factual basis for the assertion of personal 
jurisdiction in the complaint reliev es the objecting defendant of the 
burden of producing evidence negating jurisdiction). 
Analysis 
Alabama's long-arm rule, Rule 4.2, Ala. R. Civ. P., "extends the 
personal jurisdiction of Alabama cour ts to the full extent permitted by 
the Due Process Clauses of the United States and Alabama 
Constitutions." Hiller Invs., Inc. v. Insultech Grp., Inc., 957 So. 2d 1111, 
1115 (Ala. 2006). The Due Process Clau se "permits a forum state to 
subject a nonresident defendant to it s courts only when that defendant 
has established sufficient 'minimum contacts' with the forum state." 
Elliott v. Van Kleef, 830 So. 2d 726, 730 (Ala. 2002) (quoting 
International Shoe Co. v. Washin gton, 326 U.S. 310, 316 (1945)). "The 
critical question … is whether the co ntacts are such that the nonresident 
SC-2026-0255 
9 

defendant ' "should reasonably anticipate being haled into court" ' in the 
forum state." Id. (quoting Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz, 471 U.S. 462, 
473 (1985), quoting in turn World-Wi de Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson, 
444 U.S. 286, 295 (1980)). The Un ited States Supreme Court has 
recognized two types of personal juri sdiction: general jurisdiction and 
specific jurisdiction. 
 "Since our seminal decision in International Shoe, our 
decisions have recognized two ty pes of personal jurisdiction: 
'general' (sometimes called 'a ll-purpose') jurisdiction and 
'specific' (sometimes called 'case-linked') jurisdiction. 
Goodyear[ Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown], 564 U.S. 
[915,] 919 [(2011)]. 'For an in dividual, the paradigm forum 
for the exercise of general juri sdiction is the individual's 
domicile; for a corporation, it is an equivalent place, one in 
which the corporation is fairly re garded as at home.' Id., at 
924. A court with general juri sdiction may hear any claim 
against that defendant, even if all the incidents underlying 
the claim occurred in a different State. Id., at 919. But 'only 
a limited set of affiliations with a forum will render a 
defendant amenable to' general ju risdiction in that State. 
Daimler [AG

leads.caseName: In re: Suzanne M. Willmon v. First State Bank of DeKalb County, Casey S. Handrich, and Louis Crowder
leads.text:
Rel: November 20, 2026 

Notice: This opinion is subject to formal revision before publication in the advance sheets of Southern 
Reporter. Readers are requested to notify the Reporter of Decisions, Alabama Appellate Courts, 
300 Dexter Avenue, Montgomery, Alabama 36104-3741 ((334) 229-0650), of any typographical or other 
errors, in order that corrections may be made before the opinion is printed in Southern Reporter. 

SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA 

OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027 

_________________________ 

SC-2026-0424 
_________________________ 

Ex parte Suzanne M. Willmon 

PETITION FOR WRIT OF MANDAMUS 

(In re: Suzanne M. Willmon 

v. 

First State Bank of DeKalb County, Casey S. Handrich, and 
Louis Crowder) 

(Marshall Circuit Court: CV-25-900059) 

COOK, Justice. 

SC-2026-0424 
2 

This petition for a writ of mandam us raises the question of how to 
conduct discovery in a civil case when a witness invokes their Fifth 
Amendment right not to incriminate themselves. 
The petitioner, Suzanne M. Will mon, claims that certain bank 
documents were forged, leading to a foreclosure on her property. The 
focus of this mandamus petition is discovery directed to the bank 
employee who allegedly forged those documents. In April 2022, Willmon 
executed a promissory note ("the 2022 note") in favor of First State Bank 
of DeKalb County ("the Bank"), secured by a second mortgage on property 
she owned in Grant ("the Grant proper ty"). Afterward, in October 2023, 
she allegedly contacted the Bank's vi ce president to request a $60,000 
advance on the 2022 note. According to the Bank, Willmon requested that 
Casey S. Handrich, a notary who wa s employed at the Bank, execute 
various loan documents related to her request, including a renewed 
promissory note for $211,883.10 and mortgage documents adding two 
properties located in Woodville as collateral. Once the documents were 
executed, Handrich was to notarize them. Willmon now disputes all of 
this and claims that those documents were forged by Handrich. 
Later, Willmon defaulted on the note secured by the first mortgage 
SC-2026-0424 
3 

on the Grant property, which had been serviced by Selene Finance LP. 
The Bank then notified Willmon that her default also triggered a default 
under the 2022 note and the second mortgage. Thus, despite her claim 
that the documents were forged, th e Bank notified Willmon that it 
intended to sell the Grant property in a foreclosure sale on February 13, 
2025. 
 In response, Willmon filed this action against the Bank in the 
Marshall Circuit Court, requesting th at the court declare the rights of 
the parties in regard to the 2022 note and order the foreclosure sale to be 
stopped. Willmon also moved for a temporary restraining order ("TRO") 
preventing the foreclosure sale, but the sale occurred before any TRO 
could be entered. The Bank then filed its answer to Willmon's complaint, 
denying her claims and asserting a counterclaim to recover the deficient 
funds that it alleged Willmon still owed it under the 2022 note following 
the foreclosure sale of the Grant property. 
 Willmon amended her complaint to, among other things, add 
additional claims against the Bank and to add Handrich as a defendant 
to her action, and Willmon allege d claims of forgery and notary 
misconduct against Handrich. 
SC-2026-0424 
4 

 Willmon eventually took the deposi tion of Handrich. At that time, 
Handrich refused to answer any questions and invoked her Fifth 
Amendment right under the United St ates Constitution. Willmon filed 
a motion to compel, and the trial cour t initially ordered Handrich to sit 
for a deposition. 
Handrich then moved the trial court vacate its order compelling her 
to testify. She also asked the trial court to stay the proceedings against 
her and to prohibit further depositi on questions, interrogatories, and 
other matters in the case that implicated her Fifth Amendment right. 
In response, Willmon moved for sanctions against Handrich for 
failing to comply with th e trial court's previous order compelling her 
testimony. Willmon also opposed Handrich's motion to stay, arguing that 
Handrich had failed to demonstrate a concrete, nonspeculative basis for 
a stay and that a blanket stay would substantially prejudice her. 
Following additional filings and proceedings, the trial court granted 
Handrich's motion to indefinitely st ay the proceedings against her after 
it determined that Willmon's amen ded complaint included allegations 
that Handrich had engaged in crim inal conduct, thus implicating 
Handrich's Fifth Amendment right. 
SC-2026-0424 
5 

Willmon has now petitioned this Court for a writ of mandamus 
directing the trial court to, among other things, (1) vacate its order 
granting Handrich's motion to indefi nitely stay the proceedings against 
her based on her invocation of her Fifth Amendment right and (2) vacate 
its order denying her request to compel Handrich to provide responses to 
her discovery and to sit for a deposi tion in this case. For the reasons 
stated below, we grant the petition and issue the writ. 
Facts and Procedural History 
I. Willmon's Executed Promissory Note with the Bank in August 
2022 

 As stated previously, Willmon ow ned property, the Grant property, 
which had a note secured by a mortga ge that was serviced by Selene 
Finance LP. On April 30, 2022, Willmon executed the 2022 note in the 
amount of $208,390.60 in favor of the Bank. That loan was secured by a 
second mortgage on the Grant prop erty. The note was due and payable 
in full on February 26, 2023. 
 When Willmon was unable to pay the 2022 note in full by the 
maturity date, she executed in March 2023, a "Modification, Extension, 
and Change In Terms Agreement" in the amount of $40,969 ("the March 
2023 notice of additional advances"). That loan was secured by the second 
SC-2026-0424 
6 

mortgage on the Grant property, extended the loan's maturity date, and 
allegedly increased the interest ra te from 7% to 9%. According to 
Willmon, she paid that loan back in full on August 15, 2023. 
 II. The October 2023 Documents 
 On October 1, 2023, W illmon contacted the Bank 's vice president, 
Jacob Stubblefield, to request a $ 60,000 advance on the existing 2022 
note in order to purchase a tractor for her land in Kentucky and to get 
her property in Kentucky surveyed . The Bank claims that it was 
unwilling to extend the additional $60,000 to be secured by the tractor, 
which would have been located in a di fferent state, and, instead, offered 
to extend the additional $60,000 loan if it was secured by an additional 
advance notice under the second mortgage on the Grant property. 
 According to the Bank, in her te xt exchange with Stubblefield, 
Willmon agreed to the terms of the proposed loan and also agreed to 
execute an additional mortgage adva nce notice to be recorded in the 
Probate Office of Marshall County to secure the additional $60,000 loan. 
The Bank then arranged to have the loan documents prepared on October 
23, 2023, so that they would be read y for Willmon to execute them in 
Grant on October 24, 2023. 
SC-2026-0424 
7 

The Bank contends that, on Octo ber 24, 2023, Willmon allegedly 
contacted Handrich, a notary who was employed by the Bank, and asked 
her to execute various loan documents related to her request, including a 
renewed promissory note for $211,883.10, a notice of additional advance 
for $60,000, and mortgage documents adding two properties located in 
Woodville as collateral ("the October 2023 loan documents"). 
 Once the documents were execut ed, Handrich notarized them. The 
additional mortgage advance notice was thereafter recorded on October 
27, 2023, with the Marshal County Probate Office. 
 Willmon, however, vigorously disp utes this account of events and 
maintains that she never asked Hand rich to execute the October 2023 
loan documents. According to her, Handrich forged her signature on 
those documents without her knowledge, consent, or power of attorney 
and without discussion of the terms. 
 Despite Willmon's claims, howe ver, the Bank notes that the 
$60,000 loan proceeds were deposited into Willmon's checking account on 
October 24, 2023. Willmon then executed and delivered two checks -- one 
in the amount of $45,327.81 for the tr actor and a second in the amount 
of $15,000 for the survey of her property in Kentucky. 
SC-2026-0424 
8 

 Willmon acknowledges that the $60,000 loan proceeds were 
deposited into her account and that she executed and delivered the two 
checks described above. However, she claims that she believed that those 
funds were an advance on the 2022 no te that was secured by the second 
mortgage on the Grant property. 
III. Willmon Defaults on the First Mortgage on the Grant Property 
and the Bank Begins Foreclosure Proceedings 

 In December 2024, Willmon advised the Bank that she had ceased 
making the payments on the note se cured by the first mortgage on the 
Grant property and that that loan was in default. The Bank then received 
a payoff statement from Selene Fi nance LP that indicated that no 
payments had been made on the note secured by the first mortgage on 
the Grant property since March 2024 and that the outstanding amount 
due as of the date of the payoff statement was $123,927.02. 
 On January 29, 2025, the Bank, as a protective advance under the 
second mortgage, paid Selene Finance LP $126,121.38 to release the first 
mortgage on the Grant property. According to the Bank, Willmon's 
failure to maintain payment of the note secured by the first mortgage 
constituted a default under the second mortgage on the Grant property 
used to secure the 2022 note and under the October 2023 loan documents. 
SC-2026-0424 
9 

As a result, the Bank commenced fo reclosure procedures on the Grant 
property. 
 Willmon claims that she was unawa re of any of this until January 
30, 2025, and maintained that th e October 2023 loan documents were 
forged. Despite her claim that the documents were forged, the Bank 
notified Willmon that it intended to sell the Grant property securing the 
loans at a nonjudicial foreclosure sale on February 13, 2025. 
On February 12, 2025, Willmon's co unsel sent a dispute letter to 
the Bank's foreclosure counsel, as serting that the October 2023 loan 
documents were forged, disputing the debt, and demanding cancellation 
of the February 13, 2025, foreclosur e sale. Over Willmon's objections, 
that foreclosure sale went ahead as scheduled. According to the Bank, 
the Grant property was sold to the highest bidder -- Louis Crowder -- for 
$175,000, which, Willmon alleges, is less than the $ 200,000 appraised 
value of the property.
1 
 After applying the gross sale proceeds toward the expenses of the 

1According to Willmon, Crowder wa s on notice of the dispute 
between her and the Bank through the existence of her underlying 
lawsuit against the Bank and, thus, she says, cannot claim to be a bona 
fide purchaser of the Grant property. 
SC-2026-0424 
10 

sale in the amount of $7,637.86, as provided under the second mortgage, 
there remained net foreclosure pr oceeds of $167,362.14, which were 
applied first to reimburse the Bank fo r the protective advance to pay off 
the defaulted first mortga ge, plus interest, and second to the original 
unpaid balance of the 2022 note, le aving an unpaid deficiency balance 
owed by Willmon of $179,107.83. As explained below, this amount would 
later become the basis of the Bank's deficiency counterclaim against 
Willmon. 
 IV. Willmon's Underlying Action Against the Bank 
 On February 12, 2025, Willmon file d a declaratory-judgment action 
against the Bank in the Marshall Circuit Court, requesting that the court 
declare the rights of the parties in regard to the loans and order the 
nonjudicial foreclosure sale of the Grant residence to be stopped. Willmon 
attached three exhibits to her complaint, including (1) a copy of the notice 
of the foreclosure sal

leads.caseName: TruConnect Communications, Inc. v. Maximus Inc.
leads.text:
1 
Filed 11/19/26 
CERTIFIED FOR PARTIAL PUBLICATION* 
 
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 
 
FIRST APPELLATE DISTRICT 
 
DIVISION ONE 
 
 
TRUCONNECT 
COMMUNICATIONS, INC., 
 Plaintiff and Appellant, 
v. 
MAXIMUS INC. et al., 
 Defendants and 
Respondents. 
 
 
      A172474 
 
      (City and County of San  
       Francisco Super. Ct. 
       No.CGC-21-589607) 
 
 
 The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) hired respondents 
Maximus Inc. and Solix Inc. to design and implement a new software 
platform for a program to provide telephone service to lower-income 
Californians.  Appellant TruConnect, Inc. sued Maximus and Solix for 
damages it allegedly suffered because the new platform was defective.  The 
trial court sustained a demurrer to TruConnect’s claims after it concluded 
that defendants did not owe TruConnect a duty of care and were not unjustly 
enriched.  We conclude that the trial court was correct, and we therefore 
affirm.  
 
*  Pursuant to California Rules of Court, rules 8.1105(b) and 8.1110, this 
opinion is certified for publication with the exception of parts IIB and IIC. 
 2 
I. 
FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL 
BACKGROUND1 
 TruConnect provides free wireless telephone service to eligible low-
income Californians under a government-subsidized program called 
“LifeLine.”  The Federal Communications Commission established LifeLine 
in 1985, and the CPUC oversees the program in California.  TruConnect’s 
only business is purchasing wireless services from carriers that have their 
own transmission facilities, then reselling those services to TruConnect’s own 
subscribers through LifeLine.  The company earns more than 90 percent of 
its revenue through services provided to California LifeLine enrollees.   
 The CPUC is authorized to administer LifeLine under the Moore 
Universal Telephone Service Act (Pub. Util. Code, § 871 et seq.).2  The 
commission in 1983 adopted General Order 153 to implement the program in 
California.  The CPUC reimburses LifeLine providers for providing service.  
TruConnect is the second largest provider of LifeLine services in California.  
 Because of the logistical complexities of enrolling subscribers and 
providing reimbursement, the CPUC contracts with a third-party 
administrator to process enrollments and track reimbursements.  TruConnect 
was pleased with the company that served as the administrator from 
December 2011 through March 2019.  In summer 2018, the CPUC hired 
Maximus as a new third-party contractor to administer the LifeLine 
program.  TruConnect offered to help Maximus develop its LifeLine 
 
1 The following facts are taken from the allegations of TruConnect’s 
second amended complaint, which we accept as true on appeal from the 
sustaining of a demurrer.  (Doe v. City of Los Angeles (2007) 42 Cal.4th 531, 
543.) 
2 All unspecified statutory references are to the Public Utilities Code. 
 3 
administration platform to ensure a smooth transition.  Maximus declined 
TruConnect’s offer and instead hired Solix as a subcontractor.  According to 
TruConnect’s operative complaint, Maximus and Solix “negligently designed 
and implemented a software platform for administering the LifeLine program 
that proved grossly inadequate when the platform was launched on April 2, 
2019.  Hundreds of thousands of TruConnect’s LifeLine applicants and 
renewing subscribers who met the program’s objective eligibility 
requirements were denied approval due to the platform’s failure.  As a result, 
TruConnect suffered tens of millions of dollars in lost revenues and incurred 
millions of dollars in personnel time necessary to fix Maximus’ defective 
platform.”   
 It took “months” to solve several problems with the new platform.  The 
operative complaint alleges that both the CPUC’s deputy executive director 
and Maximus “asked TruConnect to commit its team of software engineers 
and operational and technical staff to the task of salvaging the platform.”  
TruConnect personnel “spent hundreds of thousands of hours working to 
resolve the platform’s countless programming defects,” which cost 
TruConnect “well in excess of $3 million dollars in time and resources.”  Both 
the CPUC and Maximus expressed gratitude for TruConnect’s assistance.  
 TruConnect first sought reimbursement from the CPUC.  The 
commission approved some initial claims for lost revenues and costs, but in 
September 2020 it adopted Resolution T-17707, which rejected 
reimbursement for lost-opportunity costs (i.e., revenue TruConnect claimed it 
lost because otherwise eligible customers were rejected by the defective 
platform).   
 TruConnect in September 2020 sued the CPUC, Maximus, and Solix.  
The company soon recognized that the trial court lacked jurisdiction over the 
 4 
CPUC, and it requested dismissal of the case less than two months after it 
was filed.  TruConnect initiated this lawsuit in February 2021 against 
Maximus and Solix only, and it later filed a first amended complaint.  
Maximus and Solix demurred to the complaint, and the trial court sustained 
the demurrers without leave to amend based on the conclusion that 
section 1759 barred the complaint.  This court reversed the ruling and 
remanded to the trial court to consider whether the lawsuit failed for any 
other reason.  (TruConnect Communications, Inc. v. Maximus Inc. (2023) 
91 Cal.App.5th 497 (TruConnect I).) 
 TruConnect then filed a second amended complaint, which is the 
operative complaint.  It alleges causes of action for negligence, negligent 
interference with prospective economic relations, quantum meruit, unjust 
enrichment, and unlawful business practices in violation of Business and 
Professions Code section 17200 et sequitur.  
 Maximus and Solix demurred to the second amended complaint on the 
ground that it failed to state a valid cause of action.  Solix demurred to the 
complaint on the ground that the CPUC was a necessary and indispensable 
party that could not be joined because the court lacked jurisdiction over it 
(§ 1759).  Maximus and Solix each joined in the other’s demurrer.  
 The trial court sustained Maximus’s demurrer without leave to amend.  
It concluded that TruConnect failed to allege that defendants owed the 
company a duty sufficient to state a claim for negligence.  And the court also 
concluded that the second amended complaint failed to state a cause of action 
under any other theory TruConnect advanced.3   
 
3 The court overruled Solix’s demurrer because it concluded that the 
CPUC is not a necessary and indispensable party to the action.  But because 
the court also concluded that the complaint did not state a cause of action, it 
dismissed the complaint in its entirety as to both defendants.  
 5 
 TruConnect appealed from the subsequent judgment.  Maximus and 
Solix have filed a joint respondents’ brief.  Because they do not distinguish 
between the companies when responding to TruConnect’s arguments, we will 
apply the same analysis to both of them.  The CPUC has filed an amicus 
curiae brief in support of defendants.  
II. 
DISCUSSION 
A. TruConnect’s Negligence Cause of Action and Derivative Claims Fail 
Since Defendants Did Not Owe the Company a Duty of Care. 
 
 As we have said, the trial court concluded that TruConnect failed to 
allege that defendants owed the company a duty of care sufficient to state a 
claim for negligence.  Although we recognize that some relevant factors weigh 
in favor of finding a duty, the greater weight of them compels us to agree 
with the trial court. 
 Negligence is conduct that “ ‘falls below the standard established by 
law for the protection of others.’ ”  (Bily v. Arthur Young & Co. (1992) 
3 Cal.4th 370, 396 (Bily), quoting Rest.2d Torts, § 282.)  “Recovery in a 
negligence action depends as a threshold matter on whether the defendant 
had ‘ “a duty to use due care toward an interest of [the plaintiff’s] that enjoys 
legal protection against unintentional invasion.” ’  [Citations.]  We review de 
novo whether this ‘ “essential prerequisite” ’ to recovery is satisfied.”  
(Southern California Gas Leak Cases (2019) 7 Cal.5th 391, 397–398 (Gas 
Leak Cases).) 
 “In California, the ‘general rule’ is that people owe a duty of care to 
avoid causing harm to others and that they are thus usually liable for 
injuries their negligence inflicts.”  (Gas Leak Cases, supra, 7 Cal.5th at 
p. 398.)  This rule is statutorily based: “Everyone is responsible, not only for 
the result of his or her willful acts, but also for an injury occasioned to 
 6 
another by his or her want of ordinary care or skill in the management of his 
or her property or person, except so far as the latter has, willfully or by want 
of ordinary care, brought the injury upon himself or herself.”  (Civ. Code, 
§ 1714, subd. (a).)  But while courts “frequently beg[in their] analysis by 
presuming a duty of care[, they] have not universally done so.”  (Gas Leak 
Cases, at p. 400.) 
 One area where courts do not begin by presuming a duty of care is with 
claims of “liability in negligence for purely economic losses,” for which there 
is instead a contrasting “general rule of no recovery.”  (Gas Leak Cases, 
supra, 7 Cal.5th at p. 400.)  Recognizing “a duty to manage business affairs so 
as to prevent purely economic loss to third parties in their financial 
transactions is the exception, not the rule, in negligence law.”  
(Quelimane Co. v. Stewart Title Guaranty Co. (1998) 19 Cal.4th 26, 58.) 
The justifications advanced for not presuming a duty of care in these cases 
“include foreseeability and the prevention of limitless liability.”  (Sharkey, 
The Irresistible Simplicity of Preventing Harm (2023) 16 J. Tort L. 143, 154.)  
Still, the presumption of no duty of care when only economic losses are 
sustained has been criticized, especially when the rule is applied in situations 
where the plaintiff victim was known by the defendant tortfeasor and the 
parties were connected, as “when they have a contractual or quasi-
contractual relationship.”  (Id. at p. 155) 
 The Legislature has created statutory exceptions to the rule.  In 
response to a Supreme Court decision that disallowed homeowners from 
suing developers and contractors in negligence for construction defects that 
had not caused property damages (Aas v. Superior Court (2000) 24 Cal.4th 
627, 632), the Legislature created a “statutory mechanism specifically 
designed for homeowners seeking redress against negligent builders” for 
 7 
economic loss without accompanying property damage.  (Gas Leak Cases, 
supra, 7 Cal.5th at p. 412, citing Civ. Code, § 895 et seq.) 
 The common law has also created exceptions, with the primary one 
being “where the plaintiff and the defendant have a ‘special relationship.’ ”  
(Gas Leak Cases, supra, 7 Cal.5th at p. 400.)  What is meant by a special 
relationship “is that the plaintiff was an intended beneficiary of a particular 
transaction but was harmed by the defendant’s negligence in carrying it out.”  
(Ibid.)  Here, TruConnect maintains it had such a relationship with 
Maximus, while defendants deny it. 
 Whether the parties have a special relationship is a critical, but not the 
exclusive, factor bearing on whether there is a duty of care, as the analysis 
“turns on a careful consideration of ‘ “ ‘ “the sum total” ’ ” ’ of the policy 
considerations at play, not a mere tallying of some finite, one-size-fits-all set 
of factors.”  (Gas Leak Cases, supra, 7 Cal.5th at p. 401.)  California courts 
“have employed a checklist of factors to consider in assessing legal duty in the 
absence of privity of contract between a plaintiff and a defendant.”  (Bily, 
supra, 3 Cal.4th at p. 397.)  These factors include “the extent to which the 
transaction was intended to affect the plaintiff, the foreseeability of harm to 
him [or her], the degree of certainty that the plaintiff suffered injury, the 
closeness of the connection between the defendant’s con

leads.caseName: Ackman, R. v. Pikewood Energy Corp.

J-S19004-26 

NON-PRECEDENTIAL DECISION - SEE SUPERIOR COURT O.P. 65.37 

ROBERTA S. ACKMAN 

 Appellant 

 v. 

PIKEWOOD ENERGY CORPORATION 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF 
 PENNSYLVANIA 

No. 78 WDA 2026 

Appeal from the Order Entered December 10, 2025 
In the Court of Common Pleas of Greene County Civil Division at No(s): 
A.D. 909-2024 

BEFORE: SULLIVAN, J., NEUMAN, J., and STEVENS, P.J.E.* 
MEMORANDUM BY SULLIVAN, J.: FILED: November 19, 2026 
Roberta S. Ackman (“Ackman”) appeals from the order sustaining the 
preliminary objections of Pikewood Energy Corporation (“Pikewood”) and 
dismissing her amended complaint in this quiet title action . Following our 
review, we affirm the trial court’s order as to Count I of the complaint, because 
Ackman develops no argument as to that issue. However, as to Count II, we 
conclude the trial court failed to properly apply the standard for the 
preliminary objections stage of litigation, and accordingly, we revers e the 
____________________________________________ 
* Former Justice specially assigned to the Superior Court. 

J-S19004-26 
- 2 - 
order sustaining Pikewood’s preliminary objections to Count II of the 
complaint and dismissing Ackman’s complaint.1 
The relevant factual and procedural history of this case is as follows. In 
September 2025, Ackman filed an amended complaint. 2 In her amended 
complaint, Ackman alleged the following: In January 2017, her cousin 
Shannon Tedrow (“Tedrow”) , a Kentucky resident, conveyed oil, gas, and 
mineral rights to property in Greene County, Pennsylvania (“the Property”), 
to Pikewood . See Ackman’s Amen ded Complaint, 9/4/25, at ¶ ¶ 3, 13 . 
However, previously, in an August 2014 Agreement (“the Agreement”) , 
Tedrow had conveyed thirty percent of “all gas and oil rights he owned [,]” in

was recorded in September 2014 . Id. at ¶ 4. Ackman attached to her 
amended complaint a copy of the Agreement. See id. at Ex. 2. 
The Agreement provided that Tedrow convey ed to Ackman a thirty 
percent interest in the oil and gas rights in exchange for Ackman performing

3 By way of background, we note that Ackman asserted she assisted Tedrow

Ackman alleged that , by virtue of her recorded 2014 Agreement with

Tedrow signed a quit-claim deed purporting to grant Ackman thirty percent of

October 2024. See id. at ¶ 11. 
Following Pikewood’s assertion of ownership of 100% of the interest in 
the oil and gas rights in the Property, Ackman filed her amended complaint , 
in which she sought to quiet title based on her receipt of legal title to the oil 
and gas rights in the Property (Count I), and, alternatively, based on her 
receipt of “equitable right to legal title [,]” both of which she asserted were 
conveyed via the 2014 Agreement (Count II). See id. at ¶¶ 26-29, 30-34. 
Pikewood filed preliminary objections to Ackman’s amended complaint, 
asserting her “claims are legally deficient and fail in several respects to state 
a viable action for quiet title.” Prelim inary Objections, 9/22/25, at ¶ 17. 
Pikewood argued that the 2014 Agreement “is unavailing because it does not 
contain any language conveying an interest in the real property to Ackman.” 
Id. at ¶ 20. Pikewood argued the Agreement “is not a conveyance, but rather 
at most a contingent agreement. Without a valid conveyance, [] Ackman has 
J-S19004-26

no basis for her claim to quiet title.” Id. at ¶ 21. Pikewood additionally argued 
the Agreement did not vest Ackman with equitable title because it was not an

Following argument by the parties in November 2025 , the trial court 
sustained Pikewood’s preliminary objections. The court adopted Pikewood’s 
interpretation of the Agreement, and concluded that it did not convey property

services are provided. . . . [T]he 2014 Agreement is a conditional agreement 
to convey, not a conveyance in and of itself.” Order, 12/11/25 , at 3-4. The 
trial court’s ruling hinged on Tedrow’s use of the word “will” in the Agreement, 
that is, the Agreement provided Tedrow was conveying the property to 
Ackman, and in exchange, she “will” perform services for him. See id. at 4. 
Because it regarded the conveyance as conditional, the court held Ackman 
had no title in the property, and Pikewood took good title under the 2017 
deed. See id. at 5-6. The court dismissed Ackman’s complaint. Ackman 
timely appealed, and both she and the trial court complied with Pa.R.A.P.

Ackman raises the following issues for our review: 
J-S19004-26

1. Whether the trial court erred in holding that the recorded 
August 4, 2014 Agreement did not convey legal or equitable 
rights to [Ackman]. 

2. Whether the trial court erred by failing t[o] consider both 
pages of the recorded Agreement. 

3. Whether the trial court erred in concluding that [Pikewood] 
took good title despite having actual and constructive notice 
of [Ackman’s] 30% interest. 

4. Whether the trial court erred in holding that the 2014 
Agreement was not a binding conveyance capable of 
transferring equitable title. 

Ackman’s Brief at 4-5 (trial court rationale omitted).4 
Our standard of review for orders sustaining preliminary objections is as 
follows: 
Our standard of review of an order of the trial court 
overruling or granting preliminary objections is to determine 
whether the trial court committed an error of law. When 
considering the appropriateness of a ruling on preliminary 
objections, the appellate court must apply the same standard as 
the trial court. 

Preliminary objections in the nature of a demurrer test the 
legal sufficiency of the complaint. . . . Preliminary objections 
which seek the dismissal of a cause of action should be sustained 
only in cases in which it is clear and free from doubt that the 
pleader will be unable to prove facts legally sufficient to establish 
the right to relief. If any doubt exists as to whether a demurrer 
should be sustained, it should be resolved in favor of overruling 
the preliminary objections.

4 As noted above, Ackman develops no argument as to Count I, but focuses 
on Count II. Therefore, our analysis is limited to Count II. 
J-S19004-26 
- 7 - 
Bargo v. Kuhns, 98 A.3d 686, 689 (Pa. Super. 2014) (internal citation and 
indentation omitted). See also Pa.R.Civ.P. 1028(a). Further, at this stage of 
litigation, the trial court must accept as true all well-pleaded material facts set 
forth in the complaint and all inferences fairly deducible from those facts. See 
Bargo, 98 A.3d at 689. Additionally, “[w]hen determining whether the trial 
court properly sustained the preliminary objections, this Court will examine 
the averments in the complaint, together with the documents and exhibits 
attached thereto.” Hoffman v. Gongaware, 186 A.3d 453, 457 (Pa. Super. 
2018) (internal citation and quotation omitted). 
Ackman asserts in all four of her issues that the trial court erred in 
sustaining Pikewood’s preliminary objections because the recorded 2014 
Agreement conveyed to her legal, or equitable, title. Because these issues 
are interrelated, we address them together. 
“Pennsylvania jurisprudence has long recognized that during the interval 
between the execution of a real estate sales agreement and the conveyance 
of title, the purchaser of the real estate is considered the equitable owner of 
the real estate. ” Greenwood Gaming & Ent ertainment, Inc. v. 
Pennsylvania Gaming Control Bd., 15 A.3d 884, 890 ( Pa. 2011). As this

The doctrine of [equitable] conversion . . . is founded on the equity 
maxim, that what is properly and sufficiently directed to be done,

what is known as an equitable title to the real estate. The buyer

leads.text:
38 E. 64th St., LLC v Nile, Inc. 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06881 
 November 19, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 38 East 64th Street, LLC, Plaintiff-Appellant, 
 v 
 Nile, Inc. et al., Defendants-Respondents, XYZ Corp. et al., Defendants. 

 Decided and Entered: November 19, 2026 
 Index No. 650912/24|Appeal No. 7544|Case No. 2025-04212| 
 Before: Webber, J.P., Kapnick, Pitt-Burke, Chan, Parker-Raso, JJ. 

 Belkin Burden Goldman, LLP, New York (Mark N. Antar of counsel), for appellant. 
 David Rozenholc & Associates, New York (James B. Fishman of counsel), for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Lyle E. Frank, J.), entered May 19, 2025, which denied plaintiff's motion under CPLR 3212 for summary judgment in its favor on its complaint and dismissal of defendants' counterclaims, and under CPLR 3211 for dismissal of defendants' affirmative defenses, unanimously affirmed, without costs. 
 In this action, plaintiff sought to recover possession and use and occupancy of the apartment rented to defendant Nile, Inc., a company owned by defendant E. Terese Carpenter, beginning in and around 2006. Plaintiff also sought attorneys' fees in accordance with the lease. 
 Under the circumstances presented, Supreme Court correctly denied plaintiff's motion. We have held for rent stabilization code purposes, where "there is a question of fact concerning whether the premises at issue are being used for mixed residential and commercial use, that question must be resolved in the first instance by the factfinder" ( Hadzovic v Buckley Sch. in the City of N.Y. , 238 AD3d 487 , 489 [1st Dept 2026]). 
 Defendants submitted evidence sufficient to raise an issue of fact as to whether the unit was used for residential purposes with the landlord's knowledge and acquiescence, thus implicating the rent stabilization regulations ( see Glebow Realty Assoc. v Dietrich , 227 AD3d 610 , 611 [1st Dept 2024]). Plaintiff does not dispute defendants' assertions that it required them to enter into a commercial lease exclusively for business use of an apartment previously subject to the rent stabilization law even though the building's certificate of occupancy permitted only residential use. Moreover, plaintiff failed to provide evidence disputing defendants' assertion that Carpenter, Nile's principal, always intended to reside, and did in fact reside, in the apartment for over 20 years ( see Matter of 20 W. 76th St. v Division of Hous. & Community Renewal , 306 AD2d 6, 7-8 [1st Dept 2003]). 
 Further, defendants stated a cause of action with respect to both their counterclaims. Defendants sufficiently alleged that Carpenter's occupancy is subject to the Rent Stabilization Law and that plaintiff illegally and fraudulently deregulated the unit, if proven would entitle Carpenter to a judgment declaring that she is the lawful rent-stabilized tenant of the unit. 
 We have considered plaintiff's remaining arguments and find them unavailing. 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: November 19, 2026

UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS 
FOR THE THIRD CIRCUIT
