Nos. 25-1629 & 25-1635 
____________ 

INTERNATIONAL CONSTRUCTION PRODUCTS, LLC, 

 Appellant in No. 25-1635 

v. 

CATERPILLAR, INC; KOMATSU AMERICA CORP.; ASSOCIATED AUCTION 
SERVICES, LLC d/b/a Cat Auction Services 

Caterpillar, Inc., 

 Appellant in No. 25-1629 

On Appeal from the United States District Court 
for the District of Delaware 
(D. C. No. 1:15-cv-00108) 
District Judge: Honorable Richard G. Andrews 

Argued on July 9, 2026 

Before: KRAUSE, FREEMAN and ROTH, Circuit Judges 

(Opinion filed: November 19, 2026) 

George W. Hicks, Jr. (Argued) 
Kirkland & Ellis 
1301 Pennsylvania Avenue NW 
Washington, DC 20004 

2 

David J. Baldwin 
Periann Doko 
Berger McDermott 
1105 N Market Street 
11th Floor 
Wilmington, DE 19801 

Paul C. Cuomo 
Baker Botts 
700 K Street NW 
Washington, DC 20001 

Joseph A. Ostoyich I 
Clifford Chance US 
2001 K Street NW 
Washington, DC 20006 

 Counsel for Appellant/Cross-Appellee Caterpillar, Inc. 

Katherine B. Forrest (Argued) 
Ekaterina Stynes 
Paul Weiss Rifkind Wharton & Garrison 
1345 Avenue of the Americas 
New York, NY 10019 

William Isaacson 
Dunn Isaacson Rhee 
401 9
th Street NW 
Washington, DC 20004 

 Counsel for Appellee/Cross Appellant International Construction 
 Products, LLC 

NONPRECEDENTIAL OPINION* 

* This disposition is not an opinion of the full Court and pursuant to I.O.P. 5.7 does not 
constitute binding precedent. 
3 

ROTH, Circuit Judge: 
International Construction Products, LLC (ICP) sued Caterpillar Inc., alleging that 
Caterpillar violated the Sherman Antitrust Act and tortiously interfered with ICP’s contract 
with IronPlanet, a third-party company, by pressuring IronPlanet to breach that contract. 
The jury rejected ICP’s antitrust claim but found Caterpillar liable for tortious interference 
with contract, awarding ICP compensatory damages of $100 million. The District Court 
denied ICP ’s motion for a new trial on the antitrust claim and Caterpillar’s motion for 
judgment as a matter of law (JMOL), and alternatively, for a new trial, on the tortious 
interference claim. Yet, the District Court vacated the jury’s damages award to ICP, 
holding that ICP failed to present evidence during trial to support a reasonably certain 
award. 
Both parties appealed. Caterpillar challenges the District Court’s denial of its 
request for JMOL on the tortious interference with contract claim, and in the alternative, 
requests a new trial on that claim because it contends that the District Court allowed ICP 
to present inadmissible evidence. ICP asserts that the District Court improperly vacated 
the jury’s $100 million damages award, and it seeks a new trial on its antitrust claim based 
on an allegedly erroneous jury instruction. Because neither party’ s arguments warrant 
disturbing the District Court’s ruling, we will affirm. 
I. BACKGROUND 
4 

ICP and Caterpillar are both in the heavy construction industry, but differ markedly 
in scale—ICP is a startup while Caterpillar is a major industry player. Although ICP and 
Caterpillar are the only parties to this litigation, other relevant companies include 
Caterpillar Auction Services (Cat Auction), a used construction equipment seller and 
IronPlanet, an online marketplace for such equipment. During the relevant period, 
Caterpillar owned stakes of approximately 30% in Cat Auction and 10% in IronPlanet. 
In early 2014, Cat Auction was in talks to merge with IronPlanet. In March 2014, 
ICP contracted with IronPlanet to import newly-made construction equipment 
manufactured by Lonking, a Chinese competitor of Caterpillar, and sell it on IronPlanet’s 
e-commerce platform. Internal Caterpillar emails show that employees expressed concerns 
about the ICP-Iron Planet contract, and relayed them to Cat Auction leadership given their 
ongoing merger discussions with IronPlanet. During the first month of the contract 
between ICP and IronPlanet, ICP made one sale of the Lonking equipment on IronPlanet’s 
e-commerce platform. A month later, IronPlanet terminated the contract and removed 
ICP’s online store from its website. 
In January 2015, ICP sued Caterpillar in the District of Delaware, alleging that 
Caterpillar pressured IronPlanet to terminate its contract with ICP. The complaint asserted 
claims under the Sherman Antitrust Act and for tortious interference with contract under 
Illinois law.
1 After an eight day trial, the jury rejected ICP’s antitrust claim, but found that 

1 During trial, the District Court observed that the “parties appear to have agreed that 
Illinois law applies” with respect to the tortious interference with contract claim. Appx. 
808 n.12. On appeal, ICP disputes that characterization, contending that the law of North 
Carolina could apply because it is ICP’s home state. ICP further argues that “the [D]istrict 
5 

Caterpillar tortiously interfered with ICP’s contract with IronPlanet and awarded ICP $100 
million in damages. Caterpillar moved for JMOL on the tortious interference with contract 
claim, while ICP moved for a new trial and a motion to alter or amend the judgment with 
respect to the antitrust claim. The District Court denied ICP’s motions and partially granted 
Caterpillar’s motion, vacating the jury’s $100 million award. The two parties appealed. 
II. DISCUSSION2 
A. Tortious Interference with Contract Claim 
In order to succeed on its tortious interference of contract claim, ICP had to prove 
by a preponderance of evidence that: (1) a contract existed between ICP and IronPlanet; 
(2) Caterpillar knew of the contract; (3) Caterpillar intentionally and unjustifiably induced 
IronPlanet to breach the contract; (4) IronPlanet subsequently breached the contract 

[C]ourt’s application of Illinois law was premised on the assumption that there was no 
conflict of laws” between Illinois and North Carolina law “on any material issue,” and that 
the District Court’s vacatur of the jury’s damages award undermine d that premise. ICP 
Reply Br. 16. This argument comes too late. At no point before the District Court did ICP 
assert that the tortious interference claim could be governed by North Carolina law. 
Instead, at the motion -to-dismiss stage, ICP argued that either Illinois or Florida law 
applied; at summary judgment, it made no choice-of-law argument; and at trial, it jointly 
submitted with Caterpillar proposed jury instructions applying Illinois law. Having charted 
that course throughout the litigation, ICP cannot now change maps on appeal . By 
affirmatively arguing below that Illinois or Florida law governed the claim—and never 
suggesting that North Carolina law applied—ICP waived the choice-of-law argument it 
now pursues on appeal. See Barna v. Bd. of Sch. Dirs. of Panther Valley Sch. Dist., 877 
F.3d 136, 147 (3d Cir. 2017) (“Waiver . . . is the intentional relinquishment or abandonment 
of a known right.”) (citation modified) (quoting United States v. Olano, 507 U.S. 725, 733 
(1993)); see also Williams v. BASF Catalysts LLC, 765 F.3d 306, 316 (3d Cir. 2014) 
(“[P]arties may waive choice-of-law issues. ”). Consequently , we analyze the tortious 
interference with contract claim under Illinois law. 
2 The District Court had jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1337, and 1367. We have 
appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1291. 
6 

because of Caterpillar’s wrongful conduct; and (5) the contractual breach resulted in 
damages to ICP.3 Caterpillar argues it is entitled to JMOL on this claim because ICP failed 
to present evidence sufficient to prove the third, fourth, and fifth elements. In the 
alternative, Caterpillar requests a new trial based on its assertion that the District Court 
allowed ICP to present inadmissible evidence. ICP, in turn, challenges the District Court’s 
vacatur of the $100 million in damages the jury awarded for this claim. 
1. Caterpillar’s Motion for JMOL4 
i. Third Element 
Caterpillar first asserts that ICP did not sufficiently prove that Caterpillar induced 
IronPlanet to breach the contract because it failed to present evidence showing any direct 
communications between Caterpillar and IronPlanet. Although the trial record is devoid 
of such evidence, that absence does not necessarily compel judgment in Caterpillar’s 
favor. The record contains ample circumstantial evidence from which a jury could 
conclude that Caterpillar pressured IronPlanet to breach its contractual agreement , 
including numerous internal Caterpillar emails, emails between Caterpillar and Cat 
Auction, and emails between Cat Auction and IronPlanet, all discussing Caterpillar’s 
concerns with the potential Cat Auction-IronPlanet merger in light of the IronPlanet-ICP 
contract. 

3 See Healy v. Metro. Pier & Exposition Auth., 804 F.3d 836, 842 (7th Cir. 2015). 
4 We exercise plenary review and apply the same standard as the District Court when 
reviewing an appeal of a JMOL—that is, we evaluate whether there was “insufficient 
evidence from which a jury reasonably could find liability.” Lightning Lube, Inc. v. 
Witco Corp., 4 F.3d 1153, 1167 (3d Cir. 1993). 
7 

Next, Caterpillar argues that even if there was sufficient evidence to demonstrate 
that it induced IronPlanet to breach the contract, its inducement was justified because 
Illinois law provides for a privilege excusing interference with a contract when “the 
defendant was acting to protect an interest which the law deems to be of equal or greater 
value than the plaintiff’s contractual rights.”5 Caterpillar contends it has two interests that 
qualify for this privilege: (1) its own business interest in refusing to deal “with IronPlanet 
if IronPlanet was going to facilitate the sale of new, Chinese equipment, in direct 
competition with Caterpillar’s business model and operations”; and (2) its shareholder 
interest as a partial owner of Cat Auction and IronPlanet. 6 Neither of these interests are 
applicable here, however. 
While refusal to deal may provide a privilege against a tortious interference claim, 
that privilege does not apply when the defendant goes beyond merely refusing to deal and 
instead uses its economic leverage “as a means of affirmative inducement, compulsion or 
pressure to” cause a third party to breach its contract.
7 As discussed above, the jury heard 
substantial evidence that Caterpillar did just that by leveraging its influence over the Cat 
Auction-IronPlanet merger negotiations to induce IronPlanet to breach its contract with 
ICP. 
Nor can Caterpillar invoke its shareholder status to claim the privilege, which does 
not apply when the shareholder defendant “acted in its own interests and contrary to the 

5 Nation v. Am. Cap., Ltd., 682 F.3d 648, 651 (7th Cir. 2012) (citation modified). 
6 Caterpillar First-Step Br. 45–51. 
7 Restatement (Second) of Torts § 766 cmt. l (1979). 
8 

interests of its principal.”8 Sufficient evidence supported the jury’s finding that Caterpillar 
acted to protect its own interests—not those of either Cat Auction or IronPlanet—when it 
interfered with the contract. After all, the evidence showed that the introduction of new, 
Chinese-made construction equipment into the United States only threatened Caterpillar’s 
interests; Cat Auction and IronPlanet, by contrast, operated in the used construction 
equipment market and would not have been similarly affected. The jury also had sufficient 
evidence to conclude that Caterpillar acted contrary to both Cat Auction and IronPlanet’s 
interests because IronPlanet viewed its agreement with I CP as a means to expand its 
offerings, and Caterpillar’s interference with the merger negotiations undermined Cat 
Auction’s stated intention to merge with IronPlanet. 
ii. Fourth Element 
Caterpillar argues that because IronPlanet had a valid basis to terminate the contract, 
ICP failed to prove that IronPlanet breached any contractual obligations. Specifically, 
Caterpillar

IN THE SUP
REME COURT OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON 
) 
BRADSHAW DEVELOPMENT, ) No. 104579-4 
INC. dba ANYTIME FITNESS, ) 
) 
Respondent, ) 
) 
v. ) En Banc 
) 
WASHINGTON STATE ) 
DEPARTMENT OF LABOR ) 
AND INDUSTRIES, ) 
) 
Petitioner. ) Filed: November 19, 2026 
_______________________________) 
GONZÁLEZ, J.—Under a Washington statute, state safety inspectors may 
“enter a worksite at an entry point designated by the employer or, in the event no 
entry point has been designated, at a reasonably recognizable entry point” to 
request consent to inspect and investigate violations of workplace safety 
regulations. RCW 49.17.070(3). We are asked whether, under this statute, state 
safety inspectors were authorized to follow a customer into a key card accessible 
fitness center’s front entrance, illuminated with an “open” sign, to request consent 
to inspect and investigate claims that the fitness center was operating in violation 
FILE 
IN CLERK’S OFFICE 
SUPREME COURT, STATE OF WASHINGTON 
NOVEMBER 19, 2026
THIS OPINION WAS FILED 
FOR RECORD AT 8 A.M. ON 
NOVEMBER 19, 2026
SARAH R. PENDLETON 
SUPREME COURT CLERK 

Bradshaw Dev., Inc. v. Dep’t of Labor & Indus., No. 104579-4 
2 
of a COVID- 19 emergency workplace safety regulation. We hold that the 
inspectors did not violate this statute. 
We are also asked whether the inspectors’ entry violated the search and 
seizure provisions of the federal constitution. We conclude that Bradshaw 
Development Inc. has not demonstrated an expectation of privacy in the fitness 
center’s front entrance area, which impliedly invited the public to enter to make 
legitimate business inquiries, and the inspectors did no more than a reasonably 
respectful person would have done. Accordingly, we hold the inspectors’ entry did 
not violate the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution. 
While the protections of article I, section 7 of the Washington Constitution 
are often broader than the Fourth Amendment’s, an independent state constitutional 
analysis has not been adequately presented in this case. Therefore, we do not reach 
the state constitution under these facts. We reverse, vacate the trial court’s order 
dismissing the inspectors’ citation, and remand to the trial court for further 
proceedings. 
B
ACKGROUND 
P
roclamation by Governor Jay Inslee No. 20-25.4 (Wash. May 31, 2020)1 
temporarily restricted certain business activities to fight the spread of COVID-19. 
1 https://governor.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2023-01/20-25.4%20COVID-
19%20Safe%20Start.pdf[https://perma.cc/4HY6-S2CM] 
Bradshaw Dev., Inc. v. Dep’t of Labor & Indus., No. 104579-4 
3 
See C lerk’s Papers (CP) at 722- 28 (describing Washington’s phased reopening 
plan). In support of that proclamation, the Department of Labor and Industries 
(L&I) enacted an emergency workplace safety rule to prohibit employers from 
allowing employees to perform work where business activity has been prohibited 
by an emergency proclamation. Former W AC 296-800-14035 (Wash. St. Reg. 20-
12-017, effective May 26, 2020); see also CP at 31-32, 1144.
Wesley Bradshaw owns Bradshaw Development Inc., operating as Anytime 
Fitness. Gyms and fitness centers were among the businesses that were 
temporarily closed in Yakima County in June 2020. L&I received a complaint that 
Anytime Fitness in Selah was open, and operating as usual, in violation of the 
emergency proclamation. On June 15, 2020, L&I workplace safety inspectors 
visited that Anytime Fitness location to determine if the business was violating the 
emergency workplace safety rule. 
On arrival, the L&I inspectors “saw a lit neon ‘open’ sign in the window of 
the building but the doors opened only to individuals who had key cards.” CP at 
32. This was the gym’s “only obvious entrance. ” Id. at 28. The inspector
s
un
successfully attempted to reach anyone at the gym by telephone at the posted 
number. They entered the locked gym by safely following someone carrying a 
Bradshaw Dev., Inc. v. Dep’t of Labor & Indus., No. 104579-4 
4 

gym bag.2 Inside, the L&I inspectors saw people exercising, sitting in an office, 
and apparently assisting a customer with a new gym membership. The inspectors 
asked an employee for consent to conduct an inspection of the facility. 
The first person the inspectors spoke with declined to give consent and 
asked them to wait where they were for the general manager. As they waited for 
about 20 minutes, the inspectors “observed several people enter the building as 
well as a chalkboard on which was written, ‘Welcome back.’” Id. at 32. The 
inspectors left after the general manager arrived and said he did not consent to 
them conducting an inspection. 
Based on the inspectors’ report, L&I cited Bradshaw Development Inc. for 
willfully violating former WAC 296-800-14035 and assessed a penalty of $9,639. 
The Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals reinstated the citation after an industrial 
appeals judge vacated the citation based on insufficient evidence.3 See id. at 32-
34. The Board explained that the inspectors “had the right to enter the building for 

2 To describe the inspectors’ entry, after recognizing the inspectors entered “in a safe manner,” 
the Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals used the colloquial term “tailgating,” using quotation 
marks, without defining it. CP at 28. Based on the testimony, the term describes an inspector 
“grabb[ing] the door and follow[ing]” a key card holder inside the locked gym. Id. at 1195. The 
dissent effectively makes its own factual finding that the inspectors were acting in a sneaky 
manner, suggesting their actions were contrary to policies established and enforced by Bradshaw, 
but the Board did not find that to be the case, and the evidence is not sufficient to support that 
conclusion. We are not the fact finder. We should constrain ourselves to making legal 
judgments. 
3 L&I had also cited Bradshaw for willfully violating the emergency workplace safety rule three 
times in July 2020. The inspectors did not enter any of the Anytime Fitness locations in July. 
The Board adopted the industrial appeals judge’s decision to vacate those three citations based on 
insufficient evidence and the State did not cross-appeal. CP at 32-34. 
Bradshaw Dev., Inc. v. Dep’t of Labor & Indus., No. 104579-4 
5 

the sole purpose of obtaining consent to inspect the premises” and properly relied 
on their observations inside the gym while awaiting consent, along with the owner 
Wesley Bradshaw’s refusal to answer questions, to find the violation willful. Id. at 
27-29. 
Bradshaw sought review in Yakima County Superior Court, which adopted 
the Board’s findings of fact but vacated the citation on statutory and constitutional 
grounds.4 That court agreed with the Board that RCW 49.17.070 allowed the L&I 
inspectors to enter the gym for the purpose of obtaining consent but concluded any 
observations inside the gym were inadmissible because, it concluded, “A business 
that limits entry to keycard holders is not open to the public. Therefore, Anytime 
Fitness had a reasonable expectation of privacy in the commercial premises.” CP 
at 1297. 
The State appealed, and the Court of Appeals affirmed on different grounds. 
Bradshaw Dev., Inc. v. Dep’t of Lab. & Indus., 34 Wn. App. 2d 705, 571 P.3d 300 
(2025). The Court of Appeals held that neither the statute nor the state and federal 
constitutions allowed the inspectors to enter a commercial premises’ key card 
accessible doors without permission through “tailgating”; therefore, any of their 

4 If the Board’s findings were challenged, we would review them to determine whether they are 
supported by substantial evidence in the record as a whole. Potelco, Inc. v. Dep’t of Lab. & 
Indus., 191 Wn. App. 9, 21, 361 P.3d 767 (2015). Here, in the absence of a proper challenge, the 
Board’s factual findings are binding. 
Bradshaw Dev., Inc. v. Dep’t of Labor & Indus., No. 104579-4 
6 

observations inside the gym were inadmissible. See id. at 721-24. The State 
successfully sought our review. 5 Wn.3d 1042 (2026). The American Civil 
Liberties Union of Washington Foundation (ACLU of WA) has filed an amicus 
brief in support of Bradshaw. 
ANALYSIS 

1. ENTRY UNDER THE STATUTE 
The Washington Legislature has enacted legislation “in order to assure, 
insofar as may reasonably be possible, safe and healthful working conditions for 
every [person] working in the state of Washington.” RCW 49.17.010. All workers 
in Washington are entitled to safe workplaces and, for workers in some industries, 
workplace safety is a fundamental right protected by our constitution. See id.; 
WASH. CONST. art. II, § 35; Martinez-Cuevas v. DeRuyter Bros. Dairy, 196 Wn.2d 
506, 519-20, 475 P.3d 164 (2020). To implement these assurances and protect 
these rights, our legislature enacted WISHA,5 along with many other statutes, and 
authorized L&I workplace safety inspectors to “enter a worksite at an entry point 
designated by the employer or, in the event no entry point has been designated, at a 

5 Washington Industrial Safety and Health Act of 1973, chapter 49.17 RCW. WISHA requires 
the State’s worker safety program to equal or exceed federal workplace safety standards. RCW 
49.17.010. 
Bradshaw Dev., Inc. v. Dep’t of Labor & Indus., No. 104579-4 
7 

reasonably recognizable entry point” to request consent to inspect and investigate 
violations of workplace safety regulations. RCW 49.17.070. 
Bradshaw contends RCW 49.17.070, read in light of its context and history, 
prohibits L&I inspectors from entering a locked business by following a customer 
inside and the L&I inspectors were required to get a warrant under RCW 49.17.075 
to enter the gym. To determine whether the inspectors were statutorily authorized 
to enter, we must look at the plain meaning of RCW 49.17.070, .075, and related 
statutes. Dep’ t of Ecology v. Campbell & Gwinn, LLC, 146 Wn.2d 1, 9-10, 43 P.3d 
4 (2002). We “must not add words where the legislature has chosen not to include 
them.” Rest. Dev., Inc. v. Cananwill, Inc., 150 Wn.2d 674, 682, 80 P.3d 598 
(2003); see also State v. Abrams, 163 Wn.2d 277, 282, 178 P.3d 1021 (2008) 
(courts “‘cannot press statutory construction to the point of disingenuous evasion 
even to avoid a constitutional question’” (internal quotation marks omitted) 
(quoting Miller v. French, 530 U.S. 327, 341, 120 S. Ct. 2246, 147 L. Ed. 2d 326 
(2000))). 
Our legislature directs L&I inspectors, once they present their credentials to 
the owner or other person with authority, to “enter without delay and at all 
reasonable times” to investigate workplace safety “during regular working hours 
and at other reasonable times, and within reasonable limits and in a reasonable 
manner.” L
AWS OF 1973, ch. 80, § 7, codified as RCW 49.17.070. Originally, both 
Bradshaw Dev., Inc. v. Dep’t of Labor & Indus., No. 104579-4 
8 

state and federal law purported to allow inspectors to enter without a warrant or 
exception to the warrant requirement. See 29 U.S.C § 657(a). Before our 
legislature amended the state statute to add procedural protections, the United 
States Supreme Court had held the federal law “is unconstitutional insofar as it 
purports to authorize inspections without warrant or its equivalent.” Marshall v. 
Barlow’ s, Inc., 436 U.S. 307, 325, 98 S. Ct. 1816, 56 L. Ed. 2d 305 (1978); see 
also See v. City of Seattle, 387 U.S. 541, 545, 87 S. Ct. 1737, 18 L. Ed. 2d 943 
(1967). 
In 2006, our legislature made its intent clear: 
The legislature intends that inspections performed under the 
Washington industrial safety and health act ensure safe and healthful 
working conditions for every person working in the state of 
Washington. Inspections must follow the mandates of Article II, 
section 35 of the state Constitution, and equal or exceed the 
requirements prescribed by the occupational safety and health act of 
1970 (Public Law 91-596, 84 Stat. 1590). The legislature also inten

SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO. A -0032-25 

73 DUN ONE, INC ., 

 Plaintiff -Appellant, 

v. 

DOROTHY A. GOULD, a/k/a 
DOROTHY GOULD, VICKI 
M. WHEELDON, a/k/a VICKI 
WHEELDON, a/k/a VICKI 
MARIE TURNER -WHEELDON, 
individually and as co-executors 
for the ESTATE OF DOROTH Y 
A. TURNER, deceased , JANICE 
VOGT and VICKI M. WHEELDON , 
a/k/a VICKI WHEELDON, a/k/a 
VICKI MARIE TURNER - 
WHEELDON, VICKI MARIE 
TURNER, individually and as 
co-trustees of the PAUL N. 
TURNER RESIDUARY TRUST , 
and GOULD HOLDINGS, LLC, 

 Defendants -Respondents. 
___________________________ 

 Argued October 6, 2026 ‒ Decided November 19, 2026 

Before Judges Rose and Bishop -Thompson.

APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court ." Although it is posted on the 
internet, this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited . R. 1:36-3. 

2 A-0032 -25 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, 
Chancery Division, Camden County, Docket No. C -
000097 -23. 

John M. Cinti argued the cause for appellant (Mintzer 
Sarowitz Zeris & Willis, LLC, attorneys; John M. Cinti, 
on the briefs). 

Carl Taylor argued the cause for respondents (Parker 
McCay, PA, attorneys; Michael E. Sullivan, on the 
brief). 

PER CURIAM 

This appeal arises from a dispute over a right of first refusal (ROFR) and 
testamentary transfer involving commercial premises (Premises) owned by 
defendants Estate of Dorothy A. Turner and Paul N. Turner Residuary Trust . 
Plaintiff 7 3 Dun One, Inc. is a tenant under a lease (Lease) that granted it a n 
ROFR to purchase the Premises upon defendants' receipt of a bona fide written 
offer from a third -party. The Lease further obligated plaintiff to pay its 
proportionate share of the real estate taxes assessed again st the Premises. 
Plaintiff a ppeals from an order dismissing its amended complaint and 
granting summary judgment in favor of defendants Dorothy A. Gould, Vicki M. 
Wheeldon, Janice Vogt , Estate of Dorothy A. Turner, Paul N. Turner Residuary 
Trust, and Gould Holdings, LLC (collectively, defendants) and dismissing its 

3 A-0032 -25 

amended complaint .1 Plaintiff further appeals from the July 22, 2025 order 
fixing the amount of real estate taxes and prejudgment interest owed to 
defendants. Because we conclude there are no genuine issues of material fact 
preclud ing judgment as a matter of law under Rule 4:46-2(c), we affirm . W e 
nevertheless remand for the limited purpose of directing the motion court to 
make findings of fact and conclusions of law required by Rule 1:7-4 concerning 
the outstanding real estate taxes and interests for years 2023 to 2025. 
I. 
We derive the following procedural history and relevant facts from the 
motion record, viewed in the light most favorable to plaintiffs as the non -moving 
party. See R. 4:46-2(c); Templo Fuente De Vida Corp. v. Nat'l Union Fire Ins. 
Co. of Pittsburgh, 224 N.J. 189, 199 (2016). 
Paul N. Turner and Dorothy A. Turner (collectively, the Turners) owned 
commercial property in Berlin Township . In May 1994, plaintiff executed the 
Lease with the Turners for the Premises , where it operated a franchise , then 
known as Dunkin' Donuts . Relevant to this appeal, Section 14.0 "Lessee's Right 
to Purchase" provides: 

1 Because Paul and Dorothy Turner, as well as Dorothy and Joseph Gould, share 
the same surname, we refer to them by their first name for clarity. In doing so, 
we intend no disrespect. 

4 A-0032 -25 

Lessor grants to LESSEE a right of first refusal to 
purchase the PREMISES at the same price and upon the 
same terms, provisions and conditions as shall be 
contained in any written bona fide offer for the 
purchase thereof which LESSOR shall at any time 
during the term of this LEASE, or any extension 
thereof, be ready and willing to accept, LESSOR shall 
give LESSEE written notice by certified mail and a 
complete copy of such bona fide offer, which includes 
all of the terms, provisions and conditions therein 
contained and LESSEE shall have thirty . . . days from 
and after the receipt of such notice from LESSOR in 
which to exercise such right. One or more waiver of 
LESSEE' S right to purchase the PREMISES under the 
terms of any such bona fide offer shall not constitute a 
waiver of LESSEE 's right to receive notice and an 
opportunity to purchase the PREMISES under this 
paragraph, if the terms of such offer should thereafter 
be altered or with respect to any subsequent bona fide 
offer to LESSOR, its successor and assigns, during the 
remaining term of this LEASE. 

 Paul died in July 2004. H is one-half interest in the property passed to his 
residuary trust, and defendants Janice Vogt and Vicki Wheeldon were appointed 
co-trustees. Dorothy retained the remaining one -half interest and later executed 
a will. 
In November 2020, both Dorothy's estate and Paul's trust entered a lease 
purchase agree ment with Gould Holdings for t he commercial p roperty and all 
existing leases thereon. Joseph, the company's owner and president , is the 
Turners ' son. Plaintiff and the other tenants were notified the leases and 

5 A-0032 -25 

management of the property had been assigned to Gould Holdings. Joseph 
certified , after plaintiff received that notice, he had several conversations with 
plaintiff's president regarding his new management of the property and its 
anticipated acquisition. 
Seven months later, Dorothy died , and defendants Dorothy Gould and 
Vicki Wheeldon were appointed co-executors of her estate. Dorothy's will 
directed : 
If, during my lifetime, I have not entered into a specific 
agreement with my son, Joseph R . Goul d regarding my 
interest [in]. . . , I specifically direct my Executor to 
grant my son . . . , if he survives me, [or to any entity 
over which he has substantial control, . . . ], an option, 
exercisable for a period of six months following my 
death, to purchase any interest I may have in the real 
property located at . . . Berlin, New Jersey . The option 
price shall be the fair market value of such interest as 
finally determined for estate/inheritance tax purposes 
and shall be exercised by providing written notice to 
my Executor within such six-month period. At all times 
during this six -month period, my son shall have the 
exclusive control of the property. If my son elects to 
purchase my interest in the property then, within 
[ninety ] days of providing the Executor with written 
notice of his intention to purchase such interest, 
settlement shall be held on the property. 

Plaintiff asserts it did not receive notice of the sale. However, the record 
shows Joseph notified plaintiff of his intent to obtain financing to close on the 
property , and he thereafter exercise d his purchase option. In October 2021, 

6 A-0032 -25 

Joseph applied for bank financing. The property was appraised at an "as-is" 
market value of $1,660,000. As a condition of financing, the bank required 
plaintiff, as tenant of the Premises, to execute a " Subordination, Non -
Disturbance, and Attornment " (SNDA) agreement and an Estoppel Certification. 
Joseph emailed those documents to plaintiff 's president, advising that he 
was "going to settlement Friday " to close on the p roperty. The SNDA identified 
Gould Holdings as landlord and reflected the bank would hold a $900,000 note 
secured by a mortgage on the property. J oseph, plaintiff's president, and a bank 
representative participated in a conference call regarding the transfer of title to 
Gould Holdings and the president's required signature. Plaintiff's president 
subsequently emailed Joseph and the bank representative two notarized copies 
of the SNDA and estoppel certificate , stating he had secured approval to receive 
notarized copies following closing. Gould Holdings then purchased the property 
from Dorothy's estate and Paul 's trust for $900,000. 
In April 2023, plaintiff 's president notif ied Joseph it was exercis ing its 
rights under the L ease to all remaining lease extension and renewals. The 
president also expressed a desire to discuss a twenty -year lease extension 
beyond the extension identified in the Lease. 

7 A-0032 -25 

In November 2003, the Berlin Township tax assessor apportioned the real 
estate taxes attributable to the Premises based on 2003 valuations, assigning 
$355,000 of the property's total assessed value of $875,000 to the Premises. 
Plaintiff paid $1,102.87 per month as its 40.57% contribution to the property's 
2003 real estate tax bill. Despite the periodic increases in the property's value 
for the purpose of real estate taxes calculation and the increases in the amount 
levied on the property, plaintiff continued to pay only $1,102.87 from 2003 
through a portion of 2023. The leased Premises was not assessed separately for 
tax purposes. 
Section 6.0 "Taxes" of the L ease stated: "In addition to the annual rent 
. . . , LESSEE agrees to pay, before interest and penalties accrue, all general real 
estate taxes which may be imposed on or become due and payable with respect 
to the premises during the term." Section 6.1. governs the calculation of taxe s 
when such taxes are not separately assessed. Section 6.1.1. provides: 
[The taxes on the land] shall be equal to the product of 
the sum of the total taxes attributable to land (land 
assessments multiplied by the aggregates of tax rates of 
all taking authorities) multiplied by a fraction, the 
numerator of which shall be the square footage of the 
PREMISES and the denominator of which shall be the 
square footage of all land assessed and including in the 
same tax bill as the P REMISES . . . . 

8 A-0032 -25 

Section 6.1.3 applies to the assessment of the building on the PREMISES 
and provides : 
[The taxes ] shall be determined by multiplying the total 
taxes attributable to all assessed improvement 
(including LESSEE's) by a fraction, the numerator of 
which shall be the square footage of floor space of 
LESSEE's building located on the premises and the 
denominator of which shall be the square footage of 
floor space of all structures existing . . . which shall 
have been assessed and included in the same tax bill as 
LESSEES's building. 

Between April and July 2023, Joseph and plaintiff's president engaged in 
numerous conversations and email exchange s concerning the tax 
underpayment s. In July 2023, plaintiff ceased making payments to Gould 
Holdings. 
In its initial complaint, plaintiff asserted claims for breach of contract, 
breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, specific performance , 
and unjust enrichment. Plaintiff later filed an amended complaint expanding its 
factual allegations underlying those claims . Defendants answered, asserted 
various affirmative defenses, and counterclaimed for breach of contract, unjust 
enrichment, breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing and a declaratory 
judgment concerning the underpa yment of real estate taxes. 

9 A-0032 -25 

Plaintiff moved for partial summary judgment on its breach of contract 
claim, which was denied. Defendants then moved for summary judgment and 
filed an amended counterclaim, adding all name d defendants as 
counterclaimants. Following argument, the motion court rendered an oral 
decision granting judgment in favor of defendants and dismissing plaintiff's 
complaint. A memorializing order was entered on April 4, 2025. 
Pursuant to the court's directive, defendants submitted a proposed order 
fixing the amount of taxes due for 2023 and 2024, together with supporti ng 
calculations for interest and square footage derived from the survey under 
sections 6.1.1 and 6.1.3, as well as prejudgment interest. Plaintiff filed 
objections and submitted alternative calculat ions based on the same survey and 
base tax assessment , but using revised survey dimens

leads.caseName: Team 3 Financial, LLC v. 125 Berckman St LLC
leads.court: New Jersey Superior Court Appellate Division
leads.text:
SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO S. A-3876-24 
 A-3877-24 

TEAM 3 FINANCIAL, LLC, 

 Plaintiff -Respondent, 

v. 

125 BERCKMAN ST LLC 
and NAYANA PATEL , 

 Defendants, 

and 

JAMES E. SHELTON, 

 Defendant -Appellant. 
_______________________ _ 

 Argued October 6, 2026 ‒ Decided November 19, 2026 

Before Judges Bishop -Thompson and Jablonski. 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, 
Chancery Division, Union County, Docket Nos. F -
001427 -24 and F -001430 -24. 

NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court ." Although it is posted on the 
internet , this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited . R. 1:36 -3. 

2 A-3876 -24 

Allison L. Domowitch argued the cause for appellant 
(Fleischer, Suglia, Dopke & Domowitch, PC, attorneys; 
Allison L. Domowitch, on the briefs). 

Hugh A. Keffer argued the cause for respondent 
(Fidelity National Title Group, attorneys; Hugh A. 
Keffer, on the brief s). 

PER CURIAM 

In these two matters, calendared back -to-back for the purpose s of issuing 
a single opinion, defendant James Shelton appeals from the trial court's August 
4, 2025 ord ers, denying his objection to the amount due fixed by the court and 
remanding the matter to the Office of Foreclosure to proceed as an uncontested 
matter on plaintiff Team 3 Financial LLC 's (Team 3 Financial) motion for final 
judgment. We affirm. 
I. 
Shelton holds a Texas judgment , entered on June 30, 2020 , against 
defendant 125 Berckman St, LLC (Berckman) and Bhavesh Patel 1 in the amount 
of $154,905.76, inclusive of damages, attorney's fees, and 5% interest . Shelton 

1 We refer to Nayana Patel and Bhavesh Patel by their first names to avoid any 
confusion caused by the common surname ; no disrespect is intended. The record 
does not identify any relationship between the m. In addition, Berckman and 
Nayana are not parties to this appeal because the sole issue is lien priority, which 
does involve them. 

3 A-3876 -24 

domesticated the judgment in New Jersey on October 14, 2020 , at which point 
it became a lien on real property owned by Berckman and Bhavesh. 
On July 18, 2022, Shelton conditionally agreed to accept $40,000 in full 
satisfaction of his judgment against Berckman and Bhavesh . Th e agreement, 
however, was never reduced to writing . Nonetheless, Shelton executed a 
warrant to satisfy the judgment and delivered the notarized original to the title 
company , with instructions to hold it in escrow pending payment of the 
settlement amount . He neither receive d the settlement funds nor authorize d the 
warrant's release or recording . The warrant was later released to another title 
insurance agency and recorded on October 27, 2022. The recorded warrant 
identified Joseph M. Carney as the party whose judgment had been satisfied, 
although he was not a party to the judgment. 
In September 2022, Advantage Capital, LLC (Advantage) extended a 
commercial loan to Berckman , secured by a note in the principal amount of 
$220,000, with a mortgage on the property located on Sumner Avenue in 
Plainfield. That mortgage was recorded in the Union County Clerk's Office on 
September 23, 2022. 
The following month, Advantage extended a second commercial loan to 
Berckman , secured by a note in the principal amount of $225,000, with a 

4 A-3876 -24 

mortgage on the property located on Berckman Street also in Plainfield. That 
mortgage was also recorded in the clerk's office on November 1, 2022. 
Both loans were further secured by an "Assignment of Leases and Rents." 
Nayana , the manager and sole member of Berckman, executed a guaranty and a 
pledge and security agreement for both loans. 
Thereafter , both mortgages were assigned to Advantage's affiliated entity, 
Team 3 Financial . Before the closing of Team 3 Financial's loan, the title agency 
obtained a title commitment that included a judgment search. That search 
disclosed the Shelton judgment . At the closing, the settlement agent was 
provided with the original notarized warrant , and Berckman furnished an 
affidavit of title . The settlement agent disbursed funds to clear Berckman and 
Nayana's title and thereby secure d Team 3 Financial a first -priority mortgage on 
each property . With regard to the Sumner Avenue property, the agent paid off 
a mortgage lien, property tax obligation , municipal utility authority charges, and 
a 2018 judgment , totaling $211,499.64 . As to the Berckman Street property, the 
agent paid of f a mortgage lien, property tax obligation, and municipal utility 
authority charges, totaling $207,321.42 . The loan nevertheless closed without 
any payment to Shelton , who receive d no notice of the closing. 

5 A-3876 -24 

Shelton learned of the unauthorized filing and confirmed the warrant had 
been recorded. He then moved to vacate the warrant , which was granted on June 
9, 2023. 
In November 2022, Berckman and Nayana defaulted on both loans and 
failed to respond to the notices of default . On February 8, 2024, Advantage filed 
separate foreclosure complaints in the Chancery Division against Berckman and 
Nayana concerning the Sum ner and Berckman Street propert ies. Shelton moved 
to intervene in these actions but later withdrew his motion s. Advantage 
thereafter filed amended complaint s in both matters , adding Shelton as a 
defendant. Shelton filed a contested answer and counterclaim , seeking a 
declarat ion that his interest as a judgment credit or was superior to Advantage's 
interest. On August 12, 2024, the court entered an order substitut ing Team 3 
Financial as plaintiff. 
In October 2024, Team 3 Financial moved for summary judgment in both 
actions , seeking a determination of the priorit y of the parties ' liens based on 
equitable subrogation. Shelton cross -moved for summary judgment objecting 
to the amount due to him. 
On November 22, 20 24, t he motion court granted Team 3 Financial's 
motion and den ied Shelton's cross -motion. In a n accompanying statement of 

6 A-3876 -24 

reasons, the court concluded that, under the doctrine of equitable subrogation, 
Team 3 Financial was entitled to the same priority as the mortgagees and 
creditors whose senior interest it had discharged. Because Shelton 's judgment 
was junior to th ose interests, the court held Team 3 Financial 's mortgage interest 
in both properties was superior to Shelton's judgment lien to the extent it s loan 
proceeds were used to satisfy those senior obligations. Accordingly, Team 3 
Financial's mortgage interest was superior in the amount of $207,321.42 for the 
Berckman property and $211,499.65 for the Sumner Avenue property. 
 In separate orders dated January 3, 2025 , the court granted Team 3 
Financial's unopposed motion to enforce the contractual default interest rate of 
2% per month , or 24% per year . Although t he motion was unopposed, the cou rt 
nevertheless made findings of fact and conclusions of law in a statement of 
reasons. It found the 24% default rate reasonable because it was expressly 
provided for in the note, mortgage, and related loan documents governing th ese 
commercial transaction s. The court further determined s ince defendants 
default ed on December 1, 2022, default interest accrued from that date through 
entry of final judgment and would continue to acc rue until the judgment was 
paid in full . 

7 A-3876 -24 

Team 3 Financial then moved before the Foreclosure Unit for entry of 
final judgment , which was unopposed . On March 14, 2025, the court entered 
separate final judgment in the full amount of the notes, $358,425.70 for the 
Berckman Street property and $351,459.71 for the Sumner Avenue property and 
issued a writ of execution . Both orders calculated the amount due, together with 
interest at the contractual default interest rate, costs, and attorney's fees 
calculated as of January 31, 2025 . A writ of execution was issued on April 14, 
2025. 
On May 23, 2025, the court vacated both final judgment s pursuant to Rule 
4:50-1. In its statement of reasons , the court concluded the judgment failed to 
account for Shelton's lien priority in relation to Team 3 Financial's total interest. 
The court explained the judgment s improperly merged Team 3 Financial's first - 
and third -priority interests into a single judgment , thereby extinguish ing 
Shelton's second -priority interest in contra vention of the summary judgment 
order. It further found Team 3 Financial had no right to extinguish Shelton's 
interest . 
Team 3 Financial again moved for final judgment in both matters and 
proposed the sale proceeds be distributed as follows: from the Sumner Avenue 
property, Team 3 Financial was to be paid first $337,459.71 , representing 96% 

8 A-3876 -24 

of the judgment , plus accrued interest ; from the Berckman Street property, it 
would be paid first $329,751.64 , representing 92% of the judgment, plus accrued 
interest . Shelton was to be paid second $154,905.76 , plus post-judgment interest 
accruing from June 30, 2020 , and Team 3 Financial w ould be paid the remain ing 
balance of the judgment from the sale proceeds . 
Shelton objected, arguing the final judgment sought by Team 3 Financial 
remained inconsistent with the court 's prior summary judgment and vacatur 
orders. The appendix submitted to us , however, does not include Shelton's 
objection. He contend ed the court expressly held Team 3 Financial's first-
priority interest was capped at $207,321.42. 
On August 4, 2025, the court entered final judgment and denied Shelton's 
objection . In its well-reasoned written opinion , the motion court rejected 
Shelton's argument , concluding Team 3 Financial would suffer no prejudice if 
its recovery were limited to the same contractual interest and related costs 
Advantage could have recovered had Team 3 Financial never become involved . 
The court found th at result consistent with Sovereign Bank v. Gillis , 432 N.J. 
Super. 36 (App. Div. 2013). The court further observed Shelton ha d not 
identified any prejudice resulting from the scope of the subrogation —whether 
by showin g his second-priority lien could not be fully satisfied through a 

9 A-3876 -24 

sheriff's sale or by demonstrating the terms of Team 3 Financial's note were 
materially less favorable than those of Advantage's note. The matter was again 
remanded to the Officer of Foreclosure to proceed uncontested. 
II. 
On appeal, Shelton contends the motion court erred in concluding Team 3 
Financial's lien retained first-priority over Shelton's judgment in an amount 
exceeding beyond the $207,321.42 fixed in the November 22, 2024 summary 
judgment order. He a rgues any interest accruing beyond the amount Team 3 
Financial paid to satisfy the mortgage falls outside the protection of equitable 
subrogation. Shelton further ass erts Team 3 Fin ancial neither raised nor 
address ed, in its motion for summary judgment or its motion for default interest 
rate, both the $337,459.71 and $329,751.64 priority calculation ultimately 
adopted by the court . 
Upon review of the record, we conclude the motion court properly granted 
Team 3 Financial's motion for final judgment and denied Shelton's objections; 
we affirm substantially for the reasons expressed in its well-reasoned opinion. 
We add the following c omments. 
Our scope of review of a trial court's decision to apply an equitable 
doctrine is limited. Ocwen Loan Servs., LLC v. Quinn , 450 N.J. Super. 393, 

10 A-3876 -24 

397 (App. Div. 2016). A decision to apply equitable subrogation is "left to the 
sound discretion of the trial judge, and we will not substitute our judgment for 
that of the trial judge in the absence of a clear abuse of discretion." N.Y. Mortg. 
Tr. 2005-3 v. Deely, 466 N.J. Super. 387, 397 (App. Div. 2021) (quoting Ocwen, 
450 N.J. Super. at 397 ). 
We

LUGG, J.

INTRODUCTION 
Quality HV AC borrowed $6,000,000.00 from WSFS.  H. Adam Wahl, III 
(“Wahl”) and Brookside Properties (“Brookside”) guaranteed the loan.  Quality 
HV AC defaulted, and WSFS moved to secure its financial interest.  WSFS invoked 
provisions of the guarantees to seek confessions of judgment against the loan 
guarantors – Wahl and Brookside.  The guarantors opposed.  They contend WSFS 
failed to demonstrate the guarantors knowingly, intelligently, and voluntarily waived 
their due process rights.   
A Superior Court Commissioner  concluded that Wahl knowingly, 
intentionally, and voluntarily waived , on behalf of himself and Brookside, the 
guarantors’ rights to notice and a hearing .1  Wahl appealed the Commissioner’s 
findings. 2

2 Defendants appealed the Superior Court Commissioner’s 2025 finding that “[t]he 
Confession of Judgment provisions of the . . . [guarantees] are valid and enforceable 
and WSFS is entitled to confess judgment against them.”  D.I. 27; Wilmington 
Savings Fund Society, FSB v. Wahl, 2025 WL 2206759 (Del. Super. Ct. Jul. 31, 2025) 
(Wahl I).  The Court recommitted the matter to that Commissioner to allow for the 
testimony of an additional witness.  D.I. 31.  After that witness t estified, the 
Commissioner again concluded “[t]he Confession of Judgment provisions of the . . 
. [guarantees] are valid and enforceable and WSFS is entitled to confess judgment 
against them.” D.I. 40; Wilmington Savings Fund Society, FSB v. Wahl , 2026 WL 
1747746 (Del. Super. Ct. June 16, 2026) (Wahl II).  Defendants again appealed.  D.I. 
41.  The parties agree that there is a single appeal before the Court.  D.I. 45.  This 
Order considers the facts developed at both evidentiary hearings in assessing the 
enforceability of the confession of judgment provisions.      
3

the complete record in this matter, the Commissioner’s conclusion, finding “the 
confession of judgment provisions [to be] valid and enforceable against the 
Defendants,”3 is ADOPTED.

Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Segall 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06852 
 November 18, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., appellant, 
 v 
 Stephen L. Segall, etc., respondent, et al., defendants; Binay AYY, LLC, etc., nonparty-respondent. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 18, 2026 
 2024-04710, (Index No. 35642/18) 
 Betsy Barros, J.P. 
 Angela G. Iannacci 
 Donna-Marie E. Golia 
 Lisa S. Ottley, JJ. 

 Akerman LLP, New York, NY (Ashley S. Miller and Jordan M. Smith of counsel), for appellant. 
 Joseph J. Haspel, Middletown, NY, for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Rockland County (Keith J. Cornell, J.), dated January 31, 2024. The order, insofar as appealed from, upon renewal, in effect, vacated so much of an order of the same court (Thomas Zugibe, J.) dated October 20, 2022, as denied the prior cross-motion of the defendant Stephen L. Segall for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the subject mortgage and, upon searching the record, awarded the plaintiff summary judgment dismissing that defendant's counterclaim, and thereupon granted that defendant's prior cross-motion. 
 ORDERED that the order dated January 31, 2024, is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 On December 8, 2006, Stephen L. Segall (hereinafter the defendant) and Wendy S. Segall (hereinafter together the borrowers) executed a note in the sum of $516,750 in favor of Option One Mortgage Corporation. The note was secured by a mortgage on certain real property located in New City. The borrowers executed a loan modification agreement dated October 1, 2008. The borrowers allegedly defaulted on their obligations under the note and mortgage by failing to make the monthly payments due March 1, 2009, and thereafter. 
 On June 10, 2009, the plaintiff, as the purported assignee of the mortgage, commenced an action (hereinafter the 2009 action) against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. The plaintiff elected in the complaint to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage. 
 On December 24, 2010, the plaintiff commenced a second action (hereinafter the 2010 action) against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. 
 The plaintiff's motion to discontinue the 2009 action was granted in an order dated October 13, 2011. The plaintiff's motion to discontinue the 2010 action was granted in an order [*2] dated June 26, 2013. 
 On January 21, 2015, the plaintiff commenced a third action (hereinafter the 2015 action) against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. By deed dated July 27, 2015, the borrowers conveyed the property to the defendant only. In an order dated July 19, 2017, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted the defendant's cross-motion to dismiss the complaint in the 2015 action insofar as asserted against him for failure to comply with RPAPL 1304. 
 On September 20, 2018, the plaintiff commenced this action against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. The defendant interposed an answer in which he asserted, among other things, an affirmative defense alleging that the action was barred by the statute of limitations and a counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 In October 2019, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant and for an order of reference. The defendant cross-moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 By deed dated December 17, 2019, the defendant conveyed the property to Binay AYY, LLC (hereinafter Binay). 
 In an order dated October 20, 2022, the Supreme Court denied the defendant's cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage on the ground that the 2009 and 2010 actions had been voluntarily discontinued, citing Freedom Mtge. Corp. v Engel ( 37 NY3d 1 , 29). Upon searching the record, the court awarded the plaintiff summary judgment dismissing the defendant's counterclaim. The court denied, with leave to renew, those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant and for an order of reference. 
 In July 2023, the plaintiff moved, among other things, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant, to strike the defendant's answer, and for an order of reference. Binay, as successor in interest to the defendant, and the defendant, cross-moved, inter alia, (1) pursuant to CPLR 1018 to substitute Binay in place of the defendant, and (2) for leave to renew the defendant's prior cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage, based on a change in the law, arguing that the action was time-barred under the Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821 [eff Dec. 30, 2022]). In an order dated January 31, 2024, the Supreme Court, among other things, denied the plaintiff's motion, denied, as academic, that branch of the cross-motion of Binay and the defendant which was to amend the caption to substitute Binay in the place of the defendant, granted that branch of the cross-motion which was for leave to renew, and, upon renewal, granted the defendant's prior cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. The plaintiff appeals from so much of the order as, upon renewal, granted the defendant's prior cross-motion. 
 "Pursuant to CPLR 1018, [u]pon any transfer of interest, the action may be continued by or against the original parties unless the court directs the person to whom the interest is transferred to be substituted or joined in the action" ( Wells Fargo Bank, NA v McKenzie , 183 AD3d 574, 575 [internal quotation marks omitted]). Thus, the defendant, as well as Binay, as the current owner of the premises and the successor in interest to the defendant, could defend the action in the absence of formal substitution or joinder ( see CPLR 1018; HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Welt , 243 AD3d 770 , 771). 
 "An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Santos , 218 AD3d 827, 828 ; see CPLR 213[4]). "[E]ven if a mortgage is payable in installments, once a mortgage debt is accelerated, the entire amount is due and the statute of limitations begins to run on the entire debt" ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Mor , 201 AD3d 691, 694 ). "The entire mortgage debt will be deemed to have been accelerated by, as relevant here, the commencement of a mortgage foreclosure action in which the complaint seeks payment of the full outstanding loan balance" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Connor , 204 AD3d 861, 863 ). 
 "Pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4), a person having an estate or interest in real property subject to a mortgage may maintain an action to secure the cancellation and discharge of the encumbrance, and to adjudge the estate or interest free of it, if the applicable statute of limitations for commencing a foreclosure action has expired" ( U.S. Bank NA v Schaer , 223 AD3d 928 , 929). Here, in support of their cross-motion, Binay and the defendant established, prima facie, that the six-year statute of limitations began to run in June 2009, when the plaintiff commenced the 2009 action and elected in the complaint to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v DiGiorgio , 237 AD3d 899 , 900). Since the plaintiff did not commence the instant action until September 2018, more than six years later, Binay and the defendant established, prima facie, that the action was time-barred ( see CPLR 213[4]; US Bank Trust, N.A. v Reizes , 222 AD3d 907, 910 ). 
 In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact. Pursuant to CPLR 3217, as amended by FAPA, the voluntary discontinuances of the 2009 and 2010 actions did not serve to revive or reset the statute of limitations ( see id. § 3217[e]; JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. v Turkov , 242 AD3d 1069 , 1071; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Edwards , 231 AD3d 1189 , 1193). Moreover, as neither the 2009 action nor the 2010 action was dismissed "based on an expressed judicial determination, made upon a timely interposed defense, that the instrument was not validly accelerated" (CPLR 213[4][a]), the plaintiff is estopped from asserting that the debt was not validly accelerated by the commencement of either of those actions ( see CV XXVIII, LLC v Williams , 236 AD3d 753 , 755; US Bank Trust, N.A. v Reizes , 222 AD3d at 910 ). 
 There is no merit to the plaintiff's contention that FAPA does not apply retroactively ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 ; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 ). The plaintiff's challenges to the constitutionality of the retroactive application of FAPA are also without merit ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 ; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 ; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d 818 , 822; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dagrin , 233 AD3d 1065 , 1069-1071; 97 Lyman Ave., LLC v MTGLQ Invs., L.P. , 233 AD3d 1038 , 1043). 
 The plaintiff's contention that the action was timely commenced pursuant to either CPLR 205(a) or 205-a is improperly raised for the first time in its reply brief ( see Bank of Am., N.A. v McKeon , 241 AD3d 617 , 619). 
 The plaintiff's remaining contention is without merit. 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court, upon renewal, properly granted the defendant's prior cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 BARROS, J.P., IANNACCI, GOLIA and OTTLEY, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

OPINION 
 
CHIEF JUSTICE TODD       DECIDED:  November 18, 2026 
In these consolidated appeals, we  consider whether a zoning hearing board may 
grant a use variance on the basis that the variance sought is de minimis, and, if so, 
whether the grant of a use variance was appropriate in the instant case.  For the reasons 
that follow, we hold that a use variance cannot be considered de minimis, and, thus, that 
the use variance granted in th e instant case was improper.  Accordingly, we reverse the 
Commonwealth Court’s decisio n below. 
I. Factual and Procedural History 
Appellees John Marshall and Dara Gans Marshall (“the Marshalls”) own 
approximately eleven acres of property in East Bradford Township (“Township”), Chester 
County, Pennsylvania  (the “Property ”).  The Property contains several structures, 
including a residential home  known as the Paxson House , which is occupied by the 
Marshalls and their three children ; a currently-unoccupied building known as the Tenant 
House, which previously was used as a veterinary clinic ; and a barn.

In these consolidated appeals, we consider whether a zoning hearing board may 
grant a use variance on the basis that the variance sought is de minimis, and, if so, 
whether the grant of a use variance was appropriate in the instant case.  For the reasons

If this opinion indicates that it is “FOR PUBLICATION,” it is subject to 
revision until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports. 
 
 
 
 
-1- 
S T A T E  O F  M I C H I G A N  
 
C O U R T  O F  A P P E A L S  
 
 
 
DEMMAK INDUSTRIES, LLC, doing business as 
IRIDIUM MANUFACTURING, 
 
 Plaintiff/Counterdefendant-Appellant, 
 
 
UNPUBLISHED 
November 18, 2026 
2:33 PM 
v No. 377081 
Washtenaw Circuit Court 
JAC PRODUCTS, INC., 
 
LC No. 23-001093-CB 
 Defendant/Counterplaintiff-Appellee. 
 
 
 
Before:  M. J. KELLY, P.J., and RIORDAN and RICK, JJ. 
 
PER CURIAM. 
 This contract dispute involves a complaint filed by plaintiff Demmak Industries, LLC, 
d/b/a Iridium Manufacturing (“Iridium”), against defendant JAC Products, Inc.  (“JAC”), as well 
as a counterclaim filed by JAC against Iridium. The trial court dismissed Iridium’s complaint under 
MCR 2.116(C)(8) and (C)(10), and granted summary disposition in favor of JAC on its 
counterclaim under MCR 2.116(I)(2). Iridium appeals that order as of right, arguing that the trial 
court erred in its contractual analysis and that Iridium, not JAC, should prevail in this case because 
JAC materially breached the parties’ two related contracts. For the reasons set forth, we affirm the 
trial court in part, reverse in part, and remand to that court for further proceedings. 
I.  FACTS 
 JAC is an automotive-component supplier to companies such as Toyota and Stellantis, and 
Iridium is an automotive-parts manufacturer that contracts with suppliers such as JAC.1 On March 
19, 2019, JAC sent Iridium a letter informing Iridium of the following: 
 
 
1 While not clearly explained in the record, this relationship implies that JAC is a “Tier One” 
automotive supplier, i.e., a supplier directly to the original equipment manufacturer, and Iridium 
is a “Tier Two” automotive supplier, i.e., a supplier to Tier One.   
-2- 
 This letter is to inform you that JAC Products, Inc. (JAC) has awarded 
Iridium Manufacturing with the Toyota Tonneau program per the terms and 
conditions detailed below and subject to JAC Products’ standard purchase order 
terms and conditions (available on www.jacproducts.com). . . . 
The letter continued that JAC would supply certain basic materials to Iridium and, in turn, Iridium 
would manufacture the automotive parts required by JAC on a rolling basis: 
 Subject to the JAC Products purchase orders and standard purchase order 
terms and conditions, Iridium Manufacturing will supply to JAC Products 100% of 
JAC Products’ requirements for all products covered by this award letter for the 
production life of the Toyota Tonneau program at the pricing indicated in this award 
letter. 
* * * 
 JAC will provide and deliver all aluminum extrusions for use in production 
of all parts to be supplied by Iridium, for no cost to Iridium FOB at Iridium’s 
address in Sterling Heights, Michigan. 
The letter estimated that JAC would require 31,496 units for 2019, 28,585 units for 2020, and 
20,053 units for 2021. It was signed by a representative for Iridium the following day.2 
 On July 22, 2022, JAC sent Iridium another letter3 informing Iridium of the following: 
 This letter is to inform you that JAC Products, Inc. (JAC) has awarded 
Iridium Manufacturing with the Stellantis DS program as detailed below and 
subject to JAC Products’ standard purchase order terms and conditions (available 
on www.jacproducts.com). . . . 
The letter further provided: 
 Subject to the JAC Products purchase orders and standard purchase order 
terms and conditions, Iridium Manufacturing will supply to JAC Products 100% of 
JAC Products’ requirements for all products covered by this award letter for the 
production life of the Toyota Tonneau [sic: Stellantis DS ] program at the pricing 
indicated in this award letter in accordance with the firm quantities and delivery 
schedules specific in the JAC Products’ releases. 
* * * 
 
 
2 We hereinafter refer to this letter as the “Toyota Contract.” 
3 We note that a near-identical version of this letter was signed in January 2022, but it appears that 
the July 2022 letter was intended to supersede and replace that earlier letter. 
-3- 
 Weekly volume for Stellantis DS accounting for all parts will range from 
2,200pcs a week min to 3,600pcs a week max. 
The letter was signed by Iridium’s representative the following day.4 
 The “Purchase Order Terms and Conditions”  referenced in those two letters  included the 
following relevant provisions: 
 ¶ 7. . . . Deliveries shall be made strictly in accordance with both the 
quantities and times specified in this Purchase Order. If quantities and/or delivery 
schedules are not specified on this Purchase Order or if this Purchase Order is 
designated a “blanket purchase order”, Seller shall deliver Products to Buyer (and 
Buyer shall only be responsible to purchase Products from Seller) in accordance 
with the firm quantities and at the times and locations specified on Buyer’s delivery 
schedules issued in connection with this Purchase Order. . . . Buyer may change the 
rate of scheduled shipments or direct temporary suspension of scheduled 
shipments, neither of which shall entitle Seller to a modification of the price for 
Products or Services covered by this Purchase Order. . . . From time to time, Buyer 
may provide Seller with, and Buyer’s delivery schedules may contain,  estimates, 
forecasts or projections of Buyer’s future volume or quantity requirements for 
Products or Services and/or the term of a program to which such Products or 
Services relate. Such estimates, forecasts and projections are not binding on Buyer 
and Buyer makes no representation, warranty, guaranty or commitment of any kind 
or nature, express or implied, regarding any such estimate, forecast or projection 
provided to Seller. 
* * * 
 ¶ 10. CHANGES: Buyer reserves the right at any time, by providing 
written notice to Seller, to direct changes or cause Seller to make changes under 
this Purchase Order, including, without limitation, in any one or more of the 
following: (a) drawings, designs or specific ations of the Products or Services; (b) 
increases or decreases in quantities; (c) method of shipping or packing; (d) 
inspection, testing and quality control; (e) delivery schedules; and (f) amount of 
Buyer-furnished property; and Seller agrees to promptly make such changes. . . .  
* * * 
 ¶ 16. TERMINATION FOR CONVENIENCE: In addition to any other 
rights of Buyer to terminate this Purchase Order, Buyer may at its option 
immediately terminate all or any part of this Purchase Order, at any time and for 
any reason or no reason, by giving written notice to Seller. . . . Upon te rmination, 
Buyer shall pay to Seller the following amounts without duplication: (a) the 
Purchase Order price for all Services and Products which have been completed in 
 
 
4 We hereinafter refer to this letter as the “Stellantis Contract.” 
-4- 
accordance and compliance with this Purchase Order and not previously paid for, 
and (b) Seller’s actual costs of work -in-process, parts and materials transferred to 
Buyer, to the extent such costs are reasonable in amount and properly allocable or 
apportionable under generally accepted accounting principles to the terminated 
portion of this Purchase Order. The foregoing amounts shall be Seller’s sole and 
exclusive recovery from Buyer (without regard to the legal theory which is the basis 
for any claim by Seller) on account of such termination. . . . Except as provided in 
this Paragraph, Buyer shall not be liable for and shall not be required to make 
payments to Seller, directly or on account of claims by Seller’s subcontractors, for 
loss of anticipated profit, unabsorbed overhead, interest on claims, product 
development and engineering costs, facilities and equipment rearrangement costs 
or rental, unamortized depreciation costs, general and administrative burden 
charges and other consequential or incidental damages from termination of this 
Purchase Order. . . . 
In August 2023, Iridium filed its complaint against JAC, alleging that “JAC has an 
outstanding balance of $428,252.10. This entire amount is for products that Iridium has already 
delivered to JAC.” Thus, Iridium maintained three claims against JAC: Count I  (breach of 
contract), Count II (unjust enrichment), and Count III (statutory conversion). 
 The following month, JAC filed a counterclaim against Iridium, alleging that “[d]uring the 
course of the contractual relationship between Iridium and JAC, Iridium repeatedly failed to 
provide timely delivery of quality parts” and that it had suffered damages in the approximate 
amount of $130,000. 
 In June 2025, JAC moved for summary disposition of Iridium’s complaint pursuant to 
MCR 2.116(C)(8) and (C)(10). In its accompanying brief, JAC explained additional details of the 
parties’ relationship. According to JAC, Iridium had deficient facilities and equipment, resulting 
in several issues such as a “busted door on Mill #1” and “down waterjets” in November 2022.  
JAC attempted to assist Iridium with production stability by, for example, providing Iridium with 
equipment and shifting some orders to another supplier with open capacity to reduce Iridium’s 
backlog.5 Unfortunately, these attempts were unsuccessful, and  in April 2023,  JAC invoked its 
right under ¶ 16 of the Purchase Order Terms and Conditions to terminate the parties’ contractual 
relationship. The April 2023 termination e-mail from JAC to Iridium stated, in relevant part: 
 Also, in order to recover the significant costs that JAC Products was forced 
to absorb since Iridium was not able to meet its obligated volumes, we are attaching 
an overview of these costs that JAC intends to short pay Iridium as a final matter 
of business and recover these costs.  
 A summary of these costs is as follows:  
 
 
5 JAC acknowledged that at one point during the parties’ relationship, JAC failed to timely deliver 
raw material to Iridium for a few months. However, JAC explained, it never sought to hold Iridium 
financially responsible for Iridium’s resulting late delivery. 
-5- 
 1. Iridium OT Charges - $28,000. This was the OT that JAC paid to Iridium 
to work weekends, and was not recovered from our customer.  
 2. Outside Processing Break in Charges - $60,000. This was $2,500 per 
occurrence from our coating supplier to break in to run the parts that Iridium was 
behind on, in order meet our customer requirements.  
 3. Premium Freight Due to Iridium capacity shortfall - 989 Hinges -
