leads.text:
Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., etc v Segall 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06852 
 November 18, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., appellant, 
 v 
 Stephen L. Segall, etc., respondent, et al., defendants; Binay AYY, LLC, etc., nonparty-respondent. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 18, 2026 
 2024-04710, (Index No. 35642/18) 
 Betsy Barros, J.P. 
 Angela G. Iannacci 
 Donna-Marie E. Golia 
 Lisa S. Ottley, JJ. 

 Akerman LLP, New York, NY (Ashley S. Miller and Jordan M. Smith of counsel), for appellant. 
 Joseph J. Haspel, Middletown, NY, for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Rockland County (Keith J. Cornell, J.), dated January 31, 2024. The order, insofar as appealed from, upon renewal, in effect, vacated so much of an order of the same court (Thomas Zugibe, J.) dated October 20, 2022, as denied the prior cross-motion of the defendant Stephen L. Segall for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the subject mortgage and, upon searching the record, awarded the plaintiff summary judgment dismissing that defendant's counterclaim, and thereupon granted that defendant's prior cross-motion. 
 ORDERED that the order dated January 31, 2024, is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 On December 8, 2006, Stephen L. Segall (hereinafter the defendant) and Wendy S. Segall (hereinafter together the borrowers) executed a note in the sum of $516,750 in favor of Option One Mortgage Corporation. The note was secured by a mortgage on certain real property located in New City. The borrowers executed a loan modification agreement dated October 1, 2008. The borrowers allegedly defaulted on their obligations under the note and mortgage by failing to make the monthly payments due March 1, 2009, and thereafter. 
 On June 10, 2009, the plaintiff, as the purported assignee of the mortgage, commenced an action (hereinafter the 2009 action) against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. The plaintiff elected in the complaint to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage. 
 On December 24, 2010, the plaintiff commenced a second action (hereinafter the 2010 action) against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. 
 The plaintiff's motion to discontinue the 2009 action was granted in an order dated October 13, 2011. The plaintiff's motion to discontinue the 2010 action was granted in an order [*2] dated June 26, 2013. 
 On January 21, 2015, the plaintiff commenced a third action (hereinafter the 2015 action) against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. By deed dated July 27, 2015, the borrowers conveyed the property to the defendant only. In an order dated July 19, 2017, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted the defendant's cross-motion to dismiss the complaint in the 2015 action insofar as asserted against him for failure to comply with RPAPL 1304. 
 On September 20, 2018, the plaintiff commenced this action against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. The defendant interposed an answer in which he asserted, among other things, an affirmative defense alleging that the action was barred by the statute of limitations and a counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 In October 2019, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant and for an order of reference. The defendant cross-moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 By deed dated December 17, 2019, the defendant conveyed the property to Binay AYY, LLC (hereinafter Binay). 
 In an order dated October 20, 2022, the Supreme Court denied the defendant's cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage on the ground that the 2009 and 2010 actions had been voluntarily discontinued, citing Freedom Mtge. Corp. v Engel ( 37 NY3d 1 , 29). Upon searching the record, the court awarded the plaintiff summary judgment dismissing the defendant's counterclaim. The court denied, with leave to renew, those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant and for an order of reference. 
 In July 2023, the plaintiff moved, among other things, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant, to strike the defendant's answer, and for an order of reference. Binay, as successor in interest to the defendant, and the defendant, cross-moved, inter alia, (1) pursuant to CPLR 1018 to substitute Binay in place of the defendant, and (2) for leave to renew the defendant's prior cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage, based on a change in the law, arguing that the action was time-barred under the Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821 [eff Dec. 30, 2022]). In an order dated January 31, 2024, the Supreme Court, among other things, denied the plaintiff's motion, denied, as academic, that branch of the cross-motion of Binay and the defendant which was to amend the caption to substitute Binay in the place of the defendant, granted that branch of the cross-motion which was for leave to renew, and, upon renewal, granted the defendant's prior cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. The plaintiff appeals from so much of the order as, upon renewal, granted the defendant's prior cross-motion. 
 "Pursuant to CPLR 1018, [u]pon any transfer of interest, the action may be continued by or against the original parties unless the court directs the person to whom the interest is transferred to be substituted or joined in the action" ( Wells Fargo Bank, NA v McKenzie , 183 AD3d 574, 575 [internal quotation marks omitted]). Thus, the defendant, as well as Binay, as the current owner of the premises and the successor in interest to the defendant, could defend the action in the absence of formal substitution or joinder ( see CPLR 1018; HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Welt , 243 AD3d 770 , 771). 
 "An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Santos , 218 AD3d 827, 828 ; see CPLR 213[4]). "[E]ven if a mortgage is payable in installments, once a mortgage debt is accelerated, the entire amount is due and the statute of limitations begins to run on the entire debt" ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Mor , 201 AD3d 691, 694 ). "The entire mortgage debt will be deemed to have been accelerated by, as relevant here, the commencement of a mortgage foreclosure action in which the complaint seeks payment of the full outstanding loan balance" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Connor , 204 AD3d 861, 863 ). 
 "Pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4), a person having an estate or interest in real property subject to a mortgage may maintain an action to secure the cancellation and discharge of the encumbrance, and to adjudge the estate or interest free of it, if the applicable statute of limitations for commencing a foreclosure action has expired" ( U.S. Bank NA v Schaer , 223 AD3d 928 , 929). Here, in support of their cross-motion, Binay and the defendant established, prima facie, that the six-year statute of limitations began to run in June 2009, when the plaintiff commenced the 2009 action and elected in the complaint to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v DiGiorgio , 237 AD3d 899 , 900). Since the plaintiff did not commence the instant action until September 2018, more than six years later, Binay and the defendant established, prima facie, that the action was time-barred ( see CPLR 213[4]; US Bank Trust, N.A. v Reizes , 222 AD3d 907, 910 ). 
 In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact. Pursuant to CPLR 3217, as amended by FAPA, the voluntary discontinuances of the 2009 and 2010 actions did not serve to revive or reset the statute of limitations ( see id. § 3217[e]; JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. v Turkov , 242 AD3d 1069 , 1071; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Edwards , 231 AD3d 1189 , 1193). Moreover, as neither the 2009 action nor the 2010 action was dismissed "based on an expressed judicial determination, made upon a timely interposed defense, that the instrument was not validly accelerated" (CPLR 213[4][a]), the plaintiff is estopped from asserting that the debt was not validly accelerated by the commencement of either of those actions ( see CV XXVIII, LLC v Williams , 236 AD3d 753 , 755; US Bank Trust, N.A. v Reizes , 222 AD3d at 910 ). 
 There is no merit to the plaintiff's contention that FAPA does not apply retroactively ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 ; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 ). The plaintiff's challenges to the constitutionality of the retroactive application of FAPA are also without merit ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 ; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 ; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d 818 , 822; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dagrin , 233 AD3d 1065 , 1069-1071; 97 Lyman Ave., LLC v MTGLQ Invs., L.P. , 233 AD3d 1038 , 1043). 
 The plaintiff's contention that the action was timely commenced pursuant to either CPLR 205(a) or 205-a is improperly raised for the first time in its reply brief ( see Bank of Am., N.A. v McKeon , 241 AD3d 617 , 619). 
 The plaintiff's remaining contention is without merit. 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court, upon renewal, properly granted the defendant's prior cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 BARROS, J.P., IANNACCI, GOLIA and OTTLEY, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph

BEFORE: LAZARUS, P.J., BECK, J., and NEUMAN, J. 
MEMORANDUM BY BECK, J.: FILED NOVEMBER 18, 2026 
 Appellant 1726 South 5th Street Associate LLC (“the LLC”) appeals from 
the judgment entered on July 25, 2025, by the Philadelphia County Court of 
Common Pleas (“trial court”) in favor of Appellee Carolyn Claus a/k/a Carolyn 
Closs (“Closs”) and against the LLC for possession of property located at 1217 
North 15th Street in Philadelphia (“the Property”). The LLC raises the 
timeliness of Closs’ challenge to an underlying sheriff’s sale of the Property 
J-A21002-26 
- 3 - 
and further claims the trial court erred in proceeding to trial at a hearing that 
was scheduled for oral argument, depriving the LLC of its right to produce 
testimony and evidence. For the reasons that follow, we vacate the judgment 
and remand for proceedings consistent with this decision. 
 The Property is a vacant lot in the City of Philadelphia (“City”), which 
the LLC purchased for $84,000 on December 15, 2015, at a sale by the 
Philadelphia Sheriff’s Office on account of unpaid real estate taxes.1 By way 
of background, when John L. Davis died in 1983, he left the Property to his 
brother and numerous nephews, nieces, grandnephews, and grandnieces. At 
the time of the sheriff’s sale, there were 24 record owners of the Property who 
each held an interest ranging from 14.69% to 0.37%. Closs was one of 8 
owners with a 0.37% interest.2 None of the 0.37% owners were named as a 
party to the sheriff’s sale action. 
 On February 9, 2021, the LLC filed a complaint in quiet title against the 
0.37% owners, seeking to clear title to the Property for resale. None of the 
defendants, except Closs, responded. Closs filed a counseled answer, new

matter, and counterclaim on September 30, 2022. In her new matter, Closs 
averred that because she never received notice of the sheriff’s sale action and 
was not joined as a party, her interest in the Property was not divested at the 
sheriff’s sale. She counterclaimed that the sheriff’s sale action was fatally 
flawed because the City failed to identify all owners of the Property; the LLC 
negligently and recklessly relied on the actions of the City in purchasing the 
Property at the sheriff’s sale; the failure to notify and join her as a party to 
the sheriff’s sale action prevented her from exercising her ownership rights to 
the Property and did not divest her interest in it; and the LLC had, through its 
attorney, denied her claim to the Property. Closs sought dismissal of the 
complaint with prejudice, grant of her counterclaim, and conveyance of the 
Property to her and the other defendants. 
 In its answer to the counterclaim, the LLC averred that Closs would be 
unjustly enriched if she were granted relief because she had only a 0.37% 
interest in the Property, yet the LLC paid $84,000.00 to satisfy delinquent 
taxes on the Property. The LLC further asserted that it has continued to pay 
taxes, insurance, and water/sewage charges, and has maintained exclusive 
possession and control of the Property since the sheriff’s sale. 
 On November 16, 2022, the trial court entered default judgment against 
the non-answering defendants.3 On March 30, 2023, the LLC moved for

the trial court denied on July 25, 2023. 
 Before a pretrial settlement conference scheduled for September 11, 
2024, the trial court granted a motion to withdraw as counsel filed by Closs’ 
attorney. Closs then filed a pro se motion seeking court-appointed counsel, 
in which she claimed, inter alia, that she was on active military duty when the 
underlying sheriff’s sale took place on December 15, 2015.4 She attached a

the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (“SCRA”), 50 U.S.C. §§ 3901-4043.5 
 On October 22, 2024, Closs filed a motion to dismiss in which she 
asserted that genuine issues of fact existed, the SCRA applied, and the City’s 
failure to notify her of the sheriff’s sale action violated her right to take 
possession of the Property while she was on active military service.

On December 4, 2024, the LLC filed a trial brief in which it argued it has

action was untimely filed beyond the six-year statute of limitations period set 
forth in 42 Pa.C.S. § 5527(b). Closs filed a trial brief on January 3, 2025, in 
which she reiterated her request that the sale of the Property be “reversed.” 
That same date, Closs filed a joinder complaint against the City, asserting the

counsel for the LLC the reason for the proceeding, to which counsel 
responded: “Your Honor had scheduled oral argument. We did not have a 
motion pending, but I think at this point, the most appropriate thing would be 
for myself to make an oral motion for judgment in quiet title pursuant to 
Pennsylvania Rule of Civil Procedure 1066.” N.T., 1/15/2025, at 3. Counsel 
for the LLC argued that Closs’ counterclaim to set aside the sale of the Property 
was untimely filed beyond the statute of limitations; the LLC, as owner with a 
99.63% interest, has superior title to the Property; and Closs’ joinder 
complaint, filed at the late stage of litigation, was highly prejudicial to the 
LLC.7 Closs argued that the City could have located her through an internet 
search; had she received notice, she would have paid the delinquent taxes on 
the Property; and the SCRA applied to her. The trial court questioned both 
counsel for the LLC and Closs and marked several exhibits8 before eventually 
swearing Closs in. See id. at 30. Once sworn, the trial court continued to

leads.caseName: PPG Industries, Inc. v. Westlake Corporation
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF CHANCERY OF THE STATE OF DELAWARE 
PPG INDUSTRIES, INC., 
Plaintiff, 
v. 
WESTLAKE CORPORATION, AXIALL 
CORPORATION, WESTLAKE US 2 
LLC (f/k/a EAGLE US 2 LLC), and 
EAGLE SPINCO INC., 

Defendants. 

C.A. No. 2024-0648-NAC 

 POST-TRIAL MEMORANDUM OPINION 
Date Submitted: August 4, 2026 
Date Decided: November 18, 2026 
David A. Dorey, Gregory P. Ranzini , BLANK ROME LLP, Wilmington, Delaware; 
Andrew Fletcher, Jason Snyderman, John A. Gibbons, BLANK ROME LLP, 
Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; Counsel for Plaintiff and Counterclaim Defendant PPG 
Industries, Inc. 

Jennifer C. Wasson, Tyler E. Cragg, POTTER ANDERSON & CORROON LLP, 
Wilmington, Delaware; William R. H. Merrill, Ryan V. Caughey, Ace M. Factor, 
Alexxa Leon , SUSMAN GODF REY LLP, Houston, Texas; David B. Goodwin, 
Christine S. Haskett, COVINGTON & BURLING LLP, San Francisco, California; 
Counsel for Defendants and Counterclaim Plaintiffs Westlake Corporation, Axiall 
Corporation, Westlake US 2 LLC (f/k/a Eagle US 2 LLC), and Eagle Spinco Inc. 

COOK, V.C.

In 1998, cargo ship DG Harmony caught fire off the coast of Brazil. After 
attempting to fight the flames, the crew abandoned ship, and the fire destroyed the 
vessel and most of its cargo. A flurry of lawsuits followed. In a consolidated action, 
the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York found that 
calcium hypochlorite manufactured by PPG Industries, Inc. caused the fire. PPG 
settled the claims for $81.5 million, with insurance contributing $56.5 million after 
PPG satisfied a $25 million self-insured retention amount. 
In 2006, Di Gregório Navegação Ltda . (“Di Gregorio”) —a Brazilian cargo 
transportation company that sub-chartered the DG Harmony—filed a lawsuit against 
PPG in Brazil. Despite being named in the consolidated New York action, Di Gregorio 
never appeared. In 2009, the New York court entered an order of default judgment 
against Di Gregorio, specifically enjoining the Brazil lawsuit. Notwithstanding the 
New York court’s order, the Di Gregorio litigation in Brazil continued, and, in 2010, 
the Brazil court found PPG liable against Di Gregorio. 
In 2013, PPG spun off its commodity chemicals business through a transaction 
involving Georg ia Gulf Corporation, later renamed Axiall Corporation. The 
transaction was governed by a series of agreements, including a Separation 
Agreement and a Contribution Agreement. Those agreements addressed the transfer 
of assets and assumption of liabilities, the parties’ indemnification rights and 
obligations, and their rights and responsibilities concerning insurance. As relevant 
here, the Separation Agreement allocated responsibility for the Di Gregorio litigation 
2 
to entities in the spun- off business. And PPG retained the insurance policies 
potentially covering the Di Gregorio litigation. 
For years after the transaction, the spun-off entities defended the Di Gregorio 
litigation and communicated with PPG’s insurers , including submitting invoices for 
defense costs. In 2023 and 2024, the Di Gregorio litigation was coming to a head. A 
decision on damages was imminent, and everyone started taking positions. Desp ite 
years of communication —including about strategy and settlement —the insurers 
refused to engage with the spun -off entities without an assignment from PPG , and 
they denied coverage for the Di Gregorio litigation. PPG refused to assign any rights 
to the insurance until any judgment in the Di Gregorio litigation was satisfied. The 
spun-off entities demanded an assignment before they would pay anything in the Di 
Gregorio litigation. 
In May 2024, the Brazil court entered a substantial damages award against 
PPG. The next month, PPG filed this action asking the Court to order the spun- off 
entities and their subsequent acquirer (collectively, Defendants here) to substitute 
PPG out of the Di Gregorio litigation and post a bond or satisfy the judgment. 
Defendants countered, asking the Court to order PPG to assign insurance rights to 
them. 
This decision denies PPG’s requests for specific performance and grants 
Defendants’ in part. Even assuming PPG has proven a breach of contract, it has not 
shown, by clear and convincing evidence , that specific performance is appropriate . 
PPG waited to request substitution for 11 years after the spinoff, and it would violate 
3 
principles of comity for this Court to order Defendants to take any action in the Di 
Gregorio litigation when that litigation was specifically enjoined by the New York 
court’s 2009 order. Defendants are entitled to an assignment of insurance proceeds, 
but, under the Separation Agreement’s terms, only for the costs of defending PPG in 
the Di Gregorio litigation that they have already incurred and paid. 
The parties agree that the spun-off entities are ultimately responsible for any 
enforceable judgment and related losses. And Defendants continue to defend the Di 
Gregorio litigation and have committed to hold PPG harmless against any attempts 
to enforce the Di Gregorio judgment. The parties also agree that the spun-off entities 
are entitled to an assignment of insurance proceeds at some point. Boiled down, the 
parties tussle over the logistics of their contractual obligations, with the crux of th e 
dispute concerning sequencing and timing. Like colleagues arriving at the entrance 
to the office, PPG and Defendants are dancing over who goes first and who will hold 
the door. In the end, they’ll both make it inside. 
I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND 
The following facts were stipulated to by the parties or proven by a 
preponderance of the evidence at trial.1 

1 See Dkt. 147, Pre-Trial Stipulation and Order (”PTO”). The trial record includes live 
testimony from two fact witnesses and four experts, 234 joint exhibits, and three deposition 
transcripts. Trial testimony is cited as “TT [Page]:[Lines] (Name).” See Dkts. 179 –80. 
Exhibits are cited by the numbers provided on the parties’ joint exhibit list as “JX ,” unless 
otherwise defined. See Dkt. 170. Pincites refer to pagination stamped with the parties’ joint 
exhibit numbers. Deposition transcripts are cited as “[Name] Dep. [Page]:[Lines].” 
4 
A. The Parties 
Plaintiff PPG Industries, Inc. is an industrial conglomerate based in 
Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Through a Separation Agreement dated July 18, 2012, 2 
PPG agreed to spin off its commodity chemicals business in a transaction (the 
“Spinoff”) with Georg ia Gulf Corporation, which was subsequently renamed Axiall 
Corporation. 
Defendant Eagle Spinco Inc. was PPG’s counterparty to the Separation 
Agreement and is a wholly owned subsidiary of Axiall.3 
Defendant Eagle US 2 LLC (now Westlake US 2 LLC) is a subsidiary of Eagle 
Spinco.4 Eagle US 2 was a party to the Contribution Agreement dated January 22, 
2013, with PPG as its counterparty. 5 The purpose of the Contribution Agreement 
was “solely to effect the transfer of” assets and liabilities contemplated by the 
Separation Agreement.6 
Defendant Axiall Corporation is Eagle Spinco’s parent company. Axiall 
acquired Eagle Spinco in 2013. This decision refers to Axiall, Eagle US 2, and Eagle 
Spinco as the “Spinco Group.” 

2 JX 23. 
3 PTO ¶ 2. 
4 Id. ¶ 3. 
5 JX 41. 
6 Id. § 1.2. 
5 
Defendant Westlake Corporation is Axiall’s, Eagle Spinco’s, and Eagle US 2’s 
ultimate parent company. 7 Westlake acquired Axiall in 2016. 8 Westlake is not a 
party to the Separation or Contribution Agreements. This decision refers to Westlake 
and the Spinco Group as “Defendants.”9 
B. The DG Harmony Fire and Ensuing Litigation 
In November 1998 , an explosion occurred aboard the container ship DG 
Harmony off the coast of Brazil. 10 The explosion caused a total loss of the ship and 
its cargo. Among DG Harmony’s cargo was PPG -manufactured calcium 
hypochlorite. 11 Following the DG Harmony fire, numerous parties sued PPG, 
alleging that its calcium hypochlorite caused the explosion and subsequent fire. The 
claims were consolidated in the United States District Court for the Southern District 
of New York. In 2009, the court entered a judgment, finding PPG liable for the 

7 PTO ¶ 5. 
8 JX 92; JX 98. 
9 As explained below, however, the Court concludes that Westlake is not a proper 
defendant in this action. 
10 PTO ¶ 15. 
11 Id. ¶ 16. 
6 
explosion and the resulting fire. 12 PPG eventually settled the lawsuits for 
approximately $81.5 million.13 
C. The Di Gregorio Litigation 
On January 11, 2006, Di Gregório Navegação Ltda (“Di Gregorio”)—a Brazilian 
cargo transportation company that sub -chartered the DG Harmony—filed a lawsuit 
against PPG in the 13th Civil and Work Accident Court of the District of Manaus, 
State of Amazonas, Brazil (the “ Di Gregorio Litigation”).14 PPG hired the Brazilian 
law firm Mattos Filho, Veiga Filho, Marrey Jr. e Quiroga Advogados (“Mattos Filho”) 
as defense counsel in the Di Gregorio Litigation.
15 
Di Gregorio was a named party in the consolidated New York litigation but did 
not appear.16 In June 2006, PPG filed a lawsuit against Di Gregorio in the Southern 
District of New York, seeking to enjoin the Di Gregorio Litigation. 17 On October 28, 
2009, the New York court entered a default judgment in PPG’s favor, declaring that 
PPG was not liable to Di Gregorio and enjoining Di Gregorio from pursuing any 

12 PTO ¶¶ 17 –18. For a comprehensive recitation of these facts, see In re M/V DG 
Harmony, 394 F. Supp. 2d 649 (S.D.N.Y. 2005), opinion clarified, 2007 WL 895251 (S.D.N.Y. 
Mar. 16, 2007), and aff’d in part, vacated in part, rev’d in part, 533 F.3d 83 (2d Cir. 2008). 
13 TT 162:2–10 (Bloch). 
14 PTO ¶¶ 19, 21. 
15 Id. ¶ 22; JX 10. 
16 PTO ¶ 20. 
17 JX 11. 
7 
claims against PPG for losses arising from the DG Harmony fire (the “SDNY 
Order”).18 The SDNY Order expressly enjoined the Di Gregorio Litigation.19 
Notwithstanding the SDNY Order, the Brazil court allowed the Di Gregorio 
Litigation to proceed and, in January 2010, entered judgment against PPG in the 
liability phase of the litigation. 20 PPG appealed the liability finding but was 
unsuccessful.21 
At the time of the DG Harmony fire, PPG maintained an insurance tower 
worth $350 million, subject to a $25 million self-insured retention.22 PPG notified its 
insurers about the DG Harmony fire and submitted insurance claims for liabilities 
arising from it, including the Di Gregorio Litigation. 23 Before the Separation 
Agreement was executed in 2012, PPG had received about $56.5 million in 
reimbursement from its insurance for DG Harmony-related losses.24 Just under $300 

18 JX 12. 
19 Id. 
20 PTO ¶ 24. 
21 Id. ¶¶ 25–28. 
22 JX 1–9; JX 147; TT 135:12-18, 161:6-22 (Bloch). 
23 TT 131:1–10 (Bloch). 
24 Id. 162:2–10 (Bloch); see also JX 13; JX 14; JX 73. 
8 
million of insurance remains available under PPG’s applicable insurance policy. And 
the Di Gregorio Litigation is the only remaining open claim under that policy.25 
D. The Spinoff 
In 2012, while the Di Gregorio Litigation was proceeding, PPG agreed to spin 
off and sell its chlor -alkali, derivatives, and other commodity chemicals business to 
Georgia Gulf (now Axiall) through a series of agreements, including, as relevant here, 
the Separation Agreement and the Contribution Agreement. 
Through the Separation Agreement, PPG agreed to transfer certain assets to 
Eagle Spinco, and Eagle Spinco agreed to assume certain liabilities, with the 
remaining assets and liabilities to be retained by PPG. 26 The Contribution 
Agreement effectuated the transfer of the assets and liabilities to Eagle US 2 (an 
Eagle Spinco subsidiary) in accordance with the terms of the Separation 
Agreement.27 
Among the liabilities Eagle US 2 assumed under the Separation Agreement 
was the Di Gregorio Litigation (the “Di Gregorio Liability”) .28 According to the

162:17–165:9.

leads.caseName: Mr. Storage, LLC v. JJ Briggs Consulting, LLC
leads.text:
COURT OF APPEALS 
DECISION 
DATED AND FILED 

November 18, 2026 

Samuel A. Christensen 
Clerk of Court of Appeals 

NOTICE 

 This opinion is subject to further editing. If 
published, the official version will appear in 
the bound volume of the Official Reports. 

A party may file with the Supreme Court a 
petition to review an adverse decision by the 
Court of Appeals. See WIS. STAT. § 808.10 
and RULE 809.62. 

Appeal No. 2026AP1057 Cir. Ct. No. 2026SC438 
STATE OF WISCONSIN IN COURT OF APPEALS 
 DISTRICT II 

MR. STORAGE, LLC, 

 PLAINTIFF-RESPONDENT, 

 V. 

JJ BRIGGS CONSULTING, LLC, 

 DEFENDANT-APPELLANT, 

JAMIE BRIGGS AND ALL OTHER OCCUPANTS 
OF 23 E. JACKSON ST., WAUPUN, WI 53963, 

 DEFENDANTS. 

 APPEAL from a judgment and an order of the circuit court for 
Fond du Lac County: DOUGLAS R. EDELSTEIN, Judge. Affirmed. 
No. 2026AP1057 
2 
¶1 GROGAN, J. 1 JJ Briggs Consulting, LLC (Briggs) 2 appeals pro se 
from a judgment evicting it from a commercial property following a bench trial 
and from an order denying its motion for reconsideration. Briggs raises four 
issues: (1) “[t]he circuit court applied the wrong legal standard by treating an 
occupancy permit as equivalent to lawful occupancy under WIS. STAT. 
§ 704.07(4)”; (2) “[t]he circuit court’s findings are incomplete under WIS. STAT. 
§ 805.17(2), and those incomplete findings do not support the denial of appellant’s 
counterclaim”; (3) “[t]he May 26 order should be vacated because the circuit court 
did not apply the stay undertaking and WIS. STAT. § 799.445 to the post-surrender 
circumstances”; and (4) “[t]he amended money judgment requires redetermination 
of post-judgment rent and fails to apply an ordered signage credit.” 3 This court 
will address only the first two issues raised. The third and fourth issue s challenge 
orders entered after Briggs filed its notice of appeal , and this court does not have 
jurisdiction to address those orders .4 For the reasons set forth below, this court 
affirms. 

1 This appeal is decided by one judge pursuant to WIS. STAT. § 752.31(2) (2023-24). All 
references to the Wisconsin Statutes are to the 2023-24 version. 
2 Jamie Briggs is the owner of the business and will be referred to as “Jamie” when the 
opinion refers directly to her. 
3 Briggs presents a fifth “issue” in its brief requesting a new circuit court judge if this 
court remands the matter. This is not an issue the court of appeals decides, but is a statutory right 
when certain circumstances set forth in WIS. STAT. § 799.205(4) are met. 
4 The notice of appeal filed on May 4, 2026 , challenges the eviction judgment and the 
reconsideration order, both entered in April 2026. Briggs’s third issue challenges an order dated 
May 26, 2026, and the fourth issue challenges an order dated July 17, 2026. Both of these orders 
post-date the notice of appeal , and this court cannot address them. See Chicago & N.W.R.R. v. 
LIRC, 91 Wis. 2d 462, 473, 283 N.W.2d 603 (Ct. App. 1979), aff’d, 98 Wis. 2d 592, 297 N.W.2d 
819 (1980) (“An appeal from a judgment does not embrace an order entered after the 
judgment.”). 
No. 2026AP1057 
3 
I. BACKGROUND 
¶2 Jamie entered into a year-long commercial lease agreement with 
Mr. Storage, LLC (Mr. Storage) to lease a warehouse space for its business, with 
the lease starting on January 15, 2026, and continuing through January 14, 2027. 5 
The applicable contractual provisions in the lease provide: 
3. Leased Premises 
3. … The Premises will be used for only the following 
permitted use (the “Permitted Use”): Insurance 
Company office/Retail and Studio Art space. 
…. 
5. The premises are provided to the Tenant without any 
fixtures, chattels or leasehold improvements. 
6. Term 
6. The term of the Lease is a periodic tenancy 
commencing … on January 15, 2026, and 
continuing for a term of one year ending Jan [uary] 
14, 2027. 
7. Rent 
7. Subject to the provision s of this Lease, the Tenant 
will pay a base rent of $2500.00, payable per month 
(the “Base Rent”), without setoff, abatement or 
deduction. In addition to the Base Rent, t he Tenant 
will pay for any fees or taxes arising from the 
Tenant’s business. 
…. 
35. General Provisions 
.… 

5 This lease followed a short-term lease that ran from September 15, 2025 , through 
January 14, 2026. 
No. 2026AP1057 
4 
40. This Lease will constitute the entire agreement 
between the Landlord and the Tenant. Any prior 
understanding or representation of any kind 
preceding the date of this Lease will not be binding 
on either party to this Lease ex cept to the extent 
incorporated in this Lease. In particular, no 
warranties of the Landlord not expressed in this 
Lease are to be implied. 
According to Jamie, the City of Waupun conducted an occupancy walkthrough of 
the premises she leased , and a city inspector determined that there was “not 
independent egress from the space and that it required exit signage.” As a result, 
Jamie did not pay the “full rent” because she could not “open [her] business as the 
permitted use statement in the lease.” Jamie’s failure to pay rent led to 
Mr. Storage initiating an eviction lawsuit against Briggs . Jamie filed a 
counterclaim to the lawsuit alleging that Mr. Storage had leased her premises not 
capable of occupancy: 
[Mr. Storage] leased [Briggs] premises that were not 
capable of lawful occupancy … including lack of 
independent secondary egress and required exit signage . … 
As a result, [Briggs] incurred mitigation expenses, loss of 
business use, reduced rental opportunities , … and other 
consequential damages, presently estimated at $20903.00. 
These conditions substantially interfered with [Briggs] ’s 
lawful beneficial use of the premises and frustrated the 
essential purpose of the lease. [Briggs] therefore seeks 
offset, abatement, and monetary relief. 
¶3 The circuit court held a bench trial . Mr. Storage called it s 
representative Jodi Mallas to testify . Mallas testified that by entering the lease , 
Mr. Storage did not have to complete any improvements to the property, nor did it 
promise to make any. Speaking about the occupancy permit, Mallas indicated that 
it was tied to the “particular business ” rather than the premises’ owner and the 
premises itself. Jamie testified next. She told the court that this was her first time 
occupying a business with a physical space “[u]nder a lease[.]” She also said she 
No. 2026AP1057 
5 
had no prior experience working with the city on occupancy permit compliance. 
She testified that she was unable to operate her business because she was told it 
was “not legal to operate a public facing business … without exit signage and 
independent egress.” Jamie explained she “did not pay the full re nt because I was 
not able to open the business as the permitted use statement in the lease. And the 
agreed use, as it was the only use permitted.” 
¶4 After hearing the testimony, t he circuit court found that “[n]o where 
in the terms of the lease is there assignment of responsibility, such that the 
occupancy permit would be the responsibility of [Mr. Storage].” It also found 
“[t]he space itself very well may be suitable, but [Mr. Storage] has not agreed to 
bear the cost of updating, renovating, or otherwise to ensure that that would likely 
be an additional cost or reference within the contract.” The court found : (1) the 
lease was “clear” and “unambiguous”; (2) there was no evidence the space was 
untenantable; and (3) Jamie materially breached the lease by failing to make 
payment. The court noted that the unpaid rent totaled $5,500, but ruled that it 
would offset the cost Jamie incurred for exit signage i f she submitted 
documentation of that cost within ten days. Jamie submitted an itemization of 
costs in the amount of $208.90 by the deadline . When asked about Jamie’s 
counterclaim, the court denied it, explaining it could not “discern that the 
contractual relationship placed any obligation on [Mr. Storage] to effectively get 
[Briggs’s] business permitted to run there.” Following the ruling, the court 
ordered a writ of eviction. 
¶5 Shortly after the eviction trial, Jamie filed a motion f or 
reconsideration, in which she requested clarification as to the status of her 
counterclaim, asked the circuit court to reconsider the counterclaim, and grant 
“such other relief ” the court “ deems just and equitable .” The court denied this 
No. 2026AP1057 
6 
motion, finding that “credible evidence” demonstrated a material breach for failure 
to pay rent . It also sua sponte referenced WIS. STAT. § 704.07(4), indicating that 
the statute only allows rent abatement when “ the condition of the premises 
‘substantially affects the use and occupancy of the premises [,]’” and there was no 
evidence of that in this case. It specifically held that Jamie’s “ failure to obtain an 
occupancy permit for the premises did not otherwise con vert the commercially 
available space into an untenantable location. ” The court’s reconsideration order 
affirmed the writ of eviction and the denial of “any counterclaims.” Briggs 
appeals both the eviction judgment and the reconsideration order. 
II. DISCUSSION 
¶6 Briggs argues that the circuit court applied the wrong legal standard 
and that its finding s were inadequate. “Whether the circuit court has applied the 
correct legal standard is a question of law reviewed de novo.” Landwehr v. 
Landwehr, 2006 WI 64, ¶8, 291 Wis. 2d 49, 715 N.W.2d 180. This court 
“uphold[s] a circuit court ’s findings of fact unless they are clearly erroneous. ” 
Phelps v. Physicians Ins. Co . of Wis., Inc., 2009 WI 74, ¶34, 319 Wis. 2d 1, 768 
N.W.2d 615. 
¶7 Briggs argues that “the circuit court answered a question of 
contractual responsibility for an occupancy permit rather than the statutory 
question presented under WIS. STAT. § 704.07(4)[,]” and alleges the court’s 
findings are inadequate, the case should be remanded so the court can make 
adequate findings, and the “incomplete findings do not support the denial of 
[Briggs]’s counterclaim .” Mr. Storage responds that Briggs’s first issue is 
“illogical, inadequately developed, and forfeited[,]” and that the court ’s findings 
regarding Briggs’s defense and counterclaim were adequate. 
No. 2026AP1057 
7 
A. Issue One 
¶8 This court agrees with Mr. Storage that Briggs forfeited the WIS. 
STAT. § 704.07(4) argument because it failed to rai se it at the bench trial. See 
State v. Huebner, 2000 WI 59, ¶10, 235 Wis. 2d 486, 611 N.W.2d 727 (“[I]ssues 
must be preserved at the circuit court. Issues that are not preserved at the circuit 
court, even alleged constitutional errors, generally will not be considered on 
appeal.”). And although Briggs is correct that the court addressed it in its written 
order denying the reconsideration motion, the forfeiture rule exists to prevent 
sandbagging a party that never had a chance to address the issue in the circuit 
court. See Schonscheck v. Paccar, Inc. , 2003 WI App 79, ¶¶10 -11, 261 Wis. 2d 
769, 661 N.W.2d 476 (party forfeits challenge when it fail s to fully develop the 
argument before the circuit court). Nevertheless, because the court addressed 
§ 704.07(4) in its reconsideration order, this court will briefly address it. 
¶9 Briggs’s briefing is difficult to decipher. Briggs seems to argue that 
at trial, the circuit court should have included an analysis under WIS. STAT. 
§ 704.07(4) and answered whether “the premises were capable of the Permitted 
Use,” rather than resolving occupancy-permit responsibility. But § 704.07(4) only 
applies to commercial leases that do not have a “contrary provision in writing 
signed by both parties .” Sec. 704.07(1). The lease that Mr. Storage and Jamie 
signed appears to have a contrary provision. 6 But even if it did not, § 704.07(4) 
only allows rent abatement under certain conditions, which Briggs failed to 

6 The lease provides: (1) “[t]he [p]remises are provided to the [t]enant without any 
fi

leads.text:
Judgment rendered November 18, 2026. 
Application for rehearing may be filed 
within the delay allowed by Art. 2166, 
La. C.C.P. 

No. 57,203-CA 

COURT OF APPEAL 
SECOND CIRCUIT 
STATE OF LOUISIANA 

* * * * * 

TYLER GORDON, MICHAEL 
CRAFT, AND MARY 
BLAKEMORE 
 Plaintiffs-Appellants 

versus 

CITY OF SHREVEPORT Defendant-Appellee 

* * * * * 

Appealed from the 
First Judicial District Court for the 
Parish of Caddo, Louisiana 
Trial Court No. 661,810 

Honorable Ramon Lafitte, Judge 

* * * * * 

WALTZER WIYGUL GARSIDE & WILD Counsel for Appellants 
By: Clay Garside 

JACK BAILEY LAW CORPORATION 
By: Jack Bailey, III 

CARMOUCHE, BOKENFOHR, Counsel for Appellee 
BUCKLE & DAY, PLLC 
By: Nichole M. Buckle 

* * * * * 

Before STONE, STEPHENS, and ROBINSON, JJ.

STEPHENS, J., 
This civil appeal arises from the First Judicial District, Parish of 
Caddo, State of Louisiana, the Honorable Ramon Lafitte, Judge, presiding. 
The plaintiffs, Tyler Gordon, Michael Craft, and Mary Blakemore, have 
appealed from the trial court’s judgment affirming the Shreveport City 
Council’s decision approving a special use permit. For the reasons 
expressed below, we affirm the trial court’s judgment. 
FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
 On October 17, 2025, Bohler Engineering filed a development 
application with the Shreveport/Caddo Metropolitan Planning Commission 
(“MPC”), seeking a special use permit for a proposed data center. Bohler 
requested that the data center be developed on approximately 254 acres 
zoned I-1 PUD, Light Industrial Planned Unit Development (“PUD”), an 
area known as Resilient Technology Park located off Greenwood Road. The 
application requested approval for seven buildings, each measuring 400,000 
sq. ft., to be used as a data center, along with various support buildings such 
as water storage, a substation, a lift station, and offices. The Bohler Project 
Team held a community meeting about the project on November 13, 2025, 
where an open floor discussion occurred at the Bill Cockrell Community 
Center in Shreveport involving the project’s purpose, design elements, and 
anticipated timeline, as well as community considerations and feedback.1 
Following Bohler’s development application, the MPC staff issued a 
report which included findings that data centers are permitted within the I-1 

1 The staff report indicated that 11 members of the neighborhood community were 
present as well as elected officials, several members from the applicant team, and two 
MPC staff members. The community members raised concerns about the impact to the 
water and electrical supply, traffic, and noise generated by the proposed data center. Job 
creation potential and other benefits to the community were also discussed. 
2 

base zoning district, but that a special use permit is required when the site is 
located within 200 feet of a residentially zoned district. The report described 
that the proposed site at Resilient Technology Park was rezoned on several 
occasions and had previous plan approvals for various developments, but 
these prior developments never occurred.2 The report also detailed that the 
proposed site abuts residentially zoned districts on the north and east sides; 
therefore, a special use permit application was required. The MPC staff 
explained that the closest residential dwelling is approximately 250 feet 
from the property boundary of the proposed site. The MPC staff report 
ultimately concluded that the proposed development properly mitigated the 
impact of the proposed use, and approval was warranted. In the report, all 
12 criteria of development standards and design specifications were deemed 
satisfied as follows: 
Section 16.3.E.1: the design, location, and operating plans of an SUP 
must be such that the public health, safety and/or welfare is protected. 
Since the property in question is part of a PUD, the site plan 
incorporates several amenities beyond the minimum requirements

leads.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF NORTH CAROLINA 
No. COA26-348 
Filed 18 November 2026 
Moore County, No. 25CV000125-620 
NATE HOLTON and CHRISTINE HOLTON, Plaintiffs, 
vs. 
VALUEBUILD HOMES, LANDMARK HOMES OF PINEHURST, LLC, 
VALUEBUILD HOMES  - FAYETTEVILLE, LLC, VALUEBUILD HOMES  - 
CHARLOTTE, LLC, VALUEBUILD HOMES  - RALEIGH, LLC and 
PROFESSIONAL WARRANTY SERVICE CORPORATION, Defendants. 
                     vs. 
LANDMARK HOMES OF PINEHURST, LLC, Defendant/Third-Party Plaintiff, 
                     vs. 
WSMASONRY, LLC, WILLIAM DONNELL SMITH D/B/A WS MASONRY, RANDY 
HENDERSON AND CECIL HENDERSON, Third-Party Defendants. 
Appeal by Plaintiffs from order entered 16 October 2025 by Judge Vince Rozier 
in Moore County Superior Court.  Heard in the Court of Appeals 28 October 2026. 
Robbins May & Rich LLP, by Claire C. Toulouse and William M. Van O’Linda, 
Jr., for Plaintiffs-Appellants. 
 
McAngus, Goudelock & Courie, PLLC, by Jeffrey B. Kuykendal, for Defendants-
Appellees. 
 
 
COLLINS, Judge. 
HOLTON V. VALUE BUILD HOMES 
Opinion of the Court 
 
- 2 - 
Plaintiffs appeal from an order granting summary judgment in favor of 
Defendants on claims arising from the alleged defective construction of Plaintiffs’ 
residence.  Plaintiffs contend the trial court erred by concluding their claims were 
barred by the applicable statutes of limitation and repose and by dismissing their 
claims for negligence and unfair and deceptive trade practices.  Because the 
undisputed forecast of evidence demonstrates that Plaintiffs knew of the condition 
underlying their claims no later than 2016 and failed to commence this action until 
January 2025, and because Plaintiffs failed to forecast evidence sufficient to support 
their remaining claims, we affirm. 
I. Background 
The forecast of evidence tended to show the following: 
Plaintiffs Nate and Christine Holton entered into a contract with Defendants 
Value Build Homes on 15 November 2015, for the construction of a residence in Moore 
County.  A certificate of occupancy was issued on 17 May 2016.  Plaintiffs thereafter 
occupied the residence.  Within thirty to sixty days after receiving the certificate of 
occupancy, Plaintiffs “noticed a substantial dip in the kitchen floor. ”  Plaintiffs 
contacted Defendants, and a representative came to the home and stabilized the 
affected area. 
On or about 14 October 2016, Plaintiffs executed an Application for Builder’s 
Limited Warranty with Professional Warranty Service Corporation.  The warranty 
HOLTON V. VALUE BUILD HOMES 
Opinion of the Court 
 
- 3 - 
provided for various levels of coverage for ten years from 17 May 2016 and required 
any and all disputes be resolved through binding arbitration. 
Years later, after consulting a crawlspace contractor in October 2023, Plaintiffs 
became concerned that the residence had been constructed on an improperly sloped 
foundation.  On 8 November 2023, Plaintiff Nate Holton contacted Defendants and 
asserted that “[t]he house was never level since day 1.”  Defendants investigated and 
took measurements at the property during 2024. 
On 17 January 2025, Plaintiffs filed this action asserting claims for breach of 
contract, express warranty, implied warranty, latent construction defect, negligence, 
and unfair and deceptive trade practices.  Defendants filed a third -party complaint 
against some of its subcontractors. 
Following a hearing, the trial court granted summary judgment in Defendants’ 
favor and dismissed all claims.  Plaintiffs timely appealed.  On 16 April 2026, 
Plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed their claims against the Professional Warranty 
Service Corporation with prejudice. 
II. Discussion 
Plaintiffs argue that the trial court erred by granting summary judgement to 
Defendants on all Plaintiffs’ claims. 
A. Jurisdiction 
Although the order on appeal is interlocutory because Defendants’ third-party 
claims remain pending, see Veazey v. City of Durham , 231 N.C. 357, 361 -62 (1950), 
HOLTON V. VALUE BUILD HOMES 
Opinion of the Court 
 
- 4 - 
the appeal affects a substantial right.  See N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 1 -277(a) (2025), 7A -
27(b)(3)(a) (2025).  The third -party claims arise from the same alleged construction 
defects as Plaintiffs’ claims and require resolution of overlapping factual issues 
concerning the existence, cause, and responsibil ity for those defects.  Because 
separate proceedings could yield inconsistent verdicts on those issues, Plaintiffs’ 
appeal affects a substantial right and is properly before this Court.  See Hamilton v. 
Mortgage Info. Servs., Inc., 212 N.C. App. 73, 79 (2011). 
B. Standard of Review 
Summary judgment is appropriate “if the pleadings, depositions, answers to 
interrogatories, and admissions on file, together with the affidavits, if any, show that 
there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that any party is entitled to a 
judgment as a matter of law.”  N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1A -1, Rule 56(c) (2025).  “In ruling 
on a motion for summary judgment, the trial court must view the evidence in the light 
most favorable to the non-moving party.”  Foxx v. Davis, 289 N.C. App. 473, 480 (2023) 
(quotation marks and citation omitted). 
“The party moving for summary judgment bears the burden of establishing 
that there is no triable issue of material fact.”  Badin Shores Resort Owners Ass’n v. 
Handy Sanitary Dist., 257 N.C. App. 542, 549 (2018).  “This burden can be met by 
proving: (1) that an essential element of the non-moving party’s claim is nonexistent; 
(2) that discovery indicates the non-moving party cannot produce evidence to support 
an essential element of  his claim; or (3) that an affirmative defense would bar the 
HOLTON V. VALUE BUILD HOMES 
Opinion of the Court 
 
- 5 - 
claim.”  CIM Ins. Corp. v. Cascade Auto Glass, Inc. , 190 N.C. App. 808, 811 (2008) 
(citation omitted). 
We review a trial court’s order granting summary judgment de novo.  Forbis v. 
Neal, 361 N.C. 519, 524 (2007).  Under de novo review, this Court considers the 
matter anew and freely substitutes its own judgment for that of the lower court.  
Archie v. Durham Pub. Schs. Bd. of Educ., 283 N.C. App. 472, 474 (2022). 
C. Statute of Repose 
Plaintiffs first contend that the trial court erred by concluding their claims are 
barred by the six-year statute of repose governing improvements to real property.  We 
disagree. 
Section 1-50(a)(5) provides that no action “arising out of the defective or unsafe 
condition of an improvement to real property ” may be brought more than six years 
from the later of the defendant ’s last act or omission giving rise to the claim or 
substantial completion of the improvement.  N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1 -50(a)(5)a, f (2025).  
“Under the statute, a plaintiff has the burden of showing that he or she brought the 
action within six years of either (1) the substantial completion of the house or (2) the 
specific last act or omission of defendant giving rise to the cause of action.”  Boor v. 
Spectrum Homes, Inc., 196 N.C. App. 699, 705 (2009)  (citations omitted).  A statute 
of repose “serves as an unyielding and absolute barrier that prevents a plaintiff ’s 
right of action even before his cause of action may accrue,” Black v. Littlejohn , 312 
N.C. 626, 633 (1985) (citations omitted), “and functions to give a defendant a vested 
HOLTON V. VALUE BUILD HOMES 
Opinion of the Court 
 
- 6 - 
right not to be sued if the plaintiff fails to file within the prescribed period,”  Monson 
v. Paramount Homes, Inc., 133 N.C. App. 235, 240 (1999) (citation omitted).  “In short, 
a statute of repose bars an action a specified number of years after a defendant has 
completed an act, even if the plaintiff has not yet suffered injury.”  Id. 
“[A] building is ‘substantially complete’ on the date upon which a certificate of 
occupancy has been issued.”  Trillium Ridge Condo. Ass’n , Inc. v. Trillium Links & 
Vill., LLC , 236 N.C. App. 478, 494 (2014)  (citation omitted) .  Here, Plaintiffs’ 
residence was substantially complete no later than 17 May 2016, when the certificate 
of occupancy was issued and Plaintiffs were able to use the home for its intended 
purpose.  Plaintiffs did not file suit until 17 January 2025.  Thus, the action was 
commenced more than eight years after substantial completion. 
Plaintiffs contend the repose period should instead be measured from a later 
“last act or omission” in 2023.  They argue that although they first became aware of 
the problem in 2016, Defendants sent someone out to stabilize the floor , so they 
thought the problem was resolved until they were told otherwise in 2023. 
“[A]lthough an act sufficient to affect the running of the statute of repose may 
occur after the date of substantial completion, ‘a “repair” does not qualify as a “last 
act” under N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1 -50(5) unless it is required under the improvement 
contract by agreement of the parties [.]’”  Trillium Ridge, 236 N.C. App. at 494-95 
(quoting Monson, 133 N.C. App. at 241).  “[A]llowing the statute of repose to toll or 
start running anew each time a repair is made would subject a defendant to potential 
HOLTON V. VALUE BUILD HOMES 
Opinion of the Court 
 
- 7 - 
open-ended liability for an indefinite period of time, defeating the very purpose of 
statutes of repose such as N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1-50(5).”  Id. at 495 (brackets and citation 
omitted). 
Here, Plaintiffs failed to forecast evidence that Defendants performed repair 
work on the residence after 2016 pursuant to the construction contract.  The evidence 
instead shows that Defendants investigated Plaintiffs’ complaints in 2024 by 
excavating near the foundation and taking measurements.  Investigative activities of 
this nature do not constitute construction work or repairs extending the statutory 
repose period.  See id. at 494-95. 
Plaintiffs alternatively rely on Christie v. Hartley Construction, Inc., 367 N.C. 
534 (2014), contending that Defendants waived repose protection by agreeing to a 
ten-year structural warranty.  Although Defendants failed to engage this argument, 
we nonetheless are unpersuaded. 
In Christie, the Supreme Court held that a home siding manufacturer  could 
contractually assume liability through an express warranty extending beyond the 
repose period.  Id. at 540-41.  We need not decide whether  the rationale in Christie 
extends to the circumstances here because Plaintiffs have failed to forecast evidence 
establishing the specific warranty obligation upon which they rely.  The plaintiffs in 
Christie did not prevail simply because a warranty existed .  Rather, they sought to 
enforce an identifiable express warranty whose terms allegedly had been breached.  
See id.  By contrast, Plaintiffs here repeatedly refer to a ten-year structural warranty 
HOLTON V. VALUE BUILD HOMES 
Opinion of the Court 
 
- 8 - 
yet identify no specific warranty provision, no particular obligation imposed upon 
Defendants, and no forecast of evidence demonstrating a breach of that obligation.  
On this record, Plaintiffs have failed to show that this action is properly characterized 
as one seeking enforcement of an express warranty extending beyond the repose 
period rather than an action arising from the allegedly defective construction of an 
improvement to real property governed by N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1-50(a)(5). 
Moreover, the record reflects that any ten -year warranty was administered 
through Professional Warranty Service Corporation, and Plaintiffs voluntarily 
dismissed their claims against that entity with prejudice.   Accordingly, Plaintiffs 
have failed to forecast evidence bringing their claims within the narrow holding of 
Christie. 
For these reasons, the trial court therefore properly concluded that Plaintiffs’ 
claims are barred by N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1-50(a)(5). 
D. Statute of Limitations 
Even assuming Plaintiffs’ claims are not barred by the statute of repose, 
Plaintiffs contend the trial court erred by concludi

leads.caseName: Procarsa Tube & Pipe Company, Inc., Industrial Procarsa, S.A. De C v. and Procarsa S.A. De C v. v. Blue Racer Midstream, LLC
leads.text:
Reversed; Rendered; Remanded and Opinion Filed November 17, 2026 
S 
In The 
Court of Appeals 
Fifth District of Texas at Dallas 
No. 05-24-01031-CV 
PROCARSA TUBE & PIPE COMPANY, INC., INDUSTRIAL PROCARSA, 
S.A. DE C.V., AND PROCARSA S.A. DE C.V., Appellant 
V. 
BLUE RACER MIDSTREAM, LLC, Appellee 
On Appeal from the 68th Judicial District Court 
Dallas County, Texas 
Trial Court Cause No. DC-21-07310 
MEMORANDUM OPINION 
Before Justices Goldstein, Barbare, and Lee 
Opinion by Justice Lee 
Blue Racer Midstream, LLC sued appellants Procarsa Tube & Pipe Co., Inc. 
(Tube & Pipe)1, Industrial Procarsa S.A. de C.V. (Industrial)2, Procarsa S.A. de C.V. 
(Procarsa)3 (collectively, appellants4) under tort and contract-based theories. Tube & 
Pipe brought a third -party action against third-party defendant Steel Professionals , 

1 Tube & Pipe is a Texas sales and distribution company that quoted the pipe, transmitted the terms and conditions, 
invoiced Steel Professionals, and acted as the sales agent/distributor. 
2 Industrial is a Mexican steel mill that physically manufactured the pipe and supplied it into the distribution 
chain. 
3 Procarsa is an API license holder and manufacturer who performed testing, certification, and applied the API 
monogram to its pipe. 
4 While appellants submitted a joint appellate brief, when necessary we treat them as distinct parties by name. 
 –2– 
LLLP5 for declaratory relief, statutory indemnity, and contribution. Following a jury 
verdict generally favoring Blue Racer, the trial court entered judgment against 
appellants in the amount of $810,590.10 plus $508,000 in attorney’s fees. Appellants 
appeal. 
Appellants raise three issues: (1) that the trial court erred in submitting Blue 
Racer’s tort claims when the economic loss rule precluded recovery in tort; (2) that 
the trial court abused its discretion by failing to submit appellants’ affirmative 
defenses based on the disclaimer -of-warranties and limitation -of-remedies 
provisions; and (3) the trial court erred in awarding attorney’s fees because recovery 
of attorney’s fees was foreclosed by contract. 
We sustain each of appellants’ issues and reverse the trial court’s judgment . 
We remand the case for a new trial on the on the contract and warranty claims. 
I. BACKGROUND 
 Blue Racer, a natural gas transp ortation and processing company , sought 
quotations from Steel Professionals and other potential vendors for epoxy-coated, 
24-inch-diameter pipe, for construction of a new pipeline. Blue Racer specified that 
the pipe comply with the American Petroleum Institute’s (API) 5L standard, which 
prescribes requirements for material strength, construction, and factory testing and 
certification before shipment. 

5 Steel Professionals is not a party to this appeal. 
 –3– 
Steel Professionals and the Upstream Supply Chain 
 Steel Professionals contacted Industrial, the steel mill that manufactured the 
pipe, regarding Blue Racer’s required specifications. Industrial, through its sales 
agent Tube & Pipe, provided Steel Professionals a quote for uncoated API 5L pipe. 
The purchase agreement included a warranty disclaimer providing that, subject to 
standard manufacturing variations, the pipe would conform to specifications, but all 
other express and implied warranties, including warranties of merchantability and 
fitness for a particular purpose, were disclaimed. 
 The agreement also contained a limitation-of-remedies provision stating that 
the buyer’s exclusive remedy for any claim, whether sounding in contract, warranty, 
tort, statute, common law, or otherwise, was replacement of nonconforming goods 
or, at the seller’s option, refund of the purchase price. The provision further excluded 
liability for incidental, consequential, exemplary, punitive, or special damages and 
stated that no contractual relationship existed with any nonparty. 
 Although the agreement defined “seller,” “we,” and “us” as Tube & Pipe, 
Tube & Pipe later asserted that the agreement was actually made on behalf of 
Industrial and functioned as a manufacturer pass-through, with Tube & Pipe acting 
solely as a sales intermediary. Steel Professionals received, reviewed, and accepted 
the original manufacturer terms and conditions and that they governed the purchase. 
 –4– 
Blue Racer and Steel Professionals 
 Because Blue Racer required fusion-bonded epoxy coating and Tube & Pipe’s 
quotation was for bare pipe, Steel Professionals modified its quote to Blue Racer to 
include the coating. Steel Professionals secured a third party to modify the pipe by 
affixing the coating. 
 The contract between Blue Racer and Steel Professionals required 
acknowledgment of all express and implied warranties and obligated Steel 
Professionals to cover damages arising from defects in the pipe. Blue Racer was 
unaware of the terms contained in the Tube & Pipe-Steel Professionals agreement. 
 Procarsa supplied material test reports certifying that the pipe complied with 
API 5L requirements when it left the factory, and each pipe segment bore Procarsa’s 
API monogram. 
Pipeline Failure 
 As construction of the pipeline neared completion, Blue Racer conducted 
hydrostatic pressure testing. Before the pipeline reached its minimum test pressure, 
one segment ruptured, creating a large crater and flooding the surrounding property 
subject to Blue Racer’s right-of-way easement. 
 The failed segment of pipe was replaced . The failure re quired additional 
testing, and Blue Racer purchase d approximately 428,000 gallons of water for a 
subsequent retest and to decontaminate the pipeline. 
 –5– 
 To clean and retest the pipeline, Blue Racer was required to: (1) cut the 
pipeline at both ends; (2) weld temporary fittings to launch and receive cleaning 
devices known as “pigs”; (3) remediate and restore the excavated right -of-way; (4) 
reconnect the pipeline; and (5) conduct additional testing. Testing was successfully 
completed and the pipeline entered service. 
 Subsequent testing of the failed pipe segment, observed by representatives of 
Blue Racer and Procarsa, revealed t hat the rupture originated from a seam defect 
created during the manufacturing process. 
Trial 
 Blue Racer sued appellants, alleging products liability, negligent 
misrepresentation, negligence, breach of express warranty, breach of the implied 
warranty of merchantability, and breach of the implied warranty of fitness for a 
particular purpose. 
 Before trial, Blue Racer moved to exclude evidence of warranty disclaimers 
and limitations of remedies allegedly asserted by Industrial, arguing that any such 
disclaimer or limitation was required to be in writing under section 2.316 of the 
Business and Commerce Code and that appellants had produced no written evidence 
establishing those terms. The trial court granted the motion. 
 Appellants sought exclusion of Blue Racer’s negligence, strict liability, and 
negligent misrepresentation claims, arguing that the damages constituted economic 
losses under the economic loss rule , not recoverable in tort . Blue Racer responded 
 –6– 
that the rule did not apply because the defective pipe caused damage to property 
beyond the failed pipe segment itself, including the remainder of the pipeline, a pig, 
and the surrounding right-of-way. The trial court charged the jury on manufacturing 
defect and negligent misrepresentation theories but declined to submit negligence. 
 Appellants also requested jury questions concerning the disclaimer of implied 
warranties and limitation-of-remedies. Their proposed questions asked the jury to 
determine whether implied warranties had been disclaimed and whether Blue 
Racer’s recovery was contractually limited. Blue Racer objected that the proposed 
questions improperly treated all defendants as a single entity and failed to identify 
which contractual provisions applied to which parties. Blue Racer further argued that 
any upstream agreement between appellants and Steel Professionals did not govern 
Blue Racer’s contractual relationship with Steel Professionals . The trial court 
declined to submit appellants’ proposed questions. 
 The jury found in favor of Blue Racer and awarded $810,590.10 in damages. 
The jury found that both Industrial and Procarsa were manufacturers of the pipe. 6 
The jury found that a manufacturing defect existed in the segment of pipe at the time 
the pipe left the possession of each of appellants and of Steel Professionals ; found 
that Procarsa, Industrial, and Steel Professionals made negligent misrepresentations; 
apportioned negligent-misrepresentation responsibility at 50% to Procarsa, 40% to 

6 This finding is not challenged on appeal. 
 –7– 
Industrial, and 10% to Steel Professionals; found each defendant liable for breach of 
express warranty; and found Procarsa and Industrial liable for breach of implied 
warranty. The trial court additionally awarded Blue Racer $508,000.00 in attorney’s 
fees. 
 This appeal followed. 
II. ANALYSIS 
We address each of appellants’ issues in order. 

BLUE RACER’S NEGLIGENT MISREPRESENTATION AND STRICT PRODUCTS 
LIABILITY CLAIMS 

 In their first issue, appellants contend the trial court erred by submitting Blue 
Racer’s tort claims to the jury because the economic loss rule bars recovery. We 
agree. 
Applicable Law 
 In actions for unintentional torts, the common law restricts recovery of purely 
economic damages unaccompanied by injury to the plaintiff or his property , a 
doctrine referred to as the economic loss rule. LAN/STV v. Martin K. Eby Const. Co., 
Inc., 435 S.W.3d 234, 235 (Tex. 2014). Whether the economic loss rule bars a tort 
claim presents a question of law which we review de novo. See House of Reaford 
Farms, Inc. v. SOMMA Food Grp., LLC, No. 05-22-01231-CV, 2024 WL 396609, 
at *2 (Tex. App.—Dallas Feb. 2, 2024, pet. denied) (mem. op.) (citing Eagle Oil & 
 –8– 
Gas Co. v. Shale Expl., LLC, 549 S.W.3d 256, 268 (Tex. App.—Houston [1st Dist.] 
2018, pet. dism'd)). 
The Texas Supreme Court has noted that whether and how to apply the 
economic loss rule to negligent misrepresentation claims does not lend itself to easy 
answers or broad pronouncements. LAN/STV, 435 S.W.3d at 245. Rather, the 
application of the rule depends on an analysis of its rationales in a particular 
situation. Id. at 245–46. The rule has two primary rationales: (1) because purely 
economic harm is not self -limiting like physical injury is, allowing its recovery in 
tort could lead to indeterminate and disproportionate liability that discourages 
economic activity; and (2) the risks of economic losses are well suited to allocation 
by contract, where parties familiar with their own economic needs may protect 
themselves through insurance or indemnity agreements and price their transactions 
accordingly. House of Raeford, 2024 WL 396609, at *3. The first rationale is 
commonly referred to as the indeterminate and disproportionate liability rationale 
and the second the deference to contract rationale. LAN/STV, 435 S.W.3d at 240–41. 
Here, we discuss the second rationale as it is dispositive of appellant's first 
issue. The economic loss rule has been applied to prevent a plaintiff from asserting 
tort claims against a defendant for disappointed economic expectations arising from 
a contractual relationship or in a setting in which a contractual allocation of risks 
reasonably should be expected or encouraged. See, e.g., id. at 241 (applying the 
economic loss rule to bar a negligent misrepresentation claim by a general contractor 
 –9– 
against an architect in connection with errors in the architect's plans that resulted in 
increased costs of performing contractor's construction contract and specification); 
Jim Walter Homes, Inc. v. Reed, 711 S.W.2d 617, 618 (Tex. 1986) (“The Reeds' 
injury was that the house they were promised and paid for was not the house they 
received. This can only be characterized as a breach of contract.”);

The appellants sued the appellee seeking specific performance of a real estate purchase and 
sale agreement whereby the appellee agreed to sell certain real property to the appellants. 
Following a bench trial, the trial court granted judgment in favor of the appellants,
awarding them specific performance but requiring them to make monthly payments to the 
appellee until the transaction closed. The appellants failed to make one of the payments as 
ordered by the trial court, and the appellee filed a motion for contempt and to alter or amend 
the judgment pursuant to Tennessee Rule of Ci vil Procedure 59.04. After a hearing, the 
trial court granted the appellee’s Rule 59.04 motion and entered an amended judgment in 
favor of the appellee finding that the appellants were no longer entitled to specific 
performance and had forfeited all previously-made payments. The appellants filed a 
motion to alter or amend the amended judgment and alleged that the appellee’s principal 
committed perjury during the hearing on the appellee’s motion to alter or amend. The trial 
court denied the appellants’ motion to alter or amend. The appellants appeal this denial. 
Although not raised by either party, we conclude that the appellee’s Rule 59.04 motion was 
untimely. We vacate the judgment and remand to the trial court for reconsideration of the 
motion pursuant to Tennessee Rule of Civil Procedure 60.02.
Tenn. R. App. P. 3 Appeal as of Right; Judgment of the Chancery Court Vacated;
Case Remanded
