leads.caseName: City of Jarrell, Texas v. BE Theon East Partnership No. 3, Ltd.
leads.text:
TEXAS COURT OF APPEALS, THIRD DISTRICT, AT AUSTIN 

NO. 03-25-00953-CV 

City of Jarrell, Texas, Appellant 

v. 

BE Theon East Partnership No. 3, Ltd., Appellee 

FROM THE 425TH JUDICIAL DISTRICT COURT OF WILLIAMSON COUNTY 
NO. 20-0125-C425, THE HONORABLE BETSY F. LAMBETH, JUDGE PRESIDING 

M E M O R A N D U M O P I N I O N 
 The City of Jarrell appeals the trial court’ s summary judgment in favor of 
BE Theon East Partnership No. 3, Ltd. (BE Theon) and ordering specific performance. The City 
asserts that th e development agreement (the Development Agreement) between the parties was 
void ab initio and that even if the Development Agreement was not void, the proper remedy was 
disannexation rather than specific performance. We will affirm. 
BACKGROUND 
 In 2008, the City and BE Theon entered into the Development Agreement 
concerning an undeveloped 24.4-acre property (the Property) that BE Theon owned near the 
intersection of Ronald Reagan Boulevard and Interstate 35 (I -35) in Williamson County. 
BE Theon agreed t o voluntarily allow the City to annex the Property, and the City agreed to 
provide water and wastewater capacity to the Property (the Water and Wastewater Provision): 
2 

Section 3.01 Construction. The City shall provide sufficient water and 
wastewater capacity and sufficient approach mains to the northwest corner of the 
Land within three years after the completion of Ronald Reagan Boulevard at its 
intersection with IH-35. “Sufficient water and wastewater” shall mean sufficient, 
as reasonably anticipated by O wner and the City’ s engineer, for the uses planned 
for the Land at the time of the City’s invitation(s) for bids for construction of such 
approach mains. To the extent that onsite water and wastewater lines are required 
to be oversized for service to properties other than the Land, the City shall pay for 
all costs reasonably attributed to such oversizing. 
The city council authorized the mayor to sign the Development Agreement, the mayor signed the 
Development Agreement, the city council approved the Proper ty’s annexation by ordinance, and 
the Development Agreement was publicly recorded in the real property records of Williamson 
County. In July 2018, the Property’ s plat map, which the city manager signed and approved, 
also was recorded in the real property records of Williamson County. It expressly states: “The 
city of Jarrell will provide water and wastewater to this site subject to the Development 
Agreement between the City of Jarrell, TX and [BE Theon], dated 11/4/2008.” 
 In August 2019, BE Theon, through its counsel, provided a letter to the City with 
the “capacities it deemed sufficient for the planned uses of the Property” as calculated pursuant 
to “the City ’s Unified Development Code .” The City did not respond to the letter and has not 
provided water or wastewater services to the Property. 
 In January 2020, BE Theon sued the City seeking specific performance of the 
Development Agreement or, alternatively, damages. BE Theon alleged that Ronald Reagan 
Boulevard at its intersection with I -35 had been completed for over three years and that the City 
had breached the Development Agreement by not complying with the Water and Wastewater 
Provision or, alternatively, that the City’ s promises in that provision were enforceable by 
promissory estoppel. BE Theon referenced a “ribbon cutting for the completion of the final, 
3 

northern portion of Ronald Reagan Boulevard and the intersection at Interstate 35 [that] took 
place on March 5, 2014.” BE Theon also referenced emails from the City manager in May 2019 
that were BE Theon ’s “first indication that the City would not fulfill its obligations under the 
Development Agreement.” 
 In February 2020, the City answered and filed a plea to the jurisdiction. The trial 
court denied the plea. The City appealed that ruling, and this Court concluded that the trial court 
did not err in denying the City’ s plea to the jurisdiction as to BE Theon’ s breach of contract and 
promissory estoppel claims. See City of Jarrell v. BE Theon E. P’ship No. 3, Ltd. (BE Theon II) , 
No. 03- 21-00651-CV, 2023 WL 2588567, at *9, 11 (Tex. App.—Austin Mar. 22, 2023, pet. 
denied) (mem. op.). In October 2020, BE Theon filed in the trial court: (1) a supplement to its 
first amended petition seeking mandamus relief against the City to compel the City to perform 
the ministerial act of providing a certificate pursuant to Subsection 212.009(d) of the Texas 
Local Government Code, see Tex. Loc. Gov’ t Code § 212.009(d); and ( 2) a traditional motion 
for partial summary judgment on its request for a writ of man damus. In March 2021, the trial 
court granted BE Theon’ s motion for partial summary judgment and ordered that a writ of 
mandamus issue. See City of Jarrell v. BE Theon E. P’ship No. 3, Ltd. (BE Theon I), 
No. 03-21-00292-CV, 2021 WL 3555974 at *1 (Tex. App.—Austin Aug. 12, 2021, no pet.) 
(mem. op.) (dismissing for want of jurisdiction appeal of order granting motion for partial 
summary judgment and writ of mandamus). 
 In March 2025, BE Theon moved for traditional summary judgment on its claim 
for breach of contract and sought specific performance and later amended its petition to abandon 
its claim for promissory estoppel. In response to the motion for summary judgment, the City 
argued that (1) the Development Agreement failed “to supply all necessary and material terms to 
4 

make this contract unilaterally enforceable by Theon,” (2) “‘ sufficient’ capacity remains 
unestablished” because “the City’s engineer has never agreed what constitutes ‘ sufficient,’” and 
(3) there is a fact question regarding when the Ronald Reagan Boulevard intersection was 
completed. After the hearing on the motion but before the trial court ruled, the City filed a 
post-hearing brief in which it argued that BE Theon’s remedy for breach would be disannexation 
and that specific performance could not be awarded because “ there is no way to discern what 
constitutes ‘sufficient’ water and wastewater capacity within the four corners of the contract 
when the parties entered it, and . . . no dollar figure to pay for this performance has ever been 
ascertained.” The trial court signed a final judgment in November 2025 granting BE Theon’s 
motion for summary judgment and ordering the City to “invite and award bids for the 
construction of water and wastewater utilities to the Property with sufficient approach mains, in 
compliance with Chapter 252 of the Texas Local Government Code, and with such utilities 
having no less than the ” capacities specified in BE Theon’s August 2019 letter. The 
City appeals. 
ANALYSIS 
 First, the City asserts that the Development Agreement was void ab initio because 
the Water and Wastewater provision “violates the reserved powers doctrine because it 
impermissibly delegates to a private developer and the City’s engineer the discretionary, 
governmental power to set the level of public expenditure required to fund water, wastewater, 
and fire-protection services in perpetuity ” and “is unenforceable as a matter of law because it 
constitutes an unenforceable agreement to agree, leaving the material terms of ‘ sufficient’ 
capacity and the corresponding cost to the City to future negotiation.” The City then argues that 
5 

the trial court’s judgment “ violates the separation of powers doctrine as applied to Texas Local 
Government Code Section 212.172(j) .” Next , the City argues that t he proper remedy for 
BE Theon is disannexation, not specific performance. Finally, the City writes in its statement of 
facts that “Whether ‘the completion of Ronald Reagan Boulevard at its intersection with IH-35’ 
occurred on the date of the March 5, 2014 ribbon -cutting ceremony . . . is a genuinely disputed 
material fact.” 
Standard of Review 
 We review the trial court ’s summary -judgment ruling de novo. See Zive 
v. Sandberg, 644 S.W.3d 169, 173 (Tex. 2022); Joe v. Two Thirty Nine Joint Venture , 
145 S.W.3d 150, 156 (Tex. 2004). Under this standard, we view “the evidence in the light most 
favorable to the non-movant, crediting evidence favorable to the non-movant if reasonable jurors 
could, and disregarding contrary evidence unless reasonable jurors could not.” Zive, 644 S.W.3d 
at 173. 
 “A party moving for traditional summary judgment must prove that no genuine 
issue of material fact exists and it is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Wal-Mart Stores, 
Inc. v. Xerox State & Loc. Sols., Inc., 663 S.W.3d 569, 576 (Tex. 2023); see Tex. R. Civ. P. 
166a(c).1 “A genuine issue of material fact exists if the evidence ‘rises to a level that would 
enable reasonable and fair -minded people to differ in their conclusions.’” First United 

1 The Texas Supreme Court recently amended Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 166a, but 
“[o]ther than the deadline changes, Rule 166a’s rewrite is not intended to s ubstantively change 
the law.” Tex. R. Civ. P. 166a cmt. to 2026 change. The amendments renumbered the rule’s 
provisions. See 89 Tex. B.J. 286, 289–92 (2026) . Because the amendments apply only to 
summary-judgment motions filed on or after March 1, 2026, and the filing of Appellees’ 
summary-judgment motion preceded the amendments, we refer to the provisions of Rule 166a in 
effect at the time of filing. See id. at 286. 
6 

Pentecostal Church of Beaumont v. Parker , 514 S.W.3d 214, 220 (Tex. 2017) (quoting Merrell 
Dow Pharms., Inc. v. Havner, 953 S.W.2d 706, 711 (Tex. 1997)). “The evidence does not create 
an issue of material fact if it is ‘so weak as to do no more than create a mere surmise or 
suspicion’ that the fact exists.” Id. (quoting Kia Motors Corp. v. Ruiz , 432 S.W.3d 865, 875 
(Tex. 2014)). 
Void ab initio 
 The City asserts that the Development Agreement was void ab initio because the 
Water and Wastewater provision “violates the reserved powers doctrine because it impermissibly 
delegates to a private developer and the City’s engineer the discretionary, governmental power to 
set the level of public expenditure required to fund water, wastewater, and fire -protection 
services in perpetuity” and “ is unenforceable as a matter of law because it constitutes an 
unenforceable agreement to agree, leaving the material terms of ‘sufficient’ capacity and the 
corresponding cost to the City to future negotiation.” 
 We first address the City’s argument that the Water and Wastewater Provision “is 
void ab initio under the reserved powers doctrine.” See Love Terminal Partners, LP v. City of 
Dallas, 256 S.W.3d 893, 897 (Tex. App.— Dallas 2008, no pet.) (“If an action is void or void ab 
initio, the transaction is a nullity.”). “Under the reserved powers doctrine, certain legislative and 
governmental powers ‘are conferred on government entities for public purposes, and can neither 
be delegated nor bartered away. Government entities cannot cede away such powers through 
contracts with others so as to disable them from the performance of their public duties.” City of 
San Antonio v. San Antonio Firefighters’ Ass ’n, Local 624, 533 S.W.3d 527, 543 (Tex. App. —
San Antonio 2017, pet. denied) (quoting Kirby Lake Dev., Ltd. v. Clear Lake City Water Auth., 
7 

320 S.W.2d 829, 843 (Tex. 2010) (internal quotation marks and citations omitted)). “A city 
contract that does so is not binding and is terminable at will.” Id. (citing Kirby Lake Dev. , 
320 S.W.2d at 842; Clear Lake City Water A uth. v. Clear Lake Utils. Co., 549 S.W.2d 385, 391 
(Tex. 1977)). 
 In Clear Lake City Water Authority v. Clear Lake Utilities , the Texas Supreme 
Court held that an agreement between the Authority and a utility company was not binding 
because it had “the effect of potentially controlling and embarrassing [the] Authority in the 
exercise of its governmental powers.” 549 S.W.2d at 392. The agreement in that case obligated 
the Authority to meet all water and sewage treatment needs for the Utilities, while pre

revision until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports. 

-1- 
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

C O U R T O F A P P E A L S 

DTE ELECTRIC COMPANY, 

 Plaintiff/Counterdefendant-Appellee, 

and 

PORTSIDE SOLAR, LLC, 

 Intervening Plaintiff-Appellee, 

FOR PUBLICATION 
November 17, 2026 
9:34 AM 
v No. 379632 
St. Clair Circuit Court 
ST. CLAIR COUNTY, ST. CLAIR COUNTY 
BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS, and ST. CLAIR 
COUNTY HEALTH DEPARTMENT, 

LC No. 25-001332-CZ 
 Defendants/Counterplaintiffs-
Appellants. 

Before: MURRAY, P.J., and PATEL and FEENEY, JJ. 

MURRAY, P.J. 
 This appeal involves a St. Clair County Health Department regulation, approved by the 
county board of commissioners, which attempts to regulate many details regarding the construction 
and operation of solar and energy facilities. Although it recognizes it has no authority to enact 
zoning regulations, the Health Department and its aligned parties 1 argue that because the issue is 
one of public health, the regulation was validly enacted under its authority to protect the health 
and welfare of county residents . The trial court did not buy that argument, and neither do we. 
Under governing Michigan law, the Health Department regulation is invalid as it is a de facto 
zoning ordinance, which the Health Department has no power to enact. And even if the Health 
Department had the power to enact the regulation, it would be preempted by state law. Regulation 
25-01 is therefore invalid and unenforceable. As a result, we affirm the trial court’s order granting 

1 Defendants/counterplaintiffs St. Clair County and the St. Clair Board of Commissioners (BOC). 

-2- 
summary disposition in favor of plaintiff/counterdefendant, DTE Electric Company, and 
intervening plaintiff, Portside Solar, LLC, pursuant to MCR 2.116(C)(9) and (10). 
I. BACKGROUND 
In September 2023, Portside submitted an application to Fort Gratiot Township for a 
special land use permit to develop a large solar energy system. Litigation over the initial denial of 
the application ensued. The following year, Portside, Fort Gratiot Township, and the Fort Gratiot 
Township Planning Commission entered into a consent judgment permitting Portside to develop 
and construct a large solar energy system in accordance with the consent judgment and the terms 
outlined in an amended site plan. The trial court ordered that the consent judgment constituted an 
approved special use permit and site plan approval required under the township’s zoning 
ordinance. 
 During Portside’s building process, the Legislature passed 2023 PA 233 that added Part 8, 
Wind, Solar, and Storage Certification, to the Clean, Renewable, and Efficient Energy Act, MCL 
460.1001 et seq, In re Implementing Provisions of Public Act 233 of 2023 , ___ Mich App ___, 
___; ___ NW3d ___ (2026) (Docket No. 373259); slip op at 2, the purpose of which was to 
promote the development and use of clean and renewable energy resources , MCL 460.1001(2). 
At the same time, the Legislature amended MCL 125.3205(1)(d) of the Michigan Zoning Enabling 
Act (MZEA), MCL 125.3101 et seq., to provide that a zoning ordinance is subject to “Part 8 of the 
clean and renewable energy and energy waste reduction act, 2008 PA 295, MCL 460.1221 to 
460.1232.” 
 In response to this legislative action, the BOC adopted regulations recommended by the 
Health Department, and Regulation 25 -01 went into effect on May 1, 2025 . The regulation 
requires any company planning on constructing an energy facility 2 in a rural area of St. Clair 
County to obtain prior authorization to do so from the Health Department. The regulation further 
requires energy developers and owners of all energy facilities to maintain and operate them 
pursuant to all applicable laws and “at least the minimum standards required in this Regulation.” 
 With respect to the requirement that the owner, operator, or developer of an energy facility 
request authorization from the Health Department before beginning construction, Regulation 25-
01, §7, requires, in part, the following to be included in the authorization request: 
 (c) A description of the Energy Facility, including a detailed site plan, which 
depicts, at a minimum: ( i) the layout of all proposed and existing structures; ( ii) 
property boundaries and dimensions; ( iii) existing and proposed landscaping and 
fencing; (iv) the location of all existing and proposed utilities; ( v) all existing and 
proposed drainage systems; ( vi) the topography of the property; ( vii) all existing 
and proposed roads and means of access; (viii) all existing and proposed easements; 

2 Regulation 25-01 defines an energy facility as “[a] Solar Energy Facility and/or a Battery Energy 
Storage Facility which is: ( i) located or proposed to be located all or in part in St. Clair County; 
and (ii) which is located or proposed to be located, in whole or in part, in or adjacent to a Rural 
Area.” 

-3- 
(ix) a scale and legend; and ( x) distances to the nearest structures located on all 
adjacent properties. 
* * * 
 (k) A soil and economic survey report under section 60303 of the natural 
resources and environmental protection act, 1994 PA 451, § MCL 324.60303. 
 (l) If the proposed site of the Energy Facility is undeveloped land, a 
description of feasible alternative developed locations, including, but not limited 
to, vacant industrial property and brownfields, and an explanation of why such sites 
were not selected. 
 (m) A stormwater assessment and a plan to minimize, mitigate, and repair 
any drainage impacts at the expense of the owner or operator. 
 (n) A fire response plan and an emergency response plan. 
 (o) A decommissioning plan that is consistent with agreements reached 
between the applicant and other landowners of participating properties and that 
ensures the return of all participating properties to their useful natural condition 
similar to that which existed before construction, including removal of all above -
surface and below-surface facilities and infrastructure. The decommissioning plan 
shall include, but is not limited to, financial assurance in the form of a surety bond 
or an irrevocable standby letter of credit, in the amount of at least $100,000 per 
megawatt nameplate capacity of the Energy Facility, as adjust ed annually for 
inflation based upon the CPI-U from the date of this Regulation. To be acceptable, 
a surety bond must be posted and maintained by a surety authorized to do business 
in Michigan and which is rate A+ or better by A.M. Best. To be acceptable, an 
irrevocable standby letter of credit must be issued and maintained by a bank 
authorized to do business in Michigan with a 1 rating pursuant to the CAMELS 
rating system. St. Clair County shall be identified as named beneficiary on such 
surety bond or irrevocable letter of credit. 
* * * 
 (s) All agreements with the owner(s) of the premises where the Energy 
Facility is proposed to be located. 
The regulation also contains requirements and standards once an energy facility is granted 
authorization to build and operate: 
 Section 8: Health Department Review of Request for Authorization 
* * * 
 After completing its review, the Health Department shall issue a written 
determination as follows: ( i) granting Authorization to construct the proposed 

-4- 
Energy Facility, with or without conditions; or ( ii) denying Authorization to 
construct or operate the proposed Energy Facility with specified reasons supporting 
the denial. If the Authorization is granted, all conditions detailed in the 
Authorization, if any must be fully complied with and all other requi red permits 
and permissions must be obtained prior to construction and operation of the Energy 
Facility. . . . 
* * * 
 Section 9: Minimum Standards Applicable to Energy Facilities 
 To be eligible to receive an Authorization, Energy Facilities must meet or 
exceed the following Minimum Standards. Regardless of whether the 
Authorization was received, all Energy Facilities are required to operate and be 
maintained in such manner which meets or exceeds the below Minimum Standards. 
 (a) Noise Mitigation. An Energy Facility shall be designed, operated and 
maintained such that when operating at full power output, as measured at any point 
at or beyond a nonparticipating property line of a parcel with an existing residential 
dwelling, it does not produce mea surable Tonal Noise, and the broadband noise 
level from the Energy Facility does not exceed 45 decibels A -weighted averaged 
over a 10 minute period (dB(A) Leq). 
 (b) Visual Pollution Mitigation . An Energy Facility shall be designed, 
operated and maintained such that it is obscured from view from adjacent roadways 
and from all points on adjacent non -participating properties including from all 
occupied stories of included buildings, including use of opaque gating or fencing 
at points of vehicular access, perimeter berms, or a buffer of at least 25’ in ground 
depth consisting of sufficiently dense natural healthy vegetation including 
deciduous trees, or a combination, thereof, which is sufficient to obscure the Energy 
Facility from view. 
 (c) Decommissioning. An Energy Facility shall enter into a 
decommissioning agreement that ensures the return of all participating properties 
to their useful natural condition similar to that which existed before construction, 
including removal of all above -surface and below -surface facilities and 
infrastructure. The decommissioning plan shall include, but is not limited to, 
financial assurance in the form of a surety bond or an irrevocable standby letter of 
credit, in the amount of at least $100,000 per megawatt nameplate capacity of the 
Energy Facility, as adjusted annually for inflation based upon the CPI -U from the 
date of this Regulation. To be acceptable, a surety bond must be posted and 
maintained by a surety authorized to do business in Michigan and which is rate A+ 
or better by A.M. Best. To be acceptable, an irrevocable standby letter of credit 
must be issued and maintained by a bank authorized to do business in Michigan 
with a 1 rating pursuant to the CAMELS rating system. St. Clair County shall be 
identified as named beneficiary on such surety bond or irrevocable letter of credit. 

-5- 
Two months later DTE filed a complaint seeking a declaratory judgment that Regulation 
25-01 is a zoning ordinance that the Health Department had no power to adopt or enforce . DTE 
asserted that, as a leading producer of and investor in renewable energy, it was developing plans 
for solar and energy storage projects in St. Clair County. In particular, DTE intended to apply for 
a permit for a solar energy project in Greenwood Township, located in St. Clair County, and if left 
undisturbed, Regulation 25 -01 would have a direct impact on its plans. Portside later filed an 
intervening complaint. Defendants filed a counterclaim against DTE , asking the trial court to 
declare that Regulation 25-01 was properly adopted as a health and safety regulation by the Health 
Department within its authority granted by the Public Health Code , MCL 333.1101 et seq., and 
that Regulation 25-01 was neither a zoning ordinance nor preempted by the MZEA. The trial court 
granted DTE’s and Portside’s motions for summary disposition, concluding that Regulation 25-01 
was a de facto zoning ordinance that exceeded the Health Department’s authority. 
II. ANALYSIS 
A. STANDARDS OF REVIEW 
This Court reviews de novo a trial court’s decision on a motion for summary disposition. 
El-Khalil v Oakwood Healthcare, Inc, 504 Mich 152, 159; 934 NW2d 665 (2019). A motion under 
MCR 2.116(C)(9) tests the sufficiency of a defendant’s pleadings. Slater v Ann Arbor Pub Sch Bd 
of Ed, 250 Mich App 419, 425; 648 NW2d 205 (2002). “[T]he trial court must accept as true all

Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Gouin 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06766 
 November 17, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Deutsche Bank National Trust Company, etc., Plaintiff-Appellant, 
 v 
 Carline M. Gouin, Defendant-Respondent, "John Doe #1 to John Doe #10, et al., Defendants. 

 Decided and Entered: November 17, 2026 
 Index No. 36590/19|Appeal No. 7498|Case No. 2025-05200| 
 Before: Moulton, J.P., Scarpulla, Shulman, Pitt-Burke, Michael, JJ. 

 McCalla Raymer Leibert Pierce, LLP, New York (Adam D. Weiss of counsel), for appellant. 
 Bronx Legal Services, New York (Stephanie A. Swinton of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Naita A. Semaj, J.), entered on or about June 11, 2025, which granted respondent's motion for leave to renew a motion to dismiss and, upon renewal, granted the motion, unanimously affirmed, without costs. 
 In this residential mortgage foreclosure action, the debt was accelerated by a prior action brought in June 2012, which commenced the six-year limitations period ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Del Rio , 233 AD3d 529 , 530 [1st Dept 2024]; see CPLR 213[4] ) . That action was dismissed as abandoned pursuant to CPLR 3215(c). Plaintiff commenced the instant action in October 2019, more than six years after the accrual date of the statute of limitations. Because the prior foreclosure action was dismissed pursuant to CPLR 3215(c), plaintiff may not invoke the savings provisions set forth in CPLR 205-a ( 630 6A LLC v U.S. Bank Trust N.A. , 234 AD3d 566 , 567 [1st Dept 2025], lv denied 45 NY3d 902 [2026]) and this case is time-barred. 
 Plaintiff's arguments concerning the non-retroactivity of the Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821), has been rejected by the Court of Appeals in Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank ( 45 NY3d 441 , 452 [2025]). In Article 13 , the Court of Appeals also rejected plaintiff's argument that retroactive application of FAPA violates the Due Process Clause of New York's Constitution ( id at 453-454). We have held for similar reasons that FAPA does not run afoul of the US Constitution ( see US Bank N.A. v Calhoun , 236 AD3d 557 , 558 [1st Dept 2025], lv denied 43 NY3d 907 [2025]; see also Rouge v US Bank Trust N.A., 250 AD3d 550 , 553 [1st Dept 2026]). 
 We have considered plaintiff's remaining arguments and find them unavailing. 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: November 17, 2026

leads.caseName: Futurewise v. Kitsap County
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON 

DIVISION II 

FUTUREWISE, No. 61665-3-II 

 Appellant, 

 v. 

KITSAP COUNTY, and the STATE OF UNPUBLISHED OPINION 
WASHINGTON, GROWTH 
MANAGEMENT HEARINGS BOARD, 

 Respondents. 

MAXA, P.J. – Futurewise appeals a Final Decision and Order of the Growth Management 
Hearings Board (the Board) dismissing one of its challenges to Kitsap County’s 2024 
amendments to its comprehensive plan and certain development regulations. This administrative 
appeal arose from Futurewise’s argument that Kitsap County (the County) was required but 
failed to revise its comprehensive plan and development regulations to protect surface and 
groundwater as required by various statutes, including RCW 36.70A.590. 
 The Growth Management Act (GMA), chapter 36.70A RCW, requires counties to create a 
comprehensive plan to guide their land use and development decision making. The GMA also 
requires counties to enact development regulations that implement and are consistent with the 
Filed 
Washington State 
Court of Appeals 
Division Two 

November 17, 2026 
No. 61665-3-II 
2 
comprehensive plan. Comprehensive plans and development regulations are subject to 
continuing review and evaluation. 
 The County conducted a periodic review and amended its comprehensive plan in 2016. 
In January 2018, the legislature enacted RCW 36.70A.590, which states that a county “may rely 
on or refer to applicable minimum instream flow rules” to comply with the provisions of the 
GMA relating to surface and groundwater resources, and that “[d]evelopment regulations must 
ensure proposed water uses are consistent with” certain other statutes involving water use. 
 In February 2018, the County enacted Ordinance 551-2018, a development regulation. 
Ordinance 551-2018 requires building permit applicants to produce evidence of water 
availability in the building permitting process. In 2024, the County conducted another periodic 
review and enacted Ordinance 637-2024, which updated the County’s comprehensive plan and 
certain development regulations. 
 Futurewise filed a petition for review to the Board challenging various aspects of the 
County’s 2024 amendments to its comprehensive plan and development regulations in Ordinance 
637-2024. Among other issues, in what the Board referred to as Issue 13, Futurewise argued that 
during its periodic review the County was required to but failed to (1) limit withdrawals of water 
from permit exempt water wells to 5,000 gallons per day and (2) improve the environment by 
enacting water regulations. Futurewise’s petition for review did not challenge Ordinance 551-
2018. 
The County responded that it was not required to update its water regulations in 
Ordinance 637-2024 because Ordinance 551-2018 already had responded to the GMA 
amendments regarding water regulations. In reply, Futurewise argued that Ordinance 551-2018 
did not bring the County into compliance with RCW 36.70A.590. 
No. 61665-3-II 
3 
 Regarding Issue 13, the Board declined to address Ordinance 551-2018 and summarily 
dismissed Futurewise’s water regulation challenge to Ordinance 637-2024 without discussion or 
analysis. 
 We hold that (1) the Board erred in refusing to address Ordinance 551-2018 because the 
County asserted that ordinance as a defense to Futurewise’s challenge to Ordinance 637-2024, 
and (2) the Board failed to decide all issues requiring resolution of Futurewise’s challenge to 
Ordinance 637-2024. Accordingly, we vacate the discussion of Issue 13 in the Board’s Final 
Decision and Order and remand to the Board for further proceedings regarding that issue. 
FACTS 
GMA Background 

 The GMA requires counties to adopt a comprehensive plan and adopt development 
regulations that are consistent with and implement the comprehensive plan. RCW 
36.70A.040(3)(d). A comprehensive plan is a “generalized coordinated land use policy statement 
of the governing body of a county or city.” RCW 36.70A.030(9). Comprehensive plans must 
include a land use element that provides for the protection of the quality and quantity of 
groundwater used for public water supplies, and a rural element that protects surface water and 
groundwater resources. RCW 36.70A.070(1), (5)(c)(iv). 
Development regulations are “the controls placed on development or land use activities 
by a county or city, including, but not limited to, zoning ordinances, critical areas ordinances, 
shoreline master programs, official controls, planned unit development ordinances, subdivision 
ordinances, and binding site plan ordinances together with any amendments thereto.” RCW 
36.70A.030(14). 
 RCW 36.70A.130(1)(a) states that a county “shall take legislative action to review and, if 
needed, revise its comprehensive land use plan and development regulations to ensure the plan 
No. 61665-3-II 
4 
and regulations comply with the requirements of [the GMA]” before certain deadlines in the 
statute. This section required the County to take action to review its comprehensive plan and 
development regulations in both 2016 and 2024. RCW 36.70A.130(4)(b), (5)(a). “Legislative 
action means the adoption of a resolution or ordinance . . . indicating at a minimum, a finding 
that a review and evaluation has occurred and identifying the revisions made, or that a revision 
was not needed and the reasons therefor.” RCW 36.70A.130(1)(c). 
The County’s Comprehensive Planning and Development Regulations 

 In 2016, the County conducted a periodic review and updated its comprehensive plan and 
development regulations, as required by RCW 36.70A.130(4)(b). But in January 2018, the 
legislature enacted RCW 36.70A.590, which states, 
For the purposes of complying with the requirements of [the GMA] relating to 
surface and groundwater resources, a county or city may rely on or refer to 
applicable minimum instream flow rules adopted by the department of ecology 
under chapters 90.22 and 90.54 RCW. Development regulations must ensure that 
proposed water uses are consistent with RCW 90.44.050 and with applicable rules 
adopted pursuant to chapters 90.22 and 90.54 RCW when making decisions under 
RCW 19.27.097 and 58.17.110. 

 In February 2018, the County enacted Ordinance 551-2018, which addressed 
requirements associated with water availability in the building permitting process. Ordinance 
551-2018 added provisions requiring a building permit applicant to provide evidence of an 
adequate water supply. Specifically, Ordinance 551-2018 stated that when a building site is 
“supplied by a permit exempt well constructed on or after January 19, 2018 . . . [t]he annual 
average withdrawal is limited to nine hundred fifty (950) gallons per day per connection for 
domestic use.” Admin. Rec. (AR) at 3165. 
In 2023, the legislature amended RCW 36.70A.020(10), adding “and enhance” to goal 10 
of the GMA, which now states, “Protect and enhance the environment and enhance the state’s 
No. 61665-3-II 
5 
high quality of life, including air and water quality, and the availability of water.” (Emphasis 
added.) 
In 2024, the County conducted a periodic review and enacted Ordinance 637-2024. 
Ordinance 637-2024 adopted an updated comprehensive plan and amended certain development 
regulations. 
Procedural History 
 Futurewise filed a petition for review to the Board challenging Ordinance 637-2024. 
Among other issues, Futurewise’s petition posed the following question as an issue presented for 
review (referred to as Issue 13): 
Did the adoption of Ordinance No. 637 -2024, the comprehensive plan, the 
Comprehensive Plan Land Use Map, Title 16 (Land Division and Development), 
and Title 17 (Zoning), protect surface and ground water as required by RCW 
36.70A.020(10), RCW 36.70A.070, RC W 36.70A.070(1), RCW 
36.70A.070(5)(c)(iv), RCW 36.70A.130(1) and (5)(a), RCW 36.70A.290(2), or 
RCW 36.70A.590? 

AR at 609.1 Futurewise’s petition did not challenge Ordinance 551-2018. 
 The Board consolidated Futurewise’s petition with other challenges to Ordinance 637-
2024. 
 Futurewise argued that the updated comprehensive plan and development regulations did 
not comply with RCW 36.70A.590 because none of its provisions limited withdrawals of water 
from permit exempt water wells to 5,000 gallons per day as required by that statute. Futurewise 
contended that because the comprehensive plan and development regulations “did not require 
compliance with applicable minimum instream flow rules” as discussed by RCW 36.70A.590, it 
violated the GMA provisions that require a comprehensive plan to include elements that protect 

1 Futurewise asserted other challenges to Ordinance 637-2024 before the Board. Those 
challenges are not at issue in this appeal. 
No. 61665-3-II 
6 
surface and groundwater resources. AR at 1977-78. Futurewise also argued that Ordinance 637-
2024 violated the amended RCW 36.70A.020(10) “[b]y failing to improve land use regulations 
to protect hydrology.” AR at 1977. 
 In addition, Futurewise argued that Ordinance 637-2024 failed to comply with (1) RCW 
36.70A.070(1),which requires that “[t]he land use element shall provide for protection of the 
quality and quantity of groundwater used for public water supplies”; and (2) RCW 
36.70A.070(5)(c)(iv), which requires that “[t]he rural element shall include measures that apply 
to rural development and protect the rural character of the area, as established by the county, by: 
. . . Protecting surface water and groundwater resources.” AR at 1977-78. 
 The County responded that it was not required to revise its comprehensive plan and 
development regulations in response to RCW 36.70A.590 and RCW 36.70A.020(10) during its 
periodic update because it already had brought itself into compliance with those regulations by 
enacting Ordinance 551-2018. In addition, the County argued that RCW 36.70A.590 did not 
require it to incorporate minimum instream flow rules under chapters 90.22 and 90.54 RCW 
because it merely stated that the county “may rely on or refer” to those rules. AR at 2289. 
Further, the County stated that the development regulations enacted by Ordinance 551-2018 
complied with RCW 36.70A.590 because they incorporated the requirements for obtaining a 
permit exempt well found in RCW 90.94.030(4)(a)(iv)(B). 
 At the hearing on the merits of Futurewise’s petition, the County also argued that 
Futurewise’s challenge to Ordinance 551-2018 was time barred. Futurewise responded that 
because the County failed to produce a publication date for Ordinance 551-2018, it could not 
establish that the statute of limitations period to challenge an ordinance under the GMA had run. 
And Futurewise emphasized that Ordinance 551-2018 did not comply with RCW 36.70A.590 
No. 61665-3-II 
7 
because it did not limit withdrawals from wells constructed before 2018 at all and did not limit 
withdrawals from permit exempt wells to 5,000 gallons per day. 
 The Board’s Final Decision and Order include a section regarding Issue 13. The Board 
recounted the parties’ arguments regarding Issue 13 and then stated, 
The Board would not anticipate the Index of Record in this matter to include the 
publication from a 2018 Ordinance, nor would the County presume to include it as 
the Issue deals with Ordinance No. 637-2024, and not Ordinance 551-2018. Thus, 
the Board is not persuaded by Futurewise’s argument regarding the 2018 Ordinance 
and find[s] issues related to that Ordinance would not be properly before this Board 
in this matter. Futurewise has not convinced this Board that this Ordinance is 
clearly erroneous. Accordingly, issue 13 is dismissed. 

AR at 3240. 
 Futurewise filed a motion for reconsideration regarding Issue 13. Futurewise argued that 
(1) the Board committed an error of fact by finding that the need for a notice of publication of 
Ordinance 551-2018 was unanticipated, (2) that the Board committed an error of law by 
implicitly concluding that the challenge to Ordinance 551-2018 was time barred
